translations.text:
The wrath of God has been stirred up. That is, we see all these schisms, disputes, and divisions, and along with them frequent and bitter persecutions, imprisonments, and harsh bonds. All these things, too, belong to the birth pains of the end. For our Savior himself was already proclaiming and saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to you.”

Again, he gave clear indications when he said plainly, “When you see all these things happening, know that it has reached the door.” He also taught his disciples beforehand and made known to them the things that are now happening among us—not only that great company of apostles, but also all the disciples who would follow them, down to the present day. He said this: “Beware of people, for they will hand you over to the courts, and in their synagogues [?] they will flog you. They will bring you before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations. But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you will speak, for what you are to speak will be given to you at that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Brother will hand brother over to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against their parents and put them to death. You will be hated by everyone because of my name.”

We plainly see that these things have now come upon all the members of the church and have been fulfilled in this time. We suffer these conflicts and evils not from outsiders and pagans, but from those who are themselves considered Christians. They freely commit pagan deeds against their fellow Christians, without the restraints of the fear of God and without mercy, acting lawlessly and savagely, without restraint.

Because of all these things, then, we have undertaken this after our earlier written account in two parts. In its two divisions, we had previously completed, as far as we were able, the histories of the church in twelve books, with much labor over a long period. Throughout these books, the material is identified by various chapter headings. We began with the times of Julius Caesar and the other early Roman emperors. Then, in succession, we collected and arranged the church histories down to the sixth year of the reign of this latter Justin, the son of Justinian’s sister. We also described Emperor Justin’s own zeal and concern for the unity of the church, from the beginning of his reign down to his sixth year. We bore careful and earnest witness to this as well, following the truth in the various matters that we previously related.

But now we have seen a fierce storm suddenly arise with great violence and force. Because of our sins, it thunders with the force of its many, frequent waves against the sturdy ship of the whole church of the orthodox. For this reason, we too have been moved to set down records, even if we can offer only a few of them. The times themselves hem us in on every side, trouble us in many ways, and prevent us from doing what we can, even on a small scale, to relate the events of church history that are now happening once again. Nevertheless, we are recording a little out of much. We will also include it in this third written account, for the information of those who come after us—though, unless I am mistaken [?], the ages of the world have already run their course and passed away. Thus these things may be known clearly and accurately to all the others who come afterward, even in the short time remaining to this troubled world [?], through the brief records that we have written for the information of those who come after us.

To begin, then, the accounts in this book, the sorrowful words of the lamentations of Jeremiah, the grieving prophet, would now be fitting—the words with which he once lamented and wept over Jerusalem and over her people who fell by the sword. In the same way, we too should now lament and weep over what has happened at this time in the church of God because of our many wrongdoings and sins. Likewise Isaiah, renowned among the prophets, would cry out with his throat and not hold back, and would raise his voice like a trumpet on seeing this harsh chastisement that has overtaken the church of God. He would also go on to repeat: “Every head is in pain, and every heart in sorrow. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, there is no sound place in it, but wounds, bruises, and swollen sores, neither bound up nor bandaged, nor softened [?] with oil.” And again he would repeat sorrowfully: “The earth has lamented, lamented, and sat in mourning; the world has lamented, lamented, and sat down and mourned. The height of the earth has lamented, and the earth has become like its inhabitants.” It would therefore be fitting for saints such as these to grieve sorrowfully with us over this great wrath, which, because of our sins, was suddenly sent upon the church of God, just as it once was upon Jerusalem.

On the terrible calamities that suddenly roared, shook, and threw into confusion the whole people of the faithful, who had been living peacefully and quietly and enjoying themselves for a long time in the imperial city and throughout its surroundings, until the sixth year of the reign of the victorious Justin. Suddenly a blast of wrath struck all the congregations of the church of the orthodox, overthrew them, scattered them, and dispersed them in every direction. My time is too short to write about these things and describe them fully.

For a long period of more than forty years, all the congregations of the whole church of the orthodox had been living quietly and peacefully in this great imperial city and throughout [?] its surroundings. With great openness, freely, without restriction or fear, all the congregations of the faithful assembled everywhere and performed all the sacraments and ecclesiastical rites. Suddenly, during the holy days of the forty-day fast, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, through the zeal and fierce malice of the man who held authority over the church of the imperial city—that is, John, woe to you, the man from Sarmin, a village in Syria—and through his many accusations against the entire body of the orthodox, the victorious Justin was stirred to fierce anger. With threats of great fury, he ordered that all the meeting houses of all the faithful should be closed, that all the altars in them should be uprooted, that all their priests and bishops should be seized and thrown into prison, and that all those who used to assemble in them should be driven away and forcibly kept out, so that they would no longer assemble. Other measures of this kind were also commanded and decreed in great anger. And although previously, until that time, peacefully and quietly throughout the whole...

Chapter Nine. “Why do you sit as a Christian with those who sent me to you, yet judge God’s servants like a pagan? You are not among living human beings unless you quickly burn me, a feeble old man, and eat me roasted.” When the prefect heard this, he was moved by respect for his old age. He ordered him to be taken out of his presence and brought to the bishop. The bishop, in the madness [?] of his anger, sent him away and imprisoned him in Heraclea, a city in Thrace. He remained there for two years, without being allowed to see any of his acquaintances. Since he was given no change of clothing and was infested with countless lice, one of his disciples went out and brought him a change. After that, no further change was allowed to be given to him, even through someone else. Later he became mortally ill. He forbade, under pain of anathema, his burial by adherents of the synod, or any of them ministering or offering prayer over him. So the orthodox [?] officers of the Roman army who were there took him out and buried him with candles and abundant perfumes. They wrapped and honored his body as that of a great martyr. They complained and spoke bitterly against the persecution of people such as these. Some of the faithful in the city planned to go out and take the holy man’s body.

There were also monasteries of men and women in the imperial capital itself and throughout its surroundings and districts. Some of these had large numbers of residents, especially the women’s monasteries, whose inhabitants had been persecuted from the beginning and had been gathered from Antioch, Isauria, Cilicia, Cappadocia, and the other regions by the late Empress Theodora, of blessed memory. Some of the monasteries numbered more than three hundred brothers. Suddenly the tempest and whirlwind of persecution overtook these too, and a thick cloud and bewildering darkness of persecution covered them.

That is, clergy together with laypeople, record clerks, and officers accompanying the assistants of the city prefect were sent against them. They went around the monasteries with savage violence. Like a pack of wolves entering and attacking a sheepfold, they too would leap into each of these monasteries to wreak destruction upon Christ’s lambs. The clergy carried their communion offerings, and they dragged and pulled the women so that they would come and receive communion from them.

But all the women fled like birds before hawks and hid in the inner rooms, wailing and saying, “We cannot receive communion from the Council of Chalcedon, which divides Christ our God into two natures after the union and teaches a quaternity instead of the Holy Trinity.” Thus, with shoving and pulling, they dragged them to receive communion, with their hands above their heads. As they wailed, they were carried by their hands, crying out with lamentation, stamping, and loud cries, and trying to flee. In this way the communion offering was forcibly thrown into their mouths, while many of them [?] with cries of lamentation.

Some threw themselves face down on the ground and pronounced an anathema against anyone who demanded that they receive communion by force. Thus they brought some of them into submission. All who resisted them and would not yield, they separated out, dragged away, and expelled from their monasteries. They were handed over to Roman officers, who pulled them about and abused them. They were taken into the city and distributed among houses and various prisons. According to the reports, many men committed acts of sexual violence against them like powerful stallions. Let these things be covered in silence on our part, since their case is reserved for the righteous Judge, who will judge their cause and exact vengeance for them.

Thus, in this savage and barbarous manner, these things were being done in all the monasteries, those of men as well as those of women.

John, then, was the instigator, promoter, and perpetrator of all these evils—the man who, as has been said, was the head of the church of the city. Out of the great bitterness of his wickedness, he would go in and make accusations, inflaming the emperor’s anger against the entire body of believers. He would come out having obtained authority to act against them. Through those who shared his wishes, he poured out all the filth of his wickedness upon every order of believers everywhere. Nor did he act only within his own city and jurisdiction: he also wrote to other regions, stirring up disturbances, persecutions, and evils. Eventually he himself went out in person and made the rounds of all the monasteries of men and women, and also private houses, forcing and pressuring people to enter into communion with him. As for those who resisted him, whether men or women, monks, clergy, or nuns, he gave orders against them in savage, merciless anger. He sent and imprisoned them all, individually, in monasteries, and pronounced harsh sentences of death against them.

He even managed to deceive, incite, and manipulate the victorious rulers themselves, so that they too fell in with him and went out, one after another, to make the rounds of the monasteries. First he himself would go with his clergy, hold assemblies and Eucharistic services in the monasteries, proclaim the divisive council there, install his own portraits in them, and appoint clergy there to offer the Eucharist every Sunday and on every festival and commemoration. Then, on another day after him, the emperor himself would make the rounds of those monasteries. After him, on another day, the empress would do the same. They also gave gifts and assigned daily allowances to those who had yielded or were yielding to them. But those who resisted they sent into exile and to oppressive prisons, or mercilessly handed them over to tortures in the governors’ headquarters [?]. In furious and bitter rage, they subjected them to scourging and bitter, harsh afflictions.

Now that bishop was filled with a spirit of hostile zeal and driven by violence and rage. Just as he was blind in the sight of his eyes, so too he was blinded in his soul by the passion of enmity and acted recklessly like a drunken man. Through every kind of savage tyranny and coercion, he had managed to subdue many priests of the orthodox and force them into communion with him. They had come forward and been received by him in their priestly rank: the priests were received by him as priests, participated in communion alongside his own priests with all the privileges of their rank, and sat in order with them in the sanctuary. Likewise, the deacons also performed all the duties of the diaconate alongside his own deacons. This happened not merely once or twice, but as many as thirty-six times, at all the festal assemblies and those that followed. They ministered with him in their own priestly rank and performed all the duties of the priesthood.

Then afterward a savage thought arose in him. Acting like a mere young boy, frantically carried away by pride and drunk with authority and self-exaltation, he issued this command: “We order that all those who have submitted to us from among our opponents be released from their former priesthood and become priests anew through us.” So he now stripped them all of their rank, after they had served as priests with him and before him thirty-six times in that same former priesthood which they had received from the orthodox. He himself ordained anew all those who had entered into communion with him, while they were agitated and distressed, anathematizing him and denouncing him and his unlawful priesthood. Some of them he appointed to the clergy of the church itself. Many, even among his own supporters, condemned the transgression and the departure from every canonical rule which he had wickedly and savagely committed.

The evil that he himself had done and carried through was not enough for him. He also wrote to the provinces and urged the bishops to act in the same way as he had. He was devising schemes and stratagems so that he would not be the only one blamed and accused for the unlawful and disorderly things he had done, but so that there would also be others implicated with him under the same blame and accusation.

Now a certain blessed and virtuous man was shown beforehand, in a vision at night, what would immediately and without delay actually happen in the church of God. He saw a great mountain stretching over a vast distance. On its southern side was a great planting of many churches, built in a row, one after another, extending a long way. They were closely packed, beautiful, splendid, and numerous. He saw that suddenly John, the bishop of the imperial city, arrived with clergy and a great crowd accompanying him. He rushed violently upon them and began uprooting and overthrowing all these churches. He also uprooted and overthrew the altars of them all, until he had finished them off.

And indeed, only a few days after this vision, this very thing was fulfilled in actual events. He went out and uprooted and overthrew all the numerous congregations of the churches of the faithful in the city itself and throughout its surroundings, just as in the revelation and vision that had been shown beforehand and soon came openly to fulfillment.

Now Paul, whom we mentioned a little earlier above, was from the province of Caria. He had been made bishop of the city called [?] Aphrodisias, the metropolis of Caria. He was a gentle, simple old man. While he was living quietly in his monastery, as we explained earlier, John the patriarch sent men, seized him, put him in irons, and imprisoned him in his own episcopal residence. By putting him under bitter pressure, he forced him into communion with himself. Then he sent him away to the province. He wrote and instructed the man who was in that city to depose him from his bishopric and ordain him anew as bishop in Antioch, a city of Caria. This was indeed carried out. They deposed him and sent him away, and when, as they supposed, they had stripped him—stripped him of his priesthood—they then ordained him anew as though he were a layman. Thus he became an object of reproach and mockery both to these people and to his own. His clergy used to call him “twice-dyed.”

Again, he also sent for the old bishop Elisha and brought him from the monastery where he had been confined, called the monastery of Dios. He imprisoned him too in his own episcopal residence, and through severe pressure they compelled him to submit to communion with him. Elisha then tried to find some way, even under these circumstances, to escape from his hands if he could. But he wanted to send him to Sardis, [?], the metropolis of Lydia. When he wanted to depose him from his bishopric and ordain him too anew, Elisha opposed him, saying, “Although I am unworthy, I have been made a bishop by the orthodox, and you shall certainly not ordain me anew. But if you think that it is proper to depose me and ordain me anew, then first undo the baptism with which I was baptized, and afterward attend to the second matter.” He replied to him deceitfully, “I am only putting the pallium on you.” But when Elisha absolutely refused to be persuaded or to submit to him, and would not accept his words, he became angry with him and sent him away to be imprisoned in another monastery, called the monastery of Abraham. A harsh sentence was pronounced against him. He remained there in distress for a long time. Then he fell seriously ill and asked to go to the hot springs, and he was released under guard.

Now, as the powerful John arrogantly exalted himself, trampling on and violating all the regulations of the church, he sent to the island called Platea, where he had banished Bishop Stephen. Stephen was one of those who had vigorously rebuked him shortly before over the annulment of ordination. John sent clerics and imperial guards against him and ordered them to toss him about like a ball until he vomited blood, unless he agreed to enter into communion with them. And so twelve imperial guards kept tossing him about like a ball until he fell among them and lay silent, already as good as dead. When they saw that he had fallen silent and was near death, they ran and brought four jars of water and poured them over him. After a long time, however, he regained consciousness and came back to life as though from the dead. In this way he was forced into communion with them. This was especially because some of the faithful who had been sending him what he needed had been discovered, arrested, and imprisoned on his account, and preparations were being made to attack them and plunder their possessions.

So they took him and entered the city, and many disturbances arose among them. Under compulsion he entered into communion with them. Afterward John demanded that his ordination be annulled and that he be ordained again as bishop of the island of Cyprus. But Stephen disputed with him and opposed him, causing an uproar and beginning to cry out in protest. He said, “If you wish to annul the priesthood I received from the orthodox and ordain me again, first annul my baptism as well, and baptize me again first. Then you can annul my priesthood and make me a priest again. For as the Lord God lives, unless you baptize me again, I will never, ever accept it.”

Thus a great uproar arose between them in the church, and many people gathered. Stephen hurried away and went in to the emperor, raising a disturbance before him too, crying out in protest and saying, “Christianity has perished! The regulations of the Christian church have been destroyed! All the regulations and canons of the church of God have been thrown into confusion, trampled on, and destroyed! What is this lawless wickedness, that the priesthood of orthodox Christians is being annulled by those who now hold power, and another is being conferred anew in its place? It is now twenty years since I, unworthy as I am, was canonically made a bishop by the orthodox, at the command of Theodosius, patriarch of Alexandria. And now that I have surrendered myself and been forced over to you, this man, acting wickedly, wants to annul the priesthood I received from the orthodox and ordain me again with his own, just as he has done to many others. Let him show from which canons he learned this! Either he has no awareness or knowledge of the church’s canons, or, though he knows them, he transgresses them and tramples on them in his arrogance, conceit, and error.

“If this command comes from you, and he does these things with your knowledge, let everyone know it. But you must understand that he also seeks to bring the reproaches and condemnations of the canons upon your imperial majesty. He is scheming to implicate and entangle you along with himself in the violation of the church’s laws. If, indeed, it is with your knowledge and at your command that he annuls priesthood and confers another anew, then command him to annul baptism as well, and to baptize people again, and only then to make them priests again. For the nineteenth canon of the three hundred and eighteen fathers, concerning the destructive heresy of the followers of Paul of Samosata and others like him, commands that they be baptized again, and that afterward those among them who are worthy should be made priests anew. This is because of the wickedness of their heresy. But now let this man first explain what grounds brought him to this, and why, in his arrogance, he has been moved to annul our ordination and ordain us again.”

When the emperor heard these things and understood that Stephen’s accusation was justified and that he was disputing with John on canonical grounds, he was astonished, as though waking from a deep sleep. He too condemned and rejected this practice, saying, “It is truly wicked, unlawful, and contrary to the entire order of the church that priesthood should be annulled and conferred again. It is disgraceful and utterly foreign to all the church’s regulations.” He then commanded that this should absolutely never happen again in the church of God. He immediately issued a formal imperial decree forbidding anyone to presume again to annul priesthood, except in cases involving the heresies specified by the canons. If bishops were found doing this, they were to be deposed and sent into exile.

When this happened, and John learned that a stern command had been issued, he and his advisers devised a plan to give a bribe so that the decree issued on this matter would be removed and never be seen again. Because of this affair, great hostility remained between John and Stephen throughout their lives.

With a cunning plan and deceptive falsehood, then—as the affair itself eventually showed—John, together with all his advisers, sent men to bring the bishops whom he had banished into exile in monasteries and other places. They deceived them by saying that they were bringing them to discuss unity with them. First he sent for Paul the patriarch, took him from the monastery of the Acoemetae, and imprisoned him in his own episcopal residence. He brought the others one after another and imprisoned them with him: namely, Paul, John, Stephen, and Elisha. They had first devised a scheme and consulted together, and they sent them a document describing the union that had taken place between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch. They sent word to them in their prison: “You must also unite with us in accordance with this union that took place between Cyril and John.”

When the bishops received this, considered it among themselves, and laughed at their foolishness, they sent them this reply: “You have taken good counsel. So, once we have done and accomplished what Cyril did, and have anathematized, expelled, and cast the Council of Chalcedon out of the church of God, just as Cyril did to the wicked Nestorius, we will not dispute with you over the remaining matters between us and you, but will unite with you without hindrance. But if you do not approve even of our doing what Cyril did, how, then, and in what manner are you scheming against us by demanding from us the union between him and John that took place afterward, when Cyril’s earlier action has not been carried out?”

After these things, John was being challenged by the bishops whom he was keeping confined in his episcopal residence. Every day they came before him to debate the faith, the corruption caused by the Council of Chalcedon, and the things that had resulted from it. They began accusing him vigorously, arguing with him and rebuking him forcefully. They pressed him with questions, saying:

“Show us, great man and holder of the leadership of the church, from what canon and ecclesiastical ordinance you learned and received authority to annul the priesthood of orthodox bishops and the other clergy, whose years in the priesthood exceeded even your father’s, and to annul their ordination and ordain them anew in the priesthood of the adherents of two natures. These proclaim and teach a quaternity instead of the hidden and holy Trinity. In what ecclesiastical ordinance did you find this, and on what basis did you decide to annul the priesthood of the truly orthodox and replace it with another, that of the adherents of the council?

“For what reason, on what charge, and as coming from what heresy, did you receive these men and depose them, in accordance with what the legislator prescribes in the canons? They accuse you and flee from communion with you because of the heresy—the heresy of two natures—and because of the blasphemies of the council and Leo’s Tome, which proclaim and teach a quaternity instead of the holy Trinity. But you have absolutely no grounds for accusing and condemning them for heresy, and yet you annul their priesthood. If, indeed, you have anything against these men whom you have unlawfully deposed from the priesthood, tell us now, and we will stop arguing and accusing you over these matters.

“For if, outside all the church’s ordinances and canons, you have given yourselves permission to act in this way, deposing true priests and ordaining them anew, it would have been consistent with this also to annul their baptism and baptize them anew, in accordance with the force of the canonical prescriptions. For consider the nineteenth—sixteenth [?]—canon of the 318 concerning the destructive heresy of the followers of Paul of Samosata. It prescribed that they should first be baptized anew, and then that those considered worthy should become priests anew. If you now think that you received them as coming from heresy—these men whom you forcibly carried off like captives and ordained anew as priests—how is it that you fulfill one requirement but have omitted the first?”

John listened to all this in silence and knew that these were grounds for reproach, since he had no way of finding relief through an answer to them. Finally, he replied:

“Since I see that you are troubled and offended over this matter of ordination—and I have listened in silence to all these things from you—if what has been done through ordination is corrected and annulled, will that satisfy you, and will you unite with us?”

They said to him:

“What correction can you possibly make after all this wrongdoing, corruption, and unlawful action that you have committed? You did not do this only here and then restrain the vehemence of your anger and hatred. Rather, you extended this lawlessness and opposition to all ecclesiastical ordinances and canons into other regions as well. Either you did not know these ordinances and canons, and so broke through them, went beyond them, trampled them down, and transgressed them; or, knowing them, you despised them, acted insolently against them, and rushed headlong into all this lawlessness.

“Do not overlook this: whenever the time comes, whether during your lives or, if it should happen so, after your deaths, all these things must undergo a rigorous examination and a canonical inquiry, if the world endures and the church of God remains standing.

“Furthermore, there is that other thing you did at the end, which deserves astonishment and should become a byword and a tale that makes people throw up their hands. Whether you did this in a rush of anger or hatred, through the arrogance of power, or with some other intention, judge now in your own minds and consider whether you acted with deliberation and sound judgment. You fell upon these men as though taking captives, seized them as though in a raid, subdued them, and subjected them to communion with you. Then, after thirty-six Eucharistic celebrations and the liturgies they celebrated with you throughout the whole Feast of Unleavened Bread and afterward, you finally attempted to annul their former priesthood. Yet you had received them in that very priesthood! You seated their presbyters in the sanctuary with your own presbyters throughout all those days of respite already mentioned. You likewise received their deacons in their own diaconal order alongside the other deacons and established them in their rank. Finally, after all these things, you senselessly resorted to some strange piece of cunning to annul their former priesthood.

“We now leave it to your own judgment and the examination of your own minds to consider on what grounds you would depose them from the priesthood and ordain them anew. This much is clear: if you indeed thought it right to act in this way without ecclesiastical order and canons, you ought to have done this before receiving them to celebrate the Eucharist with you—not turn around, after all these liturgies in which they served and shared with you in their former priesthood, and depose them and ordain them anew.”

Many things were said on both sides, which we leave aside because of their number and the length an account of them would require. The man being accused knew within himself that he was open to reproach and would not be free from accusation if his actions were examined. This applied especially to what he had done at the end, deposing those whom he had received into ministry and then turning around and deposing them. His silence about these things showed that he condemned himself, although he used foul, foolish, and disorderly words against these men.

For when the supporters of the council saw that their schemes had now failed, the victorious emperor Justin proceeded to draw up an edict, thinking that through it he would bring about unity. After carefully preparing it, he immediately sent it to the bishops who were confined in the episcopal residence, through a certain Zacharias, a sophist and chief physician of the palace. He was a native of Sura in Roman territory and had long been considered orthodox. He was therefore sent to them by the emperor with the written text of the edict they had prepared. He copied it out and said to them:

“The merciful emperor has sent you this edict, which he has drawn up for your sake, so that through it you too, together with everyone belonging to your party, may be united. He has also given you permission and commanded you as follows: ‘When you have read it, correct anything in it that you see is deficient and needs correction. And if anything is missing that is necessary for the true confession which you wish to prevail, add it without fear.’”

When the bishops received this command, they took it and read it. They saw that it was inadequate: although it contained certain things opposed to the Council of Chalcedon, it also contained things belonging to that council and supporting it. Nevertheless, because they had been instructed to do so, they drew up articles—that is, corrections—which, if their opponents had allowed them to be inserted into it, would undoubtedly have brought about unity.

The man who had brought the edict took the corrections away and showed them to his confidant and counselor John and to all the rest of their council. When they heard the corrections, they were alarmed and shaken, and great fear fell upon them, since, if these were to prevail, they would uproot the entire heresy of the two natures. The thoroughgoing Nestorians were even more alarmed and disturbed than the semi-Nestorians. They stirred up trouble and caused an uproar throughout the church, running about and agitating the clergy and the people, saying, “If these additions are accepted, the whole church will be thrown into confusion and ruined.”

Finally, they gathered their entire party together and went in to the emperor to persuade him not to insert these corrections into his edict. They also stirred up the people of the palace, many of whom were themselves unsound in their Christianity, especially the quaestor, whose name was Anastasius the Palestinian: besides being a pagan, he was also a Samaritan.

When they came before the emperor and these corrections were read to him, they pleased him, and he praised them highly. He ordered that they be inserted into the edict and written in [?]. Then all those who had come in—clergy, laymen, and the rest of the senate—raised an outcry against him, saying:

“My lord, if you put these articles into your edict and they are introduced into the church, it will immediately be overturned and ruined. While you are seeking to bring a few in and unite them—and it is only a few that you would bring in and unite—tens of thousands will leave the church.”

As they continued raising an uproar against him, he became angry and turned to face them, saying:

“These articles are sound. But I know that you are all Nestorians, sick in your consciences, and that you take no pleasure in the true faith. If you do not keep quiet, I will release the bishops and bring them out, and I will unleash them against you. They will fall upon you like wolves and tear you apart, and you will not be able to stand before them.”

Then he gave the quaestor this command: “Unless you promptly bring me twenty copies of the edict by this evening, containing these corrections, I will have your head cut off.”

Thus the entire party of the Nestorians and semi-Nestorians was thrown into alarm, and they buzzed like bees exposed to smoke. They nevertheless managed to plead with him and frighten him with the prospect of disorder in the church. When they pressed him hard, he yielded to them and left the matter to their wishes. They allowed him to include only a few minor points from these corrections. They themselves, acting heretically, added something of their own at the end of the edict: “The church’s customs are to be preserved for it.” This referred to the council, so that they could continue proclaiming it as was their custom. They devised this and inserted it craftily, to prevent unity from coming about and the wheel from turning against them as Nestorians.

For after the edict had been written in [?], as the emperor had ordered, he immediately signed it and sent it to the bishops who were in the episcopal residence, sending them this message: “Look, we have brought about unity as you wished, and now we have sent you an edict. From now on you have no reason to delay joining us. Indeed, it was also for your sake that I made this edict.”

But when those bishops read the edict and saw that the corrections they had made were not in it, but that only some extracts from them had been included, according to the wishes of those who had made the extracts, they disregarded it. For the opposing party had confused and muddled it as they wished. Out of fear of the emperor, they had not dared to remove from it the statements opposed to the two natures, but they had contrived to insert their own statements into it as far as they could. Thus it appeared to oppose the council and, again, to fight on its behalf, and statements from it and belonging to it could be seen in the edict.

Those bishops replied to the men who had brought it, saying: “If the cause of stumbling and disturbance throughout the whole church—that is, the Council of Chalcedon—is removed, the church has no need of this. But if that council continues to be proclaimed in the church, not even a thousand documents like this, posted in every place and every region, will establish unity. The division still remains where it was. For this document appears to fight both against the council and on its behalf, and anyone who examines it can recognize both positions in it.”

Every day John himself, together with those sent to them on the emperor’s behalf, solemnly warned the bishops, saying: “Look, it is you who are thwarting and obstructing the unity of the church of God. Now, after fifty years, it has come, and you are now rejecting, preventing, and hindering it, and you are unwilling to unite.”

But they would reply to them: “How are we thwarting unity, when you do not touch it with even one of your fingers, except with outward words and deceit, so that people may see you and suppose that you are truly concerned about unity? You are scheming to direct all the blame from everyone against us. What union are you actually striving to bring about? Or how can you ask us to unite with you while you hold fast to the council that uproots and disturbs the whole church of God, proclaiming it and cherishing it? If you are truly concerned to bring about unity, as you say, remove the stumbling block and the cause of stumbling from the smooth path of faith, and cast it out of the church of God. Then not only we, but all the faithful, rejoicing and freed from stumbling, will unite with you.”

There were many other things of this kind, spoken between them every day in their exchanges of argument about these matters, which we cannot encompass even in a great mass of pages. Because of the abundance of words and the bulk of the writings, we have left these out and passed over them, lest those who encounter them should find them tedious.

Even before the time of this persecution and these trials, hardships, and imprisonments at the hands of the persecutors, those bishops were also harshly reproached by the rest of the orthodox. They argued with them and said, “Why do you persist in such contentiousness and rigidity, instead of making accommodations and concessions so that there may be unity in the church of God? Instead, you remain stiff-necked and contend against those in power. You do not care that you are going to destroy us, our households, our children, and our estates. What do you care if we lose our [?] and become beggars?”

Such things had already been said to them in harsh reproaches by the orthodox, who were anxious about their wealth. Along with these things, there was also what their consciences testified against them every day: “Look, you are preventing unity from coming about.” So they fell into grief and bitter weeping by day and by night. They sat weeping and lamenting to one another with sobs, and said in sorrowful voices:

“What are we to do now? We are reproached on both sides; people testify against us and blame us. And now, here we are, imprisoned in distress, and we are not allowed to see any of our acquaintances. Those who oppose us say these things and [?], especially to the leaders and prominent people among our own. They deceitfully tell everyone, and persuade them, that they themselves are concerned about unity. Consequently, everyone believes their words to be true, and they lay on us all the blame for the failure of unity.

“Now we are caught between the two sides. As for surrendering ourselves and relying on the deceitful promises and false oaths of our opponents, we know that there is no truth in them and that they are not at all fit to bring about unity. Yet if we continue to stand against them in opposition, we are placed under a curse by both sides for all generations, as people who thwart and obstruct the unity of the church of God. Moreover, they lend an appearance of truth to these people's deceitful promises and lying words, as though they were ready to bring about unity, but we had barred unity from the church.”

These and many similar things were said among them for many days amid tears and sobs. As before God, we bear witness to their truth, since we were close at hand and eyewitnesses to everything.

For thirty-three days they were fiercely arrayed against one another in this debate: those who supported the council and held power, and those who opposed the council, whom they had imprisoned and were bitterly oppressing. Whenever the latter were sent for, they were released and came out of prison to the patriarch’s council chamber. There they sat and debated for as long as those in power wished. Whenever those in power were either defeated by them or thought fit, those bishops went out with their guards and were imprisoned again behind three cordons of guards: one of the episcopal staff [?], one of the imperial guards, and the outer one of the doorkeepers. Meanwhile, the people belonging to each of them, from every place—not only the clerics, monks, and the other free men accompanying them, but also all their servants—were imprisoned in dark and dreadful cells throughout the episcopal residence. They were all kept under guard, and not only that: they were also stripped of their possessions by the episcopal staff and the deacons, as though by robbers. Whatever clothes they wore were stripped off them, even worn-out things that were of no use to their captors. Whether shoes, belts, straps, prayer beads, or anything else was found on any one of them, they were stripped of everything. Everything found on them was taken away, and they were thrown onto the ground, stripped and suffering hardship, even for lack of food. No one was allowed at all to see them or to give anything either to them or to the bishops. Instead of the promised unity, they and all those with them suffered and endured these evils, these afflictions and trials, especially because they openly rebuked those who were tormenting them.

After all these things, finally the bishops were again sent for and brought out of their prison. Pressure was now brought to bear on them harshly and shamelessly, both by John, who presided over the assembly, and, even more than by him, by those who were sent by the emperor and acted as his representatives. They said, “How long will you go on trampling on and destroying the unity of God’s church, which our lord the emperor and we are striving to bring about? Day after day you delay and ruin this good work. Are you not plainly showing everyone that you yourselves, and no one else, are the ones preventing it? Now, once and for all, either unite with us or reveal yourselves as the people who disturb, batter, and destroy the unity of the church.”

But the bishops, who were in mourning and distress, said, “If matters are judged justly and with sound reasoning, it is not we who are obstructing unity, but you. Although your hearts are full of the filth of Chalcedonian opposition and division, you want to portray us as the obstructors, when you yourselves have neither established nor displayed even a shadow of unity. Instead, you deceitfully demand that we unite with the whole Chalcedonian falsehood. You are not striving to bring about the true unity of the church justly and rightly.

“Now, as we said from the beginning, if you truly seek unity, and are not intent on practicing deceitful misdirection and wicked cunning, first remove the cause of division from our midst, and there unity will stand in its place. Do not deceitfully make us your excuse. Since this has never even entered your minds, why do you wrong and oppress us every day, adding pain to our torments, to the distress of imprisonment, and to the other afflictions we suffer at your hands because you have no fear of God? Every day you torment us with your words and drive a thorn into our sores. You have no fear of God, though you see that our lives are already spent, wasted away and exhausted by the afflictions surrounding us on every side. If you really intend to bring about unity, as your outward words suggest, reject the Council of Chalcedon. It was this council that disturbed, divided, and split the church, as even you cannot deny. Then unity without division will stand throughout the whole church of God.”

John and those with him said again, “You yourselves are preventing even this rejection of the council that you speak of. For if you unite with us, the council too will immediately be rejected, and complete unity will come about.”

The bishops said, “As it appears to us, you are striving to make us unite with your council. Let neither you nor anyone else be mistaken about this: until the breath has left the nostrils of every one of us, the condemnation of the council and of Leo’s Tome will never cease from our mouths. Together they divide our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ into two natures after the union.”

John and those with him said, “As we have told you many times, we and our lords the emperors give you our word and our oaths, as before God, that as soon as you unite with us, the council will immediately be abolished. What has passed our lips will not be changed.”

The bishops said, “If [?], and you are prepared to do this in accordance with your oaths, why do you not do it immediately, so that not only we but everyone may unite without a stumbling block? Instead, you want to deceive us by trickery and make us unite with the heresy of the two natures, and afterward turn around and mock us. If that is what you think, you are mocking and deceiving yourselves. For we know that your intentions and thoughts are not directed toward unity. You do not even appear to be speaking the truth, although you have made yourselves ready with words, so that everyone may suppose that we have prevented unity, and so that we may be condemned as obstructors by you and by everyone else.

“We are ready to sacrifice even our lives for unity. If, then, relying on your words and promises as though the council had already been condemned and rejected, we enter into communion with you while continually keeping its condemnation on our lips—once, or perhaps, if it should happen, twice—then, a third time, before the council has been condemned and rejected, we will have no share or communion with you forever and ever.

“We know that you will not uphold the truth of your words. But so that it may be revealed and made known to everyone that you are not prepared to bring about unity, but imagine that you can deceive us and everyone else, here and now we submit ourselves to union with you, if necessary as many as two times.”

These things, together with countless others, were spoken and solemnly attested between them. So the bishops concluded by saying, “Because of the oppression inflicted on us by the supporters of the council, we now submit ourselves, so that it may be known that we are not the ones preventing unity.” For everyone on both sides was reviling them, saying, “Look, the emperors and the patriarch are taking care, making every effort, and preparing to bring about unity, while these prisoners are stopping and obstructing them.” Because of all these things, they submitted themselves in great distress. While loudly condemning the Council of Chalcedon, they were drawn into communion with them twice, as they had promised and agreed. They also protested, and throughout all those thirty-three days they insistently demanded from the emperor and the patriarch that the council now be condemned and rejected, as these men had pledged with many oaths.

But they began to go back on their words and put them off with excuses, saying, “We are writing to the pope of Rome, and if he agrees, then we will reject the council. For we cannot break with Rome on your account.” Then the bishops answered them, “Now it is time for us too to repeat the words of the prophet Jonah: ‘Was this not what I said when I was still in my own land?’”

Thus it became known and clear to everyone that those who had been imprisoned and were suffering bitter afflictions were not the ones preventing unity. On the contrary, they had surrendered themselves for its sake. Rather, it was those who held power and oppressed them, who lied in their promises and oaths to them. They wanted to direct all the blame—not only that of their contemporaries, but also that of the generations to come—against the bishops, as though they had obstructed and destroyed the unity of God’s church. This would have happened if the bishops had not sacrificed themselves for its sake, even though they were deceived.

For who is capable of writing and recounting the afflictions, mourning, lamentation, and heartbreak that overtook those who entered into communion with the people who had plotted against them and were united with them, although they were not united at all? They were now as though utterly lost and finished. Their eyes were troubled and darkened by weeping and lamenting opposite one another night and day. The mourning of a woman for the husband of her youth is only a faint illustration when compared with their mourning. They had now even stopped eating their customary food, remaining without nourishment or consolation, with no rest or interruption in their tears. Each covered his face, and they sat lamenting opposite one another in choked and bitter voices. Above all, they now lamented for themselves, because after all these struggles, imprisonments, and afflictions, they had been caught, brought low, and made to fall through such deceitful trickery. Unity had been agreed upon beforehand, but it had not been put into effect as promised.

Those who had deceived them, seeing that they were already wasting away and approaching destruction, said to them, “Why are you killing yourselves, soul and body, like people who have sacrificed to idols? Why, then, have you passed judgment on yourselves and persisted in all this weeping and lamentation, continually choking yourselves? Take food and be comforted. Live, and do not die.” Although these opponents said many such things, they remained inconsolable.

Thus they continued all the more in mourning and weeping, remaining bitterly distressed for many days, even after they had been released from prison and had come out. Then they rallied and took a courageous stand. Now they rebuked their opponents still more openly, disputed with them, and denounced them as liars and deceivers. So they were again handed over to imprisonments and tortures harsher than the earlier ones. Afterward, each of them was forcibly cast into a different place of exile, with bitter severity.

When the emperors learned of all this intense mourning and bitter suffering, they sent for the bishops, brought them to the palace, and tried to comfort them, saying, “Why have you fallen into such overwhelming grief that you have become so weakened and are like dead people? Take courage and be comforted. For we trust in God that we will satisfy you and unite you in complete unity. Do not be distressed.”

When they reproached him at length to his face about the things that had been discussed between them but had proved false and had not been put into effect, he said to them, “Since we are preparing to go to the hot springs, wait for me twenty or thirty days. Know that we will return promptly for your sake. We are prepared to discuss this very matter and to satisfy you. The whole church will be one, and we will all rejoice.” Thus they departed from him, having addressed many rebukes to him.

After thirty days, the emperor returned from the hot springs, as he had promised. Before he had yet entered the city, while he was still across the water at Chalcedon, John took his advisers and went out to meet him. As became apparent once again, he continued adding accusations against those who were imprisoned, saying, “These men have cut themselves off from us and have turned away from the church altogether.” Then they took counsel about how to win their consent and deceive them again. They drew up a list of the great cities and sent it to them through the quaestor, with this message: “Because your welfare is our concern, and we care about your honor and wish to make [?] for you, we have sent you this list of well-known cities. We have not ourselves specified in which city each of you is to be. Rather, we have left this to your own choice, so that each of you may choose whichever city pleases him.”

When the illustrious quaestor had taken the list and entered the city, he sent for the bishops so that he could give them the list. He said all these things to them, along with many others, speaking on the emperor’s behalf. But they would not look at the list and were unwilling to accept it from him. They said, “Tell the victorious emperor: We are not sacrificing our lives in order to become bishops in cities, but because of our hope in the promises of unity. For we are bishops already, even though we are unworthy. But if they are fulfilled—if they are fulfilled [?]—so that the promises of unity are fulfilled for us, together with the oaths made to us over the course of many days! It was because of these, and so that the accusations against us would not be confirmed, namely, that we were obstructing unity, that we committed ourselves to communion with those who deceived us—[?]—and thought they had misled us. They did not realize that they had misled themselves, not us. And now, unless the council is set aside and unity is established in accordance with the promises and oaths, far be it from us ever again, for all eternity, to have communion with those who commemorate it.”

When they had thus made their decision firmly and refused to accept the list, the quaestor became angry and went to report these things to the emperor. He too became angry and was stirred to great fury. He threatened them and made harsh menaces against them, which he eventually carried out.

Then the emperor, filled with anger, sent for the patriarch of the city and assailed him harshly with severe insults, saying, “You have turned the bishops away—the very bishops who, after much hard work, had barely agreed [?] to join us. Now you have turned them away from us!” In his agitation, he ordered the senate to enter the episcopal residence and judge the events that had taken place between them. The patriarch himself was also to stand trial, and if they found him at fault, he too was to be condemned.

For on the following day, in accordance with the command, members of the senate went with the quaestor to the bishop’s residence, and the bishops were summoned for judgment. They were required, as an imperial command, to remain in communion with the adherents of the council, keeping quiet and demanding nothing further.

But they stood their ground and fought the contest vigorously and courageously. Without fear they openly denounced all the deceitful promises, all the oaths that had proved false, the truth that had been wronged and trampled underfoot, and the other things of this kind. Along with this, they openly addressed the senate with great boldness, pronouncing an anathema against the entire heresy of the two natures. They spoke firmly at the beginning, in the middle, and also at the end, once more declaring their complete and everlasting separation from communion with them. Many other things were also done and said there in that contest of courageous struggle, until the senators and the patriarch became so furiously angry with the bishops that they ordered them to be dragged out of their presence, separated from one another, and sent into exile.

This was quickly carried out. They were taken out and separated, and they never saw one another again. They were sent into exile, some to monasteries, some to islands in the sea, and some to cramped and wretched places of confinement in hospices. It was decreed that they should be confined and that no one belonging to them, nor anyone else, should be allowed to see any one of them. Many, many other things were decreed against them, as though against murderers, with savage harshness and without mercy, with bitter malice and oppressive restraints.

Now perhaps those who are accomplished in lofty learning and sharp in understanding, who examine these words closely, will suppose that all these things that have been said and written were used by the writer as embellishments, in the manner of a literary composition—as though he had written these things himself, adorning his language [?]. Otherwise, how could he have known how to recount and write down, in such order, everything that happened and was said between the two sides, and to hand all these things down in writing? Moreover, as it appears, in his account he is aligned with one side, attacks the other side, and fights on behalf of one side.

But now let this be known to those who hold this opinion: the writer of all these things was not outside the contest, nor was he far removed from the struggle, receiving these things as hearsay upon hearsay, from a distance and from others, and then writing them down and handing them on in his book. Rather, he himself was one of those who stood in the contest. In the great struggle, together with the others—or even more than they—he bore sufferings courageously and endured the afflictions of persecution and imprisonment. He and the others spoke and argued before the emperor and the patriarch, not only about these few matters that he has handed down in this book, but about a hundred times more besides. Because the history would have been so lengthy and the mass of words limitless, he passed over the greater part of these things and made use of only a few of them.

Moreover, although he belonged to the side opposed to those who profess two natures, against whom he had taken his stand, as his own account also makes clear, he nevertheless observed the proper manner of historical writing, without partiality, or injustice and unfairness toward the opposing side for the sake of establishing his own side. Rather, as he had previously said and promised at the beginning of this book of his history, he became an advocate for the truth and preserved a faithful representation of both sides in what was said, put forward, and debated, even though he made use of only a few of these things. Indeed, he was not able to put on record even one hundredth of what was said and done.

At that time Conon was also arrested. He was the leader of the heresy of those who dare to count natures, substances, godheads, and gods in the holy Trinity, which is equal in substance. He too was arrested and imprisoned for a time in the episcopal residence, along with the others. They demanded that he draw up a written declaration as a heretic, but he resisted this and did not do it. When the victorious emperor learned of this, he swore by the Mother of God, saying, “Even if he appeals and enters the church and receives communion without drawing up a declaration of repentance, I will not enter it or receive communion in it.” Thus, because he was a heretic and a blasphemer, when Photius, the son of Belisarius’s wife, came to the imperial city at that time, Conon was handed over to him. He took him with him to Palestine and imprisoned him in the monastery called the New Monastery. He remained there for three years. Then he was released and went to the region of Cilicia.

This Photius was the son of the wife of Belisarius the patrician, whose name was Antonina. He had served in the army and gone on campaigns with Belisarius. Eventually, for some reason, he went and cut off his hair and put on the monastic habit, although he never adopted the monastic way of life at all. Rather, he wore a monk’s habit under an assumed name. After a short time, unable to restrain his unruliness through the fear of God, he ran to the emperor. While outwardly clothed in the monastic robe, he was sent to the regions of Syria because of the Samaritans who had rebelled. Wishing to please people while angering God his maker, and himself pursuing filthy profits through the revenues, he threw himself into plundering, robbery, oppression, uprooting, and destruction. Consequently, throughout all the regions of the East, great and small [?], even the bishops and clergy of all the cities fled from him as though from barbarian captors.

Whenever he learned that anyone, whether in a city or in the countryside, had more than his daily bread, he would seize him, plunder him, imprison him, suspend him, and torture him. He imposed assessments of pounds of gold on anyone at all, whether he possessed anything or not. Even if someone sold himself, his children, his house, and his property, there was no way for anyone to overturn the pronouncement of his mouth. For whenever he seized someone, he would say, ‘Give such-and-such a number of pounds, because the emperor needs gold to spend on the wars.’ In this way he collected gold by the hundred pounds and sent it off, so that through this he might be given authority to do whatever he wished to whomever he wished, without anyone standing against him.

He also made enormous demands on the bishops in the same way. If anyone resisted him, he was immediately hoisted up on a rope without delay, either by the back of his head, by his shoulder blades, or by one arm. Thus, as is reported, he imposed an assessment of three hundred pounds on the bishop of Ashkelon. When the bishop cried out and swore solemnly that he did not have it, he gave orders, and the bishop was suspended by a rope. He left him hanging and went away, ordering that even if he hung for three days, he was not to be taken down until the hundred-pound sums arrived. And so he was not taken down from the rope until the three hundred pounds arrived. He treated many others in the same way, until the land trembled before him, as did all the magistrates, governors, and other authorities.

When many people complained before the emperor, he would write to him, ‘It is a sin for you to send us the proceeds of plunder.’ But he would write back, ‘You, my lord, need not fear any sin because of the gold I send. This sin is on my own head.’ On his own head indeed! He had with him a company of monks who assisted in these things, as well as imperial servants, imperial servants [?], household officers, sword-bearers, and even a force of Roman soldiers.

After he had spent twelve years in this vile course of destruction, cunning, and brutality, entirely devoid of the fear of God, his end overtook him, and he received his shame, with an evil end and a cursed memory. After him there arose another man, Abraham by name, the abbot of the monastery in Jerusalem called the New Monastery.

In the midst of the persecution, a letter was written and sent to Alexandria, and rhetoricians, lawyers, lawyers [?], shipowners, and many others came up. The secret intention was to require them to enter into communion with the council, but the outward pretext was unity. In practice, both approaches were used toward them, though in the end they were required to enter into communion. They, however, disputed and argued courageously for many days, for about a whole year, without yielding or giving in at all. Eventually some of them were released, because those in authority were afraid to coerce them on account of the shipments of wheat sent from there to the imperial capital. Others were detained for as long as three years, but nothing came of it. And so they were all released.

After this, it was reported in writing to the emperor that the orthodox bishops had appointed not just one bishop, but two, in place of the blessed Theodosius. He became extremely angry and ordered all the leading clergy to be arrested and sent away. This was done. They were arrested and taken up, and remained there until after the death of John the patriarch. Then Eutychius, who had been his predecessor, became patriarch. He took office after John's death and released them after a year.

Again, people were repeatedly sent to Egypt, and many monks were summoned and came. They were thought to know hidden things and understand future events, and were to disclose how many years the emperor and empress would live, what would happen during his reign, and other such things. Some of them, when pressed and questioned about these matters, admitted that they knew nothing. Instead, they spoke about moral instruction, justice, and righteousness, saying that practicing these things pleases God and brings people near to him. These men were not accepted, because they would not stoop to give a flattering answer as requested. They were immediately dismissed and driven out of the city to return to their own country. Others, however, seeking to please people, fell into the weakness of that pretense, which was exposed in the end. These were kept in honor and lived for a long time in comfort, receiving gifts of food. Such things happened many times.

For when all the convents mentioned above were taken over forcibly and unlawfully, a few of their members entered into communion, while the rest were thrown into other convents. Those clerics were installed everywhere, to celebrate the Eucharist in each convent and administer it to those who complied. The name of the council was written up and proclaimed in them. John took down the portraits of all the orthodox fathers and put up his own portraits everywhere. For these deeds he was repaid by God according to what he had done. For after his bitter and agonizing death, and the accession of Eutychius, who had been his predecessor and took office again after his death, his portraits were torn down, and those of Eutychius were installed in their place in the churches. Most of these women's convents returned and became orthodox. Some young girls remained in them, however, and were coming in every day, receiving communion with the council. They wore the monastic habit and received communion from the clerics. But these openly broke off, and not a single one of them continued to receive communion, especially after John's death.

Now before John’s death, while he was drunk with furious zeal for persecuting the Christians and thirsted like a wolf for the blood of lambs, he went in to the peaceable and gentle Caesar Tiberius. He was eager to inflame him too with the same furious zeal as his own. After he had said many things to him against the faithful, Tiberius questioned him, saying, “I want you to answer truthfully what I ask you. Are these people whom you urge me to persecute pagans?” He could not lie and said to him, “They are not pagans.” He said to him, “Then are they heretics?” He said to him, “Neither are they heretics, my lord.” He said to him, “Then, as you yourself have testified about them, they are Christians.” He answered again, “Christians they certainly are.” He said to him, “If, according to your testimony, they are Christians, how can you urge me to become a persecutor of Christians, like Diocletian, Diocletian, and the other pagan emperors? Go, remain in your church and keep quiet. Do not trouble us about these things again.” Thus the onslaught of his savagery was held back until wrath from heaven overtook him, as we explained above, and he departed from this earthly life.

After this, again, as we explained above, when Eutychius came in and those clerics who were accustomed to plunder and robbery began to inflame him, he too went in to the gentle Caesar Tiberius Constantine and said many things to him against the whole body of the faithful. But he answered him in turn, saying, “The wars with the barbarians, who surround us on every side, are enough for us. We cannot stir up another war against the Christians as well. Go, stay where you are and keep quiet. If you can persuade them by discussion or exhortation, do so; but if not, leave them alone. Do not persecute them, and do not trouble us, for we are beset by the trials of wars on every side.” Thus he too restrained himself for the time being and kept quiet.

Now all those orthodox congregations that had been uprooted and shut down by John of Sirimis began to take courage and open up, reopening their meeting places, when God sent upon him the chastisement of fierce wrath from heaven. At first they did so fearfully, quietly, and little by little. Even while he was still alive, they gained new members and grew, especially after he had been struck by the blow of wrath and his mind was now failing because of the fire of death that had seized his heart and was blazing in his inward parts.

Finally, those who shared his wishes and served his wickedness, knowing what he wanted, would come in and say to him, “Look, these enemies of the church and the council have reopened their meeting places and have spread more widely than before. They rejoice in your illness and pray for your death. If you give us the order, we will torment them more than before and make them suffer.”

But he would angrily rebuke them in a loud voice, saying, “Get away from me, you murderers! Have your fill of my humiliation! It was you above all who brought me to this humiliation and misery. [?] The curses are enough, those that have stirred up and brought wrath from heaven—stirred it up and brought it upon me. Get out of my sight, and let no one bring this matter before me again.” Thus they would leave him with their heads bowed.

Before his death, then, as we said, and again after his death, which followed soon afterward, the congregations of the faithful now met openly, with great freedom and without fear.

This monastery of Cathara, then, was built by Narses while he was the emperor’s keeper of records in the palace, before he went to Rome. He was preparing to leave the palace, go and have his head tonsured, live there, and settle others there. He placed in it monks who had been driven out of Cappadocia. He bought a considerable number of villages for it, built a magnificent church in it [?], established a guesthouse there, and endowed it with substantial revenues. Then he was sent to Rome, where, through the help of God who accompanied him, he distinguished himself with great victories in many battles. He departed this world there, in those regions. His remains were brought back and laid in the monastery; the emperors brought him, laid him there, and performed the sacred rites for him.

After John, who had been one of the patricians in the imperial city, had completed his term as bishop of Alexandria—he had been sent there, served for [?] years, and died—a man named Eulogius, the director of a guesthouse from Antioch, was called to succeed him. He became pope there in the third year of the victorious Tiberius.

The Julianists’ bishop was Dorotheus, who had been appointed many years before and occupied the see there.

As for the bishop of the followers of Theodosius, some time after his death there was first a man named Theodore, a Syrian administrator. When the clergy and the others learned of this, they turned against him. Since they would not accept him without the canonical procedure, they took action and appointed another over him, named Peter. After completing his term and ordaining more than eighty bishops, this man died. They appointed a Syrian named Damian, and they remained divided.

In Antioch the Great in Syria, in the days of Emperor Anastasius, there was Flavian. He was accused of the heresy of the two natures and was expelled from his see after serving for [?] years. After him came the orthodox Severus, who held office for six years. At the beginning of the reign of the elder Justin, the first of that name, he left his see. After spending [?] years in the Egyptian desert, he died there. [?]

After Antioch had been without a bishop for one year, Paul the Jew finally came down. He had been the custodian of the shrine of the blessed Euphemia in Chalcedon. He introduced into the East the diptychs [?] in which the council was recorded. After he had held office for about two years, it became known that he was a Nestorian, and he too was expelled and departed.

After him came Euphrasius, a Samaritan. In his seventh year Antioch was overthrown by an earthquake, and he died in it.

After him came Ephraim of Amida, the son of Appianus, a wicked persecutor worse than Paul and Euphrasius. He lived for [?] years and died. After him came Domninus, a Roman. [?]

After him came Anastasius [?], who had been the representative of Alexandria [?]. The younger Justin fabricated charges against him and removed him. In his place a man named Gregory, the abbot of the monastery on Mount Sinai, was sent.

As for those who opposed the Council of Chalcedon [?], after a long interval they first appointed Sergius in Severus’s place, a man originally from Tella. After completing about three years, he died in the imperial city, where he was living.

Some time afterward he was succeeded by Paul, an Alexandrian, the personal assistant of Theodosius of Alexandria. He was appointed at Theodosius’s command and with his knowledge during those evil days. Through the schism that arose between him and the blessed Jacob, the church of the faithful was split and became two factions. Both sides fell into incessant conflicts and struggles with one another. After Jacob’s death, those opposed to Paul unlawfully appointed another patriarch in Antioch, a man named Peter from the city of Callinicum.

Such, in brief, has been the course of these events down to the present time when these things are being written, which is the year eight hundred and ninety-two.

In Constantinople, after Epiphanius, Anthimus was appointed to the episcopate. He had previously been bishop of Trebizond, of the city of Trebizond, and was summoned to the imperial city. After he had been there for some years, Severus of Antioch was summoned from Egypt by order of Justinian, so that they might discuss unity. Through Severus’s teaching, Anthimus learned about the wrongdoing and perversity of the Council of Chalcedon and about Leo’s blasphemies in his Tome. He abandoned the throne of the imperial city, departed, and joined Severus and Theodosius of Alexandria. After him, a certain Menas, an Alexandrian, occupied the throne of the imperial city. He had been the administrator of the hospice of Samson. After completing his years, he departed from this world. He was succeeded by a young monk, the representative of Amasea, named Eutychius. After holding office for about twelve years, he was cast out and left his see. After him came John, a Syrian from the village of Sarmin in the territory of Antioch. When he took office, he deposed Eutychius, and Eutychius deposed him. After John had completed twelve and a half years, he died. Eutychius was summoned again [?] and returned to his see. The first book of the history of the church is finished. It contains forty-two chapters.
Next, the second book of the Ecclesiastical History, containing fifty-two chapters, which are as follows.

Let us now return again to the history of those bishops who endured many trials during their third imprisonment and other sufferings. We gave a little information about them, out of much that could be told, in our first book, as—as was appropriate there to the orderly sequence of these events. They had already seen that they had been deceived and that the many promises, confirmed by numerous oaths, which had been made to them to bring about unity had been broken. After twice entering into communion through deception, they were plunged into grief, mourning, and endless distress, with lamentations and bitter wailing. Then, at last, they resolved and determined that they would never again have any communion whatsoever with the adherents of two natures, even if they should face death by sword or fire. This brought fierce anger and great wrath upon them, and they were all sent into exile for the third time, each to a separate region, so that they were very far from one another. Harsh and bitter sentences were pronounced against them, as we have already related. They remained in bitter distress, deprived of their acquaintances and far from those close to them, until they even came to the point of death.

Now those bishops made an agreement among themselves and resolved and determined that they would never again have any communion whatsoever with the supporters of the council. They contended and stood courageously against the ruling power, while countless things were done and said between them in the contest of this great struggle. Then, in bitter spite, a sentence of exile was mercilessly pronounced against each and every one of them. First, Paul the patriarch was sent to the monastery called Abraham’s and imprisoned there. While imprisoned, he found some room and a little light inside his prison and began writing about what had happened in the church at the hands of John the Sirmian. But he was watched and caught writing. The document was taken from him before it was finished and brought to John. In bitter spite, John took it, brought it in, and read it before the emperor. When the emperor heard what Paul had written about him and the patriarch, and about what they had done to the orthodox community, he too was filled with great anger and became enraged against Paul. He ordered them to take the document, go to Paul, and demand that he acknowledge whether he had written it. If he acknowledged it, they were to demand—demand—that he put his signature to it, confirming that he had written it. But if he denied it and refused to acknowledge it, he was to be flogged to the point of death until he confessed, and then left in that prison.

Those who received these orders took the document and went to him at the monastery in great anger. They showed it to him and pressed him to acknowledge whether he had written these things. But, so that he would not be caught in a lie, he acknowledged that he had written it. They demanded that he write an acknowledgment in the document in his own handwriting: “I, Paul, acknowledge that I wrote with my own hand everything contained in this document.” Thus they left him imprisoned there and went away, taking the document to the patriarch and the emperor. From that time onward, threats of death hung over him. Added to this were the accusations from Rome. Both he himself and everyone else despaired of his life, and they expected that he would die a terrible death and be removed from this earthly life.

This Stephen was the bishop whom the narrative mentioned earlier, the one whom John, bishop of the imperial capital, had wanted to depose and ordain again. Stephen disputed with him and opposed him firmly and vigorously. He hurried to the emperor, crying out and complaining against John about this, so that the emperor himself rejected the proposal and severely rebuked him. He ordered a formal decree to be issued, forbidding anyone ever again to dare to engage in this unlawful and godless practice. Stephen enjoyed considerable freedom of speech with the emperor, who appointed him to go as bishop to the island of Cyprus and bestowed many honors on him.
