On his account, the emperor also granted a substantial remission of taxes on that island.

Now that Stephen had gained this freedom of speech, he presented a petition on Paul's behalf, asking that he be pardoned and released from the harsh affliction in which he found himself. Out of regard for Stephen, the emperor promised him that, if Paul would come in and receive communion with John, all the offenses he had committed would be forgiven him. Stephen went to Paul and told him this. Because of the terror of death that had gripped him, Paul gave himself up, went in, and received communion once again. He was received into the bishop's residence.

John, however, wanted to humiliate him before everyone. He arranged for many senators and Alexandrians to assemble, since Paul was Alexandrian by birth. Before them all, he had Paul receive communion from him again, supposing that this would make it impossible for him to turn back even if he wanted to.

From then on, the emperor received Paul every day and talked with him about many things, for he was a wise and knowledgeable man who had read extensively. The emperor now sought his advice on affairs of state, and often spent time with him and spoke with him privately. This alarmed John greatly: [?] he would remove him and install Paul in his place. John was now in great anxiety and fear. He began sounding out the emperor, saying, 'If you command it, my lord, let Father Paul be sent as bishop to Jerusalem or Thessalonica, since both sees are vacant.'

But the emperor, recognizing his timidity, said to him, to make him tremble still more, 'Leave Father Paul alone. We need him here.' This alarmed him even more. Now firmly gripped by this suspicion, he became bewildered. From then on, he left Paul free to depart if he wished, and left him without a guard. Those who wished could visit him, for John was considering how to give him an opportunity to escape. This is indeed what happened: Paul escaped, and John was relieved.

Now when Paul had entered and been received through Stephen, and the Synodites had consequently come to place great confidence in him, Stephen was also sent by the emperor and the patriarch, together with senators and others, to John, who was called the superintendent of the pagans and the breaker of idols. They went to the guesthouse called Eubulus's—of Eubulus [?]. After the confinement of the two in the episcopal residence, and after they had all been separated from one another, John himself had been confined there in the house for the distressed, where none of his acquaintances was allowed to see him at all.

Those who had been sent therefore came to him and said, “Our lords, the victorious emperors and the patriarch, and the patriarchs, send you their warmest greetings. They urge you to free yourself from this distress and come and join your brothers, Mar Paul the patriarch and Mar Elisha, and bring joy to them, to the merciful emperors, and to the holy patriarch. Then you can speak again about unity.”

When John heard this, under the distress and constraint of his harsh imprisonment, he was stirred with zeal and confronted those who had come to him angrily and harshly, with anathemas, insults, curses, and many other things of this kind, which seemed too excessive to be put in writing. So they left him, embittered and distressed over him.

Again, a day later, they were sent to him, appealing to him in a conciliatory manner on behalf of the emperors and the patriarch. They said, “For the sake of the unity of the church, yield yourself and come, and let us talk. Do not remain so contentious over unity.”

Again they heard from him things even harsher than the first, as he said, “God and human beings have had enough of that first unity, which was discussed and turned into apostasy, uprooting, and downfall,” along with other things of this kind.

After they had gone back and forth many times and he had neither yielded nor been persuaded by them, they finally said to him, “We know what lies ahead for you, and we hear threats of death against you: you are not going to be put to death by an ordinary death. We are distressed over you, and we speak because we want to spare you the evils you are going to suffer.”

When he heard this, he seethed with zeal and cursed them: “If only you would eat me roasted, so that I could be rid of the sight of you! Then let me be handed over to a bitter death.”

So they left him for good. Stephen himself, however, came to him alone in secret, informing him of the deadly measures that had been decreed against him. He said to him, “As for me, so that I do not see the evils that are coming upon you, I am now leaving. Look out for yourself.”

Although much happened and much was said, he could not make him relax his resolve. So Stephen left them and departed for Cyprus.

For while John was suffering the harsh and bitter distress of imprisonment, he fell into another affliction as well: the bitter pain of gout in his feet and hands. From then on he was like a dead man, unable to turn over or move a single hand or foot. He was deprived of human care, especially that of his acquaintances. Besides this, he was tormented night and day by the ordeal of various vermin. First, he was infested with countless lice, and along with these were the fleas that filled the cell in which he was imprisoned. Night and day they wore his life away. In addition, throughout the day, swarms of flies and countless mosquitoes gathered on him because of the filth of the infirmary. He was completely unable to move his hands to drive them away, and he had no one to drive them away for him.

Then a fourth ordeal, more bitter than all the others, was added to his sufferings at night: bedbugs. Throughout the night they came out in such numbers that they covered him, his entire bed, his face, and his eyes, until his face and eyes became swollen and puffy. He could not wipe them off himself. Then there was a fifth ordeal: mosquitoes. Together with the others, they fastened on him like fire throughout the night, especially on his face and wherever they could find his body exposed. He wept and wailed because of all this misery and the burning caused by these five plagues, which surrounded his whole body, inside and out. There was no one to come to his aid, either by night or by day, as he burned under all these torments from vermin.

In addition to these, Satan brought a sixth ordeal upon him: mice. They climbed up and made themselves a nest beneath the pillow under his head. All night they burrowed and squeaked beneath his head. All these afflictions were added to his imprisonment and illness, and there was no one to help.

Yet it happens that people who have never experienced these things or fallen into them even treat the written account of them as a subject for laughter and mockery. In accordance with our Lord’s words, let such people stay awake and pray that they may not enter into temptation.

Now this John, who has been mentioned, had sunk into despondency under the pressure of his trials: he was in the depths of misery, amid the burning of his whole body from all the different, tormenting vermin that were consuming him, together with the bitter pains that continued to torture him. He looked for someone to pity him, but there was no one, and for a comforter, but none was found. This was how he himself used to relate it afterward. In many letters, and also in a solemn declaration that he made to the eastern synod and to all the ranks of the faithful, he wrote about all these things, including this vision that he saw. He solemnly testified before God that he was not departing from the bounds of truth or adding a single word either to what he had suffered or to this vision that had plainly appeared to him. He spoke as follows before everyone:

“While I was being tormented by all these trials, my spirit grew distressed, I lost heart, and I despaired of my life. One day a handsome young man, wearing a beautiful white tunic decorated with [?], suddenly came in to me. I thought he was one of the attendants who cared for the sick. It was at noon, after the meal, when everyone had gone to sleep, the doors had been shut, and everything was quiet on every side. I was burning from the torment of all those different vermin, together with bitter pains. Then he suddenly came in to me and said, ‘Peace to you, father! How are you feeling? How are you? Do not be afraid.’

“Still in my despondency, I said to him out of my great distress, ‘Why do you ask me, my son, when you can see me in all this torment?’

“But that young man said to me, ‘Take heart, abba, and do not be downhearted. Give thanks to God, who has not abandoned you, for he has not forgotten your suffering.’

“I said to him again, ‘What encouragement or comfort can there be for me? Look, I am dying a bitter death, not only from the torment of the severe pains laid upon me in accordance with my sins, but also from all these vermin that surround me and are destroying me. I have no one to remember me, so that I might at least be comforted by seeing them.’

“After this he said to me, ‘We know that you are suffering and that there is no one to care for you, and especially that you are afflicted by pain and vermin. That is why I have now come in to visit you and encourage you. I also know that you are thirsty and have no one to offer you water. I will bring you something to drink. God will help you; be strong. Know that, just as all this suffering has taken hold of you, so God will also increase your reward. Do not be downhearted or lose your strength.’

“After saying these and many other things, he went outside and returned carrying a bowl of wonderful mixed drink that shone like light. He gave it to me, and I drank it with pleasure and delight. My soul was refreshed, and I gave thanks to God. I also thanked that young man for his kindness, saying to him, ‘May God have mercy on you, my son, because you have shown me this kindness: you have visited me, comforted me, and encouraged me.’ After comforting me at length, he said, ‘Tomorrow I will visit you again,’ and went away. I was so encouraged by the sight and words of that young man that all my pains and sufferings became lighter.

“The next day he came again at the same time. Once more he asked me, ‘How have you been? Be strong and do not be distressed, because you have a great reward to receive from God in return for all this suffering. You will be released from this torment, and your people will gather around you. God is with you; do not be downhearted.’ He said many other things to me as well, and then went away again.

“On the third day, although my eyes were already looking up expectantly for his arrival, he did not come. I became very distressed and was deeply sorrowful.

“On the fourth day he came again at the same time and said, ‘I know that you were distressed because I did not come to you yesterday. Do not be distressed; I will not abandon you.’ Once again, after much counsel and encouragement, he left me. In this way he continued coming and going for eight days. I marveled at the dignity, beauty, features, speech, and knowledge of that handsome young man.

“After these eight visits, when he had come and gone, the patriarch’s secretary finally came to press me. When he had said a great deal, I answered him, ‘This is in keeping with the division in your faith, that you should behave like pagans. Indeed, you are now carrying out the work of pagans: you see me in all this torment, yet you have no fear of God that would make you give me even one of my servants whom you are holding prisoner, to attend to me.’”

He related many things that had been said between them, and how he had spoken sternly to the secretary and rebuked him. The secretary left him in a burst of anger, went and brought him one of his servants, and said, “Here is your servant to look after you, so do not curse us.” Then he went out angrily and departed. Once his servant had come, that young man no longer came to him, nor did he appear to him again.

Wondering and trying to understand, since he supposed that the young man was an attendant, he said to the administrator who was in charge of him, “One of your young attendants used to come in to me, encourage me, and visit me. But now it has been several days since this servant of mine came to me, and the other one has not come again. What can have happened to him? Perhaps he has fallen ill?”

The administrator questioned him about what sort of young man he was. He told him, “He is a handsome young man, very imposing in stature. His face is bright and fair, and he wore a beautiful tunic with decorated fringes and circular designs both above and below.”

The administrator said to him, “None of the attendants has any of the features you have described to me.”

He answered him again, “You should know that for eight days he came in and out to visit me, comforting and encouraging me, and speaking to me wisely and sensibly.”

But the administrator said again, “We have no young man at all like the one you have described.” Then he went out, gathered all the young men, and brought them before him, saying, “Here are all our attendants, and we have no others. See whether he is one of them.”

After looking carefully at them all, he said, “He is not any one of these.”

Then, on hearing this, the administrator said, “A vision from God has appeared to you and visited you, abba. One of the angels or one of the saints was sent to you to strengthen and encourage you. There is no one here like the one you have described.”

John was astonished, bewildered, and full of wonder, reflecting on the words, wisdom, and sayings of that young man whose appearance was so extraordinary. He said, “I regarded him as one of the attendants. But God knows what and who he was. He helped me greatly and brought me a mixed drink in a bowl. I marveled at it, at how radiant and wonderful it was, and all my pains were relieved. I was also astonished at the wise and sound words that came from his mouth, wondering whether someone like this could be caring for the sick in your hospital. From now on, as we marvel at the kindness shown to us, we must give thanks to God, who visits everyone in his mercy. He himself knows what that young man who appeared to me was, for through his hands he visited us and gave us relief in our sufferings.”

For this John had completed twelve months and nine days imprisoned in this way, after his earlier imprisonment on two occasions in the bishop’s residence. Yet even then the malice of John of Sirmium did not abate. He gave orders, and they took him from the hospice and sent him out again to an island in the sea. There too they imprisoned him under harsh conditions, with orders that none of his acquaintances should any longer be allowed to speak with him at all. When he had completed twenty-eight months on that island as well, the chastisement from God overtook both parties—a chastisement that was terrible, astonishing, and grievous. Thus, at last, by order of Caesar Tiberius, they sent and brought him from there into the city. He then lived in the city under guard for more than three years, until the end of John of Sirmium, the persecutor.

All these things are also found in the many letters he wrote to various people, together with his vision of the young man who used to visit him. Anyone who encounters these earlier accounts and these later ones should not be surprised if he finds that they differ from one another, with omissions and additions. For he himself made use of only a few of these things, for the glory of God, while neglecting and passing over many because of their great length. In some places he made fuller use of some of the things mentioned [?], especially in certain matters [?], whether concerning the vision or the remaining events. Here too they have been written down only briefly, to serve as short reminders, rather than to recount the histories at such length that they would be considered a great burden by those who read them afterward.

Now when this Paul of Antioch was thought to have become firmly committed to the belief in two natures, John the patriarch, who had grown very weary of him, would have been glad if the idea had occurred to him to run away. He was therefore no longer kept under guard. After spending some time in the bishop’s residence, he went down one night among the people, fled, and went into hiding in a secret place. When he was wanted, he could not be found. John, afraid of the emperor, immediately went in and informed him of Paul’s escape. When the emperor heard it, he was astonished and was filled, filled, filled with anger. He ordered all the crossings to be closed and all the ships to be searched, along with all the houses along the waterfront throughout the city, and all the suburban estates and monasteries. Even tombs were opened, and they searched for him inside sacks full of corpses.

Finally, urgent letters were written to every region and city, to the bishops and governors. His identifying features were also written down so that he could be recognized and arrested, but he was not found. At last his brother, who was the count in charge of the ships, was arrested and subjected to harsh treatment. Paul himself, however, remained hidden within the city, as they say, in a cupboard built into a wall, for nine months. Afterward he came out and went into hiding in the land of Arabia, with the knowledge of the household of Mundhir son of Harith, until the time of the terrible chastisement mentioned above.

At that time, then, when everyone was gripped by fear, many were shaken by the emperor’s harsh and terrifying threats and were drawn into communion. For on the feast day the emperor had also commanded, “Anyone who does not receive communion with me must not greet me.” Many were shaken by this and were brought into communion with them, apart from just a few. These had sentenced themselves to death. In this way many were overcome by fear.

But Andrew, the treasurer mentioned above, was ardent and burning with zeal for the faith, and from his youth he had been devoted to virtuous conduct. He persevered in fasting and prayer. From the very beginning of the persecution, many of the male and female chamber attendants, and even the empress’s chief chamberlain himself, whose name was Stephen, were led by fear into communion with the supporters of the council who sided with the emperor, although they had been orthodox since the days of Empress Theodora. Andrew alone, however, stood firm and courageous, confident as he faced a struggle with death. The imperial couple themselves, together with all the other chamber attendants of both households, who wanted to please them, were drawn up against him in battle and argument. Yet he was not at all afraid of any of them, nor did he stop or slacken in his struggle against them all. Thus the emperor himself constantly addressed him with harsh and terrifying threats of death. But he did not soften a single word, yield to him, or show fear of him at all, until the emperor became furious. Once the emperor even struck him with his own hands over the liver, because he stood openly and boldly against him, exchanging words with him.

The emperor demanded that he receive communion from those who upheld the council. But he argued and resisted him, saying, “I acknowledge that you are my masters and that I am your servant. My body is in your hands, for you to do whatever you wish with it. But you have no authority over my soul, because it is in God’s hands. As for my faith, neither you nor anyone else will ever change it, because I have put my faith in God.” Along with these things, countless other words passed between them every day.

Because both the emperor and the empress loved him for his frankness and virtue, and also for his intelligence and knowledge, they were all the more eager to bring him into submission rather than expel him from their palace. Indeed, in the presence of many people, the emperor himself would say, “What are we to do with this insolent man who opposes us and will not obey us? We have no one else here with intelligence and brains like his. We do not want to dismiss him; yet there is no way to leave him as he is, refusing to obey us.” So they put up with him for a considerable time, hoping to turn him around. When he neither yielded to them nor weakened, however, they finally gave him a categorical order: “Either obey us and receive communion with us, or leave our palace.”

As soon as he saw this, he took off his official robes and threw them down before them, saying, “You have never done me a greater kindness than this: you are releasing me from serving as a slave to human beings, and enabling me to stand in the service and slavery of the one who created me and brought me into the world, and to serve him alone as his slave.” So he left the palace and went to be confined under harsh conditions in the palace called Hormisdas’s. After many days the emperor’s curator was sent to him to unsettle and frighten him, and to see whether he had weakened and would receive communion with them rather than lose his position.

The curator went and addressed him at length, admonishing, coaxing, and pleading with him. When he saw that Andrew would not weaken, he began to threaten and intimidate him, saying, “Watch yourself, or I shall be compelled to carry out against you what I have been ordered to do.” Andrew immediately bent his neck and stretched it out before him, saying, “May you not be among the living, and may God not accept your kindness, if you have not brought your sword with you! Here is my neck: cut it off! But make no mistake, either you or those who sent you: I have never had any communion whatsoever with those who divide our Lord Jesus Christ into two, nor will I ever have it—God forbid! And may God not accept your kindness if you do not immediately take off my head and allow me to depart from this miserable life.”

When the curator heard this, he went in and reported it to the emperor and empress. When they heard it, they were astonished at him and were also distressed on his account. Still hoping that he could be persuaded, they ordered him to go and be confined in the monastery called Dalmatius’s, that of Dalmatius, which held the highest rank among all the monasteries in the city and throughout its surroundings.

So they brought him out and led him away in daylight, in everyone’s sight, to inspire fear. But he was glad and joyful and gave thanks to God as they held him and he passed through the city among all the people, on his way to imprisonment for the truth of the faith. A great crowd came running to see the empress’s treasurer, who had stripped off and thrown away his worldly authority and was being led to prison for the true faith.

Everyone marveled at him, and many praised God, who had strengthened him to despise the world in this way. Many were confirmed in the faith when they saw him so joyful and glad, and they praised God. But the [?] and the others who were escorting him kept tugging at the covering on his [?], trying to cover his head. He uncovered it, saying, “It is a great honor for me to die for the truth of Christ. Let no one rob me of my honor.” So he went and was confined in that monastery for three years. Finally, after this punishment, he was released and allowed to live outside the palace.

From the days [?] of the late Empress Theodora, her aunt, the compassionate Empress Sophia too, from her youth until three years before she became empress, received communion with the Orthodox. She completely avoided all communion with the Synodites, that is, those who profess two natures. Everyone knows this openly. A priest named Andrew used to come in [?] and celebrate the Eucharist in her house, giving communion to her and all her household. When he finished the Eucharist, she would tell him to leave one pearl on the paten and put it under the veil. No one else knew who took that pearl which was left, except the patrician Sophia herself. Because of this, everyone supposed that the compassionate Justin took it secretly, and that he too avoided communion with those who profess two natures. We cannot testify to the truth of this, but have put it on record on the basis of the report and the opinion generally held.

Her entry into communion with those who profess two natures came about for the following reason. Many people were being urged to persuade the late Justinian to make Justin, his sister's son, Caesar. But he neglected the matter and put everyone off. Finally Theodore, who had been made bishop of Caesarea, went to her—God alone knows the judgment upon him for his many evil deeds—and said to her: “You should know that it is not without reason that your uncle has so far refused to listen to anyone and make his nephew Caesar. He is displeased with you because you have set yourself against him: you receive communion with those opposed to him, but do not receive communion with him. How can he bring you both to imperial rank alongside him when you appear to be opposed to him? Instead, listen to me: go and receive communion in the church. You will please the emperor, and he in turn will please you both.” And so she was persuaded by him [?], and only three years before she became empress, she received communion [?] with the Synod for many years.

These three consuls, then, whose names were John, Peter, and Eudaemon, held their bodily lives in contempt for the sake of spiritual life and the true faith in Christ. They took courage, stood firm, and openly declared that they would not share communion with those who divide Christ. Deadly anger fell upon them, and faces were turned away from them. From then on they constantly expected affliction and the loss of their estates, their houses, and everything they possessed. Although everyone had pronounced their complete destruction certain, God sheltered them, seeing that for his name and for the truth of the true faith in him they were struggling with death.

For many senators, chamberlains, and other officials had been gripped by fear over communion with the Chalcedonians. The emperor heard the complaints about the force and compulsion imposed on many people. Eventually, before the senators, he wanted to present himself as someone who compelled no one, although everyone was being subjected to force more severe than any other. God put it into his mind to say: “We have not compelled anyone, nor do we compel anyone. Those who would not agree to receive communion with us, we have left to their own choice.” This intention and declaration brought relief to these men, and they were not subjected to any trial over the matter of faith. Instead, they eventually attained high offices and great freedom to speak openly. Thus the illustrious Eudaemon became a count, count of the private estates. The illustrious John was related to Emperor Anastasius and was also the grandson of Empress Theodora. These men, together with Peter, who was himself related to the family of Peter, the patrician and curator of the empress’s estates, were eventually sent to negotiate a treaty with the Persians on behalf of the whole Roman state. They continued to hold firmly to their true faith, as they had from the beginning, with great openness.

But John the patriarch had removed their names from the diptychs. “Diptychs” is repeated here [?]. This itself brought them great joy, and they said: “Now we know that God is pleased with us and has looked upon us, so that we should not be commemorated at the Eucharistic offering of those who divide Christ into two after the true and indivisible union.”

A fierce campaign was mounted from every side against these two well-known women, together with many other women of patrician rank and others. Harsh threats breathed fire and menaced them with death. The others faltered in the struggle because of the severity of the persecution’s oppression. For the sake of their furnishings, houses, children, and estates, they were driven into communion, though only outwardly. But these two remained firm and stood ready for death, surrendering their lives to death and scorning possessions, children, and houses.

One of them, whose name was Antipatra, was the mother-in-law of John the consul, who was mentioned in the preceding account together with her daughter, Georgia, John’s wife, who was herself a woman of consular rank and zealous for the faith.

The other, whose name was Juliana, was the daughter of Magnus the consul, who had himself once been sent into exile with his sons. Juliana herself had also been with him. He was related to Emperor Anastasius. She was also the sister-in-law of Emperor Justin himself, being his brother’s wife.

After much conflict and a heroic struggle, they cast both her and Antipatra into convents across the water at Chalcedon. Strict orders were issued concerning them and sent to the convents where they were confined: if they would not agree to receive communion, their hair was to be cut off, and they were to put on the black monastic habit. They were to be required to perform all the menial work of monastic life. Indeed, even harder tasks than these were imposed on them. They were required to sweep the convent and carry out the refuse, to scrape and wash their latrines, to serve in the kitchen, and to wash lamps and jars. Other such things were harshly demanded of them.

Thus, when they could no longer endure and bear all these afflictions, they too were driven into Chalcedonian communion, though only outwardly, so that they might be released and escape the constraint of confinement in these convents—if indeed they deserve to be called convents. So they were released and returned to their houses, thereafter maintaining their former way of life. Then the time of discipline from God overtook both sides, and so there was relief for these women and for everyone.

Now this priest Sergius, who was the writer’s cell companion, together with another priest Sergius, who was also his disciple, while John was imprisoned in the cramped quarters of the hospital of Eubulus, were taken away after they had struggled many times and had been seized and imprisoned. Finally, through the treacherous betrayal of others—that is, of someone close to them who was ostensibly imprisoned with them, this betrayer who resembled Judas—he too was again seized and dragged off to the bishop’s residence. They stood up to their captors, disputed with them, and argued fiercely with them. Their captors became enraged with them, stripped them before a large crowd, stretched them out, and flogged them severely in everyone’s sight. But they could not weaken their resolve. They stood firm and struggled so vigorously and courageously that even their persecutors marveled at them. Then they took them away and imprisoned them in the deacon’s quarters, after their other earlier, harsh and oppressive imprisonments: twice in the bishop’s residence and once in the monastery called the House of Rabbula. That is, this was Sergius the cell companion mentioned above. They remained there for forty days during the harsh days of cold and frost in February.

The patriarch John would send for Sergius the cell companion and have him brought to him. He would admonish, harass, and entreat him to stay with him in his episcopal residence and become his cleric—a cleric—swearing to him, “I will not force you to receive communion with us. But because I have heard that you are a chaste man and a monk, remain with us and live as you please. But if you yield and receive communion with us, I will immediately make you bishop of whatever city you like.”

But he resisted courageously, and neither promises nor harassment could make him relax his firm adherence to the truth. When John saw his determination and that he would not yield, he sent him away and imprisoned him in the monastery called the House of Rabbula. Those monks were not corrupt in their faith like those of the other monasteries. They did not favor the Council of Chalcedon, nor did they proclaim it at all.

Now while this priest Andrew was again imprisoned outside the city wall at Phorcas, he sent clerics and Roman soldiers against him. They broke open his prison and brought him out. Pulling at him and dragging him along, they led him into the city’s main avenue. When he saw a large crowd, he began shouting, “Help! Help! People, I am a Christian, and orthodox as well! If these men who are pulling at me are not pagans, but say that they are Christians, why have they become persecutors and murderers of Christians? Why are they dragging me through your midst while you remain silent, without zeal for Christ?” He shouted many other things like these—such things he kept shouting—so that a large crowd gathered and turned upon his captors with fierce indignation, as though they would kill them. When the captors saw the anger and indignation of the whole crowd against them, they fled and hid. In this way the people rescued the blessed Andrew from them.

Eventually, however, they seized him again and sent him away to be imprisoned in the monastery of the Sleepless Monks—of the Sleepless Monks. After he had spent some time there and many things had happened, he escaped from there too. Later they again watched for him, seized him, and imprisoned him in the bishop’s residence. After much disputing, he escaped from there as well.

For although various charitable institutions for men and women could be seen in this great imperial city, there were two charitable institutions that were especially large and well known. All of them belonged to the orthodox. The first and largest was the one established by the godly Paul of Antioch. With great zeal he also founded and established charitable institutions in the great and famous cities of both East and West. In these the Lord’s saying is visibly fulfilled: “This is my rest: give rest, so that I may give rest to the weary.” Absolutely no one who accepted the Council of Chalcedon was admitted to any of them.

When this time of persecution arrived, a great, distinguished, and well-known man named Thallus was at the head of one of them. He had greatly expanded and increased this ministry through many spiritual and godly undertakings, about which there would be much to tell and write. While it was flourishing in this way, as it still does today, through the devil’s envy it was denounced before the emperor and the bishop. The accusation was that all its members opposed the Council of Chalcedon, that many monks and clergy were mixed among them, and that gatherings, assemblies, and celebrations of the Eucharist took place there. Blessed Thallus was therefore compelled to send away all the clergy and monks who were with him, so as not to give those who hated good things a pretext. Thus only the laypeople continued to carry out the ministry. When those in authority learned this, they left him alone throughout his lifetime, also out of respect for him, since they admired the man’s conduct. His life came to an end recently, in the year eight hundred and eighty-eight. After him a banker named Romanus took charge.

At this same time, a clergyman stood at the head of the other of the two charitable institutions. His name too was Comitas, and he too was zealous and virtuous. He had been a clergyman at the church of Our Lady Mary at Blachernae, at Blachernae, and had left because of the faith, together with others. He had also gathered many people together and required them to conduct themselves according to the monastic rule, while he himself attended to all their needs.

A large house was left to him as an inheritance so that there might be a charitable institution in it. This indeed came about, and the entire ministry to the poor was carried out in that house. But during the same time of persecution, he too was accused of holding assemblies. The house was taken away from him, and imperial seals—imperial seals—were hung on it. The charitable institution was uprooted from it, and he was sent into exile on an island in the sea. Everyone with him, down to the youngest, was scattered. A few of them, however, persevered and went and obtained another place for themselves. There they continued their ministry in an orderly way and bathed the poor.

As a result of this persecution, which had been stirred up in the imperial city and was being carried out so zealously, tyrannically, and unceasingly, a fierce persecution was now stirred up throughout all the territories of the Romans, wherever orthodox believers were found. Persecution was stirred up against them through letters from John the patriarch and the others. It rose like the waves of the sea, and like the Babylonian furnace with its great blaze. But unlike that furnace, it was not fueled with reeds, branches, and other materials. This one was fueled with anger, fury, and zeal for destruction and killing, and it blazed terribly and fiercely. With these came all their accompanying evils: the plundering of movable belongings and the seizure of property on this pretext; and, secondly, confinement in cramped prisons and harsh bonds, tortures, beatings, banishments, and the rest, in every region and city and their districts.

Since, then, we undertook to write only about events of which we were eyewitnesses and with whose many trials we were closely involved, being ourselves among those affected throughout the period we have described, it has nevertheless now seemed right to us to include in these records of remembrance events that happened also in Persian territory. These were recounted before many people in the capital of our Roman Empire, not by ordinary or insignificant men. Although we ourselves did not witness these events or have direct knowledge of them, and cannot testify to their truth because we were far from the places where they occurred, they were publicly recounted by the great catholicos of Dvin, the great city in Persian Armenia, and the other bishops with him. They had fled and come to seek refuge in the Christian empire, and were received with great honor by the victorious emperors. With solemn oaths, they related the following before many witnesses:

When their magi and the leading men of the Persian kingdom learned that, by the command and will of the Roman emperor, everyone throughout his dominions, in every region and city of his entire realm, was being required to submit and embrace his faith, and that he had commanded everyone who resisted and refused to obey his command and will to be persecuted, imprisoned, and stripped of their possessions, and finally put to death, they said: “Look, these things are being done throughout the territories of the Romans. Henceforth it is right for us too to act in the same way in these territories of ours, and to turn all the religions under our authority to our own religion.”

Then all the Magi gathered and said to Khosrow their king, “O king, live forever! We have learned that the emperor of the Romans demands, compels, and forces everyone throughout his dominion to adopt his religion and his faith. He demands that the many people throughout all his territories worship—worship according to his religion. Everyone who refuses to obey him he expels and drives out of his entire dominion. Let your own divinity likewise command that the same be done in your dominion: that all religions turn to your religion, and that everyone in your dominion practice your worship. Those who dare to oppose your command must not live.”

When King Khosrow heard these things from the Magi, he yielded to their words and accepted their advice. Immediately he too began with the Christians. First he sent and seized three bishops, along with many clergy and a large crowd of people [?]. He commanded them to renounce their faith and join him in worshiping fire, the sun, and the other objects of his worship. But they disputed with him and courageously stood against him, declaring, “We are Christians, O king [?]. We worship and honor God, the maker of heaven, earth, the seas, and everything in them. We will not abandon him, the creator of everything, and worship his creatures. Do not be mistaken, O king. You have authority over our bodies, to do whatever you wish to them. But our souls belong to him and are in his hands, and you have absolutely no authority over them.”

When the king heard these things, along with many other words befitting the bishops’ witness, he gave orders, and immediately they were flayed and died. He also committed many other evil acts against the Christians, and destroyed many monasteries and churches. He bound and imprisoned many people, and his heart became arrogant. He blasphemed against Christ, saying, “Let us see what Christ, the Christians’ God, will do to me! I do not know who or what he is.”

These bishops recounted these things, along with many others that the king of the Persians said and did at this time, before Armenia surrendered to the Romans. They said that for this same reason he ordered fire temples to be built throughout Persian Armenia.

After all this, the catholicos and those with him related, he sent a governor to our country, accompanied by two thousand armed horsemen. He first came to us in our city, carrying an order to build a fire temple there for the king’s worship. As the catholicos recounted: “When he showed me and the citizens the order, I burned with zeal, and I and all the citizens stood against him. We said, ‘We are servants of the King of Kings, and we pay him taxes. But we are Christians, and in matters of faith we will not submit, even if we must die for the truth of our faith. This also happened in the days of Shapur, King of Kings. He wanted to build a house of worship here, but the inhabitants of the country gathered, and there was war for seven years. Then he established a law and issued us an order that the matter of Christianity should never again be challenged or investigated.’

“We also showed him a copy of that decree of King Shapur, but he was not persuaded. Instead, following his orders, he forcibly set about marking out the site, digging, and laying foundations. He began building, while also making vigorous preparations for battle. Although I pleaded with him at length, he would neither listen to me nor pay me any attention at all. Finally, I sent word of this everywhere, to all the inhabitants of the country. When they heard, they burned with zeal for their faith in Christ. They all gathered as one man, about ten thousand armed for battle, ready either to live or to die for Christ, and absolutely determined not to allow a house of Magian worship and paganism to be built in their country.

“When all the nobles and leaders of the country had gathered, we went with them to that governor, to the place where he had begun building the fire temple. We spoke with him at length, standing against him and saying, ‘We are Christians and subjects of the King of Kings. But in matters of faith we cannot and will not submit to human beings. Even if the king himself comes, a house of pagan worship will never, ever be built in our country before we have all died. Instead, leave the country without war or bloodshed, and go to the king. Tell him of our firm resolve concerning our faith. He is free to do whatever he decrees. For until we have all died, we will not allow a house of Magian worship to be built in our country.’”

After they had spoken at length with one another, the governor, who was preparing to build as he had been ordered, argued with the inhabitants of the country and warned them, saying, “See! You are opposing the command of the King of Kings and insulting him. He will order a terrible death for you. Consider what you are doing!”

But when the governor saw their readiness and their preparations to oppose him, and saw also that they were stronger than he was, he departed, threatening and warning them. In great anger he went and reported all these things to the king. When the king learned of them, he was stirred to anger and became fiercely enraged. He sentenced all the inhabitants of the country to death and sent fifteen thousand troops against them with the governor. He ordered that, if they opposed his command, they should be put to the sword, and that the sanctuary of the fire temple should be built there.

When the inhabitants of the country learned of this, they all gathered together, about twenty thousand, prepared for battle and ready to fight to the death for their Christianity. When the troops arrived and all drew up against them for battle, the inhabitants called upon the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and went out against them. Christ shattered the troops before the inhabitants of the country, and they put every one of them to the sword, to the last man. They killed the governor, took his head, and carried it to the patrician Justinian, who was then stationed on the frontier in the city of Theodosiopolis. All these things happened, as did the other events that followed; to give an account and narrative of them now would take a long time.

For when these things happened, and all the people of Greater Armenia saw that a fierce war had been stirred up against them by the wicked kingdom of the Persians, the whole country united as Christians. They hurried to seek refuge in the Christian empire, saying, “From now on we are servants of the Christian empire, and we have hurried to seek refuge in the Roman Empire, so that it may deliver us from the savagery of the religion of the Magi.” The catholicos and the other bishops with him recounted these things, along with many others, before our merciful emperors and before the entire senate. We have made use of only brief accounts of some of them. They spoke of the battles and the great devastation that had occurred there at various times, and of how the armies afterward clashed again, and how the Persians were defeated many times and their elephants were captured. For the present, however, we leave these things aside because they are so numerous.

All these things, then, together with many others, were recounted in our Roman imperial capital by the catholicos of Dvin, in the land of Persian Armenia. He, the bishops, and the many nobles with him recounted them before many people. When he arrived with the other bishops and some of the leading men of Armenia, they were all received with great honor. They received imperial gifts and honors, and [?] high offices were granted to all who had come with him from there, along with large houses and imposing imperial residences. Much gold and appointments to office were also sent to those in the country itself, together with a three-year remission from the Roman emperor. Orders were given to assist them and fight the Persians on their behalf and on behalf of the whole land of Armenia, while holding the country. This continued for a long time, and the people of the Magi fell before the Christians many times when they attacked them. These wars continued for six years. As for what happened afterward, we will recount a little of the many events when we reach their time. The catholicos himself, after two years, died in the imperial capital and did not return to his country.

From the very beginning of the arrival of the catholicos of Armenia and the other bishops and leading men with him, as people who had fled the wicked and pagan kingdom of the Magi and had come to seek refuge in the Christian empire, immediately upon entering and being received and greatly honored, they entered into communion with the patriarch of the city, confidently and without making any inquiry. They were unaware of the cause of the division and dispute that existed throughout all the churches of the territories of the Roman Empire because of the wrongdoing of the council held at Chalcedon. When this became known in their own country, the other bishops and all their countrymen became angry with them. They wrote harsh things to them, which the circumstances require us to pass over in silence. So they withdrew and separated themselves. From then on, they all held their own assembly together in one of the large residences that had been granted to one of their leading men. There they used to gather in a large congregation after the death of their catholicos.

Now, as we consider how many things have happened in our times and days, especially recently, and how they exceed all bounds and written accounts, especially the events following the surrender of Persian Armenia to the Romans, which took place in the year 880 of Alexander: how, because of this, continual and frequent wars broke out on every side, the sword devoured, and much blood was shed; and how, again, the Magian grew proud in his cunning and attacked the Roman forces in Armenia, hoping to destroy and annihilate them. When he could not accomplish this, he turned away from them and crossed into Roman Armenia, hoping to conquer Caesarea in Cappadocia and take its people captive. But when the armies surrounded him and checked his advance from Cappadocia as well, they turned and attacked him. They carried off absolutely all his baggage, and he returned in disgrace. Had the commanders agreed with one another, he would not even have returned alive.

And how, again, the emperor of the Romans enriched and exalted the Armenians—Armenia [?]—with gifts, grants, military appointments, and military service; and how, again, all Persian Armenia surrendered, was conquered, and was occupied—surrendered, was conquered, and was occupied [?]—by the Romans. Although they had often distinguished themselves, won victories, and conquered other powerful peoples, in the end, because of their commanders’ bad management, or because they had angered God in many ways, the entire Roman army trembled and fled before a single contemptible marzban who did not have even thirty thousand men with him, although they themselves numbered no fewer than a hundred thousand. They lost their weapons and horses and were put to shame.

After these things, the Persian grew proud and powerful, took possession of all Armenia, and conquered it. The whole country asked him for a pledge, and he gave it to them. In turn, the whole country surrendered to him, apart from those of its people who were in Constantinople, after a period of seven years during which they had rebelled against him and fought with him.

And how, again, after these things, high-ranking envoys of both kingdoms were sent to examine the matters that had caused conflict between the two kingdoms and also to discuss peace once more. This indeed took place. For more than a year they sat facing one another, discussing, examining, and arguing with one another, without accomplishing anything. At first the Persian demanded that he receive gold and make peace. In response to this, the emperor of the Romans rose up boldly, saying, ‘This man demands gold from us as though from someone who fears him and is subject to him. Let him know that, as long as we live, he will not receive a single mina, not even what he has been receiving from us until now. Unless he acts with the equal honor of one kingdom toward another, we will not make peace with him.’ In the end, the Persian came around even to this, but nothing came of it.

Along with these were many other similar things, whose histories many books could not contain, and the remaining events concerning wars, the world, and the church. Because they were so numerous, we have left some of them out.

At this time, then, the power and fulfillment of the apostolic teaching were fittingly seen in action—the teaching that says, “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the injustice and wickedness of human beings who suppress the truth through injustice,” and so on. For at this time Christians, on frivolous pretexts, stirred up harsh and severe persecutions against Christians, without mercy and entirely without fear of God. They acted savagely and barbarously, not as Christians, resembling a lion roaring to destroy, and a lion’s cub sitting in hiding. For this reason the Lord rose up before them and brought them to their knees, as was openly revealed and made known before everyone’s eyes.

These people dealt with their own flesh and blood—that is, with the whole community of the orthodox—with every kind of lawless cunning and angry zeal, rather than in a peaceful, just, and Christian manner. They stirred up fierce, merciless persecutions and ordered God’s servants—elderly, sick, weak, and respected men—to undergo bitter imprisonment in dark, cramped conditions. They decreed cruel banishments, entirely devoid of the fear of God, ordering that those whom they arrested and imprisoned should be tormented by hunger, thirst, and deprivation of contact with their acquaintances. They threatened those in the places to which the exiles were sent, requiring them to treat the exiles without mercy and to oppress them by every possible means, so that, under compulsion, harsh afflictions, and trials, they would be forced to submit to their oppressors’ will. Others they coerced, subdued, and enslaved according to their wishes. They even unlawfully, and entirely outside canonical order, annulled the priesthood of orthodox men who had held it for many years, and made them priests and bishops all over again. There were many other things of this kind, which we have too little time to recount.

As became known, not even God’s justice bore and endured these things. Instead, swiftly and speedily, a sentence of judgment and wrath was sent from heaven against all this cruelty and savagery—that is, against those who practiced it without the restraints imposed by the fear of God. It was sent against John the patriarch and against the emperor who was incited by him and whom he instructed to do these things. Both were struck by a single rod of wrath, and both received the same sentence of being handed over to evil spirits. There were also many other terrible and shameful things that happened in the meantime, which, out of respect for the priesthood and the imperial office, we will for the moment cover with silence. For no short time these things were done, displayed, and spoken through each of them by the demons to whom each had been utterly handed over. Though these things are very terrible and grievous, they are not false, according to the testimony of all the people of these times.

After the terrible chastisement that had been sent upon the bishop and the king, Bishop John himself, through the activity and prompting of the one who was working within him, prepared all the more to persecute the faithful. Every day he prepared savage and harsh threats against them from every side, without understanding or orderly thought. Although he was repeatedly afflicted by an evil spirit, he acted in such a way that the righteous Judge would become still angrier with him and send upon him yet another internal affliction and pain in his bowels, together with the bitter pain of gout. From then on he was tormented beyond healing, and every day pain upon pain and affliction upon affliction were added to him. Although many physicians gave him a great deal of care, no relief or improvement at all could be seen in him.

But just as the magicians before Pharaoh acknowledged, “This is the finger of God,” so he too now recognized, even if only under compulsion, the chastisement that had been sent upon him from heaven. With choking tears he began to say to the physicians, “Why, my sons, do you still wear yourselves out over wretched me? You cannot heal my afflictions, because all these afflictions have been sent upon me from heaven by a righteous sentence, because I provoked God's anger. Human beings cannot heal them. Only now have I understood and realized that, just as I struck many people without mercy, so now I alone have received merciless blows from that One.”

Some time before, the physicians had stopped treating him, as he himself had urged them to do, since he could no longer take any food. Even if he drank mixed drinks, he would quickly vomit them up. In the end, even his internal organs began to break apart and pass out of him. His torment was not only very bitter and severe but also prolonged. Weeping over himself, he would say before many people, “I know, my Lord, that I have done evil before you. The curses of your servants, elderly and honored men, have overtaken me and stirred up your anger against me, because I treated them without mercy.”

From the first year of his persecution onward, he was continually chastised and could not lift his head. Yet even so, he did not desist from the harshness of his schemes. Finally, after severe weakness and all this bitter torment had racked him for about two years, he departed this life, in the thirteenth year of the reign of King Justin, still suffering from those illnesses. Although he received relief from time to time, he was repeatedly chastised again until the day of his death.

We have already touched briefly above on the subject of this chapter. Now, however, we must show the just sentence of God, who has shown that deeds receive their recompense not only at the judgment to come, but already here.

John of the imperial city, who was mentioned above, was possessed by savage impetuosity and was [?] with frivolity and restlessness like a young boy. He was also crazed and drunk with power. As he persecuted and seized monasteries and also the churches of the orthodox Church, he took down and removed all the portraits of the orthodox fathers, and set up and installed his own portraits everywhere. While he had no thought of dying, the end of his life suddenly overtook him. Eutychius, who had previously been removed, was summoned and came in, taking his place.

When John had died and Eutychius had been summoned and had come in, Eutychius, at the emperors’ urging, let all their former disputes drop and disregarded them. But he erased and removed John’s own portraits, which were numerous everywhere, from the episcopal residence and from all the churches, down to the individual ones that had been overlooked and were found here and there. Indeed, in all the cities and episcopal sees, when people learned Eutychius’s wishes, they erased all John’s portraits, both paintings and panel portraits, so that they would not be accused. They raised and installed portraits of Eutychius, as we have said, even down to the small ones that had been left scattered about.

God repaid Abimelech for the evil he had done—he killed, and they killed [?] his brothers, seventy men, on one stone. In the same way, this became a cause of astonishment, amazement, and wonder to everyone: how quickly God repaid John already here, and how he was treated just as he had treated others. The Lord brought Nabal’s recompense back upon his own head. Thus John’s portrait was erased after his death, just as he himself had dared to take down the portraits of the saints and put up his own. He occupied his throne for approximately thirteen years.

This Theodulus, a deacon of the church, had appeared from his youth to be gentle, humble, and quiet, so that many regarded him as virtuous. When he gained access to Emperor Justinian, and the emperor saw his gentleness and quietness, he entrusted him with a great deal of gold to distribute to the poor, prisoners, and monasteries around the city and throughout all the regions. He would even give him hundred-pound sums of gold and send him to distant places to distribute them. Thus, little by little, he too amassed hundred-pound sums for himself. [?] Justin, in turn, continued to trust him in the same way. When the persecution broke out, seeking to curry favor in his capacity as a trusted man, he joined John and the others in inflicting many evils on the whole community of the faithful. He himself would first be sent to the monasteries, where he misled many with deceitful oaths, only to be caught lying in the end. Thus he clothed himself in an angry zeal, even greater than John's, on behalf of the council and the entire heresy of the two natures. With authority he seized, imprisoned, and tortured people as he pleased. He slandered all the faithful before both the emperor and the patriarch, stirring them to fierce anger. He received orders and authority and used them however he wished. Indeed, John himself was considerably afraid of him and kept out of his way. He had also received authority over all the Arians everywhere.

While he too was thus rising in prominence and engaging in persecution, God sent severe afflictions upon him as well, so that he could no longer walk upright. Yet he continued to act insolently and pursue the persecution with furious zeal. His own relatives, those of his wife, and his secretary, together with others, boarded a boat to cross the sea. Their boat sank, and they drowned in the sea; only two or three of them escaped. After this loss and disaster that overtook him, his wife also died. He himself became bedridden with a severe illness and suffered for three years. Under the distress of these severe afflictions, he now confessed with bitter tears, saying, 'Woe to me! The curses of the persecuted have overtaken me, and the cry of those whom I oppressed has come before God. All this illness has been sent upon me in anger from heaven.'

A short time before, moreover, some incident had occurred in which he offended his treasurer, who had charge of everything he possessed. The treasurer went in secretly and informed the emperor about the hundred-pound sums of gold he possessed. This, at least, was what was said; we ourselves do not know for certain. There were twenty-four or thirty of them. After the emperor had secretly sent and taken them, he sent for Theodulus and said to him, 'Since we need money to spend on the wars, deacon, if you have two or three hundred-pound sums of gold, give them to us, and we will repay you.' But he said to him, 'My lord, where would I get hundred-pound sums of gold?' He said to him, 'By my life and my salvation, have you none?' But he denied it and swore that he did not possess even one hundred-pound sum. Then the emperor gave an order, and the hundred-pound sums were brought in, together with his treasurer. The emperor said to him, 'Do you recognize these? How could you swear falsely by us and by God? Your shame is enough for you. Get out of here!'

Thus, like the shame of a thief when he is caught, he went out in disgrace and hid himself for shame. He became an object of reproach and contempt to everyone who encountered him. When this disgrace was added to all his illness, he was left prostrate and laid low from that time onward, and remains so even now.

For this quaestor of the emperor was himself also of Samaritan descent. When the Samaritans in Palestine were tried by Photius, they made him [?]. Proceedings were brought against him, and he came to the emperor. He ran here and there and bribed people on every side; the proceedings were covered up, and no investigation was made against him. He too was a bitter enemy and adversary of all the faithful. He threatened them harshly, accused them, and continually stirred up trouble against them, taking the place of John the patriarch when he was away. Whenever John came in, the two of them would agitate the emperor. When the emperor summoned them and accepted what they said, he would become enraged and issue dreadful, harsh orders against the party of the faithful. For, as everyone knew, he continually received no small amount of gold from John. He was an adviser and instigator of every evil, like his accursed teacher Aetherius, who had been removed from office and with whom he had formerly been in league [?]. He was eager to follow in that man's footsteps in everything.

But justice could no longer bear [?] this man's wickedness either. Although he presented himself as a Christian, like the pagans and Samaritans he secretly struck at Christians by every means and on every pretext, using his authority as a justification. He was bound in a secret conspiracy with the rest of the hidden pagans to destroy the unity of the church. When God saw the deceitfulness of his schemes, and that he thought he could deceive God and human beings, he exposed his deceit before the eyes of the whole church in its fullness.

On the day of the veneration of the holy cross of our Savior, when it had been brought out and set up in the Great Church, the whole senate and the entire city gathered to venerate it. The quaestor entered with the senate to make an outward show that he too was a worshiper. As the ranks stood in order and approached in turn, he reached the holy cross. Before he could bow down, a demon entered him, lifted him up, and dashed him to the ground before the holy cross, which he had approached to venerate deceitfully rather than sincerely, making a mockery of Christianity. He began foaming at the mouth, writhing under the demon's torment, struggling violently and crying out for a long time. Finally the patriarch gave orders, and a number of men gathered around, picked him up, carried him inside, and threw him into an inner room in the church.

The whole church in its fullness cried out, “Lord, have mercy,” for a long time. They marveled at the exposure of this man's fraud and at the rebuke that the Lord of the cross had administered to him in full view of the great crowds. Terror fell upon many who were deceivers and hypocrites. He himself never raised his head again. He lived for about another year and a half, more or less, tormented in this way by that demon, and so departed from this present life.

Now, when those who held authority, whether secular or ecclesiastical, had chosen and approved this course—to uproot the meeting places of the faithful and overthrow their altars—shortly afterward, at that very time, the long-haired barbarian people called the Avars made their preparations and advanced against the city as far as the outer wall. All the churches throughout the land of Thrace were plundered, and their communities went into exile before them along with the whole country. Their altars were stripped and uprooted, and the altar canopies were torn down and brought low, right up to the city wall.

Some of them, recognizing the judgment of justice, said, “What the members of our own party unjustly did to those who do not agree with us, uprooting their churches—look, God has now done it to us in his anger! Our own churches too have been uprooted and thrown into confusion.” Everyone marveled at these things and praised God, who repays everyone according to their deeds.

After the death of Patriarch John, Eutychius, who had held office before him, was summoned from his monastery in Amasea, in the northern region. He entered the city and was received with great ceremony by the emperors and the whole city. Great things were also being reported about him: that he performed miracles and worked mighty deeds. The whole city rejoiced at his arrival, as though they had found relief from all John's falsehood, deceit, and [?], which had been quite disorderly. For he was a young man and had been one of the lawyers. Only a short time before, he had been tonsured and become a cleric, and then suddenly became bishop of the imperial city. Yet he had not changed from his youthful ways or from any of the ways of the lawyers.

Eutychius, however, was a modest monk. Before his removal, he had occupied the throne of the imperial city for twelve years. After he left, John in turn occupied it for twelve years and had also entered his thirteenth. Thus Eutychius returned, intending not to sit on his throne before he had anathematized John and abolished his commemoration from God's church.

Now, after John of Sirimis died and Eutychius was summoned and returned, the archdeacon of Rome spoke before the emperor with great boldness, saying: "Let Your Clemency know that, according to the canons and ecclesiastical regulations, if John was patriarch and acted in every respect as patriarch throughout his life, Eutychius is not patriarch and cannot possibly enter the church and occupy the throne. But if, on the other hand, Eutychius is accepted and enters as patriarch and occupies the throne, John and everything done by him stand outside the entire church. Everything done by him is invalid: whether the appointment of a bishop or any of his other ordinations, whether he administered baptism or consecrated a church or an altar, together with all his other acts, they are annulled and invalid. His very name must likewise be erased, and he must be publicly excluded from God's church and removed from every rank of the priesthood. This is especially so because the two of them deposed and anathematized one another from the church, together with all who commune with them. According to the canons, one of them is deposed and without authority—without authority and excluded from the church."

When the archdeacon said all these things before the emperor, and said that the pope of Rome would accept no other arrangement, he was harshly rebuked and told to be silent and disregard the strict application of the canons. So he fell silent and let the matter go. The order prescribed by the canons was trampled underfoot and transgressed.

Although everyone had thought that Eutychius would undertake a major inquiry when he was summoned and returned, their wrongdoing came back upon their own heads: he went up and sat on the throne without dispute. Both parties, together with those who commune with them, drank and drained the murky dregs of their mutual anathemas—that is, John's and his own—just as they had pronounced them. Everyone was seized with amazement at these things.

When Eutychius returned and took possession of the see, he neglected the canonical inquiry, fearing that some opposition might arise against him through it and that he might lose his good fortune. Nevertheless, he showed his hatred and resentment toward John by ordering all his portraits to be torn down and removed from the episcopal residence, which John himself had magnificently rebuilt after its destruction by fire. His portraits were erased and torn down, both there and everywhere else. The proclamation of his name was being suppressed, until the emperor took exception to this abolition of his name. Eutychius expelled and humbled all John's associates and relatives, and poured insults and abuse upon him. Everyone who wanted to please Eutychius, seeing his lack of restraint, would abuse John in his presence, and he listened with pleasure. In the end he went so far in this madness as to say openly before everyone: "John was not bishop of Constantinople. He was merely keeping my place, while he himself was an outsider."

Everyone who heard this mocked it, knowing that Eutychius himself had gone out and been cast aside, and that John had succeeded him, occupied the see, and carried out his deposition.

For while Eutychius was away in exile in his monastery, he extracted and compiled books of excerpts, supposedly as proof from the Fathers, teaching a quaternity instead of the Holy Trinity, after the manner of the Council of Chalcedon and Leo’s wicked Tome. That is, he too taught as they did, saying, “There are two natures in Christ, even after the union. This is also what all the Fathers confess.” Thus, immediately after he returned and took his seat on his throne, he began eagerly and diligently sending his books to all the leading men and prominent women, urging them to read and understand them and to confess two natures. He sent these writings with particular eagerness to those who took offense at the confession of two natures and who, together with all the Fathers, confessed one incarnate nature. When many read them and were appalled at his foolishness, including his own bishops and others, the whole city began to be disturbed. In particular, all those who had not drunk from the murky dregs of Nestorius’s gall complained bitterly against him, especially his own bishops. Eventually they were stirred to great agitation and uproar against him, gathering at the bishop’s residence and saying to him, “You should know that unless you withdraw your books and abandon this opinion, you are creating a schism in the church of God, even among us, your own people.” So he withdrew his books, and the disturbance ceased, although he persisted in his opinion.

After this, the overbearing Eutychius, who by birth had originally belonged to the heresy of the Sabbatians, did not delay in throwing himself into another pit, that of those who deny the resurrection of bodies. Wickedly and eagerly, he embraced this teaching too, openly professing and teaching it, saying, “These human bodies do not come to the resurrection. Rather, other bodies, newly created, are the ones that rise at the resurrection.” He did not teach these things merely by word of mouth, but also composed written discourses and published them publicly. He persisted in disputing about these matters. Because of this, disturbance, complaint, insults, and abuse were again stirred up against him throughout the city, especially among his own people and those who shared his faith. They said to him, “Unless you stop this teaching, we will all anathematize you.” Even so, they did not turn him from his opinion. He merely stopped teaching it, while everyone regarded him as a heretic and a madman.

Through vain presumption, Eutychius had become filled with hatred and implacable hostility toward the entire body of the faithful. He pursued them and set his face toward wiping them out and destroying them. Church advocates, excubitors, Roman soldiers, clerics, candidati, and others would fall upon each one of them during their services like brigands and barbarians, not like Christians. They would seize them, pull them about, and drag them away, overturn their altars, throw down their offerings, and spill their consecrated elements. They plundered and carried off their liturgical equipment and all the other utensils they could find for their use, as well as their books. They even carried off their clothing and footwear, and whatever money they had for their needs. They disdained absolutely nothing they found, but plundered, seized, and stole it. Finally, they would drag them away, together with everyone they found with them, and take them off to prison. There they would hand over what they had and what they did not have, and only then would they get out. In this way they seized one congregation after another every day. When many reproached them for throwing down and trampling on the Christians’ Eucharistic offering like pagans, they eventually began throwing it into the fire and burning it. All these evils continued without restraint, until no congregation could be found meeting openly anywhere in the city.

The cause of all these evils, then, was a certain Probinus, a slave of Andrew. When the persecution began, Andrew, who had been the empress’s treasurer, left the palace and his post for the sake of the true faith. His possessions were seized, and he was imprisoned in the monastery of Dalmatius, [?], and was not released. He had this barbarian as a slave, and had himself brought him up and diligently taught him to read and write. He was trusted throughout his household. But in the end he rebelled against him and went over to Eutychius, who appointed him as an informer and [?] and [?] against all the clergy and all the religious communities. To bring misery upon his master, he would take church advocates, imperial guards, Roman soldiers, and clerics with him, and go around dragging everyone away and taking them to prison. First they would plunder them barbarously, seize their possessions, and take everything they had. From many they also took large amounts of gold. Even if someone had, so to speak, gone into a hole and hidden himself, this man would cunningly get inside, seize him, rob him, and imprison him. He became a trial and an adversary to all the clergy, all the religious communities, and all the faithful in the imperial city, including us along with the rest. The evils this man inflicted upon the whole church of the faithful are beyond recounting and too endless to relate.

These sisters, then, were sisters by birth. While they were still little girls, their mother died, and their father placed them in a convent. He too died and left them—that is, their convent—everything he owned. As time passed, they grew up and reached adulthood. Then the persecution under John overtook them, and afterward the persecution under Eutychius. When they were pressuring the whole convent to receive communion from them, they seized some of the sisters and distributed them among convents in the city.

These two sisters, however, stood firm like adamant, especially the older one. They subjected her to every kind of torture and affliction, confining her in cramped quarters and making her suffer hunger and thirst. But she grew still stronger, more radiant, and more fervent in faith. She rebuked and reproached all the women in whose convent she was confined, saying, “You, all your priests, and all who share your views are strangers to the Holy Trinity, since you hold to a quaternity in its place, together with the Council of Chalcedon. That council outwardly anathematizes Nestorius, but in practice and in truth it holds to his faith and, like him, confesses two natures. You are with it, along with everyone who agrees with it.”

Thus she defeated them all. They went to the bishop with complaints, crying out, “Unless you order this affliction to be removed from us, you should know that we will all leave our convent. We cannot endure her insults, her reproaches, and her arguments.”

So he sent word to the exarch of the convents to send for her, put her on trial, and have her tortured. They were to take her away and place her in another convent, harsher than that one, and the women there were to be ordered to torment her until they subdued her.

When the exarch’s visitor went to her and they began accusing and threatening her, she boldly laughed at them, mocking them and saying, “What is this, you pagans and murderers? Are you threatening me, a weak woman? If you have come only to threaten me and do not kill me, as is your custom and that of the man who sent you, you are not men, nor do I count you among the living.”

Then they angrily beat her with a stick as though she were a camel. But she mocked them still more, anathematized them, and called out to them, “Woe to you, pagans, persecutors, and murderers of Christians!” She challenged them to kill her, saying, “You are pagans, not Christians. Christians do not persecute Christians. You yourselves show that you are pagans, and you yourselves display the deeds of your paganism.”

When these men too were defeated by her, they dragged her away and confined her in another convent, ordering the women there to torture her severely. After she had spent only a few days there, these women too began crying out and fleeing from her. In this way they put her in many convents, but they could not overcome her strength.

Eutychius ordered, “Bring her here to the church.” When the members of the exarch’s household heard this, they went in and said to Eutychius, “You should know, my lord, that if she comes to you, unless you cut out her tongue or take off her head, there is no insult or mockery that she will not hurl in your face. When she is beaten and flogged, she only does it all the more, since she is ready to be killed and eager for death.”
