Finally, they brought her into the church. Many people took turns confronting her and heaped threats and intimidation upon her, but she mocked them all as though they were lifeless corpses. She rebuked them at length, until they had all been defeated by her on every side. At last they released her to return to her convent.

Thus she became the means of deliverance for her whole convent, since they no longer attacked its sisters. Shrinking back from her struggles, they said, “If one sister from that convent stood firm through all these struggles and did not give way, who could overcome their strength if they all joined together?”

Now the powerful Eutychius, as in other matters, presumptuously contrived to present himself as a teacher. He plotted to abolish and invalidate the original order of the churches’ services and to establish and impose his own destructive work, which he wrote out on sheets on Maundy Thursday and sent to all the churches. He ordered that the original hymn should be discontinued and his own used instead, threatening and intimidating those who dared to use the earlier one and leave his aside. This agitated and disturbed not only the clergy of all the churches and the monastic communities, both men’s and women’s, but also the whole city and the entire senate. Matters reached the point where a great uprising against him nearly broke out, not only among the churches and monasteries but throughout the city. These things were even brought to the emperor’s attention by some members of the senate.

The bishop himself, meanwhile, hurried in to the emperor in a furious rage to complain to him about these matters. The emperor then rebuked him severely, saying, “How much longer will you refuse to restrain yourself and remain quiet? Look, you have agitated and disturbed the whole city! How can you change their ancient customs? Watch out, or they will stone you!”

He said to him, “My lord, I composed something of my own that is much more suitable than the earlier one.”

The emperor said to him, “Understand that even if you had brought your hymn down from heaven, they would absolutely refuse to accept it. Go and stay in your church, and adhere to what the ancient fathers established in it.” In this way he restrained his impetuosity, and his threats ceased and fell silent.

Now this John, who was called “the one in charge of the pagans,” and who was bishop of Ephesus, after all the trials, imprisonments, persecutions, and exiles he had endured, was finally required to surrender the charter of an estate that had been given to him by Callinicus, the praepositus, the emperor’s chief chamberlain and a patrician. When John received it, he spent considerable sums on it and renovated it. He built a church there, constructed three cisterns, and designated it a monastery. When persecution arose under John, he took from him the monastery he had established, installed Chalcedonians in it, and banished him to an island in the sea.

When John died and Eutychius took office, he demanded that he surrender his deed of gift for the estate and the rest of his documents concerning it. Nor did he demand only these, but also the liturgical vessels, books, and other belongings. After persecution and affliction lasting many days, he seized him and confined him in prison, demanding and taking from him all the documents concerning the estate. While he was imprisoned, he assembled against him the whole body of church advocates, together with laymen, who brought proceedings against him concerning the liturgical vessels and the other things.

But he was strengthened by grace and said to them, “What liturgical vessels, then, and what belongings are you demanding? The things that you or others gave there? Whoever gave me liturgical vessels has the right to come and demand them back from me. For look, you have unjustly and forcibly taken all the legal documents concerning the estate that were found in my possession, without any fear of God. Read them and see whether the name ‘monastery’ occurs in them, and whether it is written in them that I received liturgical vessels. Yet this is what I am being required to surrender! For I did wrong in designating it a monastery. Otherwise, it was not even a monastery.”

In this way, with God’s help, he refuted them, and they all stopped pressing him about these matters. They did, however, demand and take from him five bread allowances, which he had purchased for three hundred darics—darics—saying, “You purchased these in the monastery’s name.” While he was in prison, he handed over the estate, and then he was released and escaped the affliction of imprisonment.

The story of Paul, then, deserves great sorrow. He was a clear-minded, quiet, humble, and blameless man, who had long lived, like Jacob, in the tent of his monastery in the region of Caria. When John of Sirmium learned about him, he immediately sent to Asia, had him brought in bound and shackled in irons, and confined him under harsh conditions in his episcopal residence. Through these bonds and many torments, he forced him to submit to him and receive communion from him. Out of regard for his gray hair and the man's dignity, he did not reveal the deceit in his heart or what he had planned against him. But after subjecting him and showing himself well disposed toward him, he sent him to the bishop of Aphrodisias. He wrote—he wrote to the bishop of Aphrodisias [?]—saying, “Depose this man from his episcopate and ordain him again. Appoint him in the city of Antioch, which is under your authority.”

When the bishop received Paul and the letters, he immediately seized him, while Paul remained unaware of their deceit. He said to him, “The patriarch has instructed me to depose you from your episcopate and ordain you again.” When Paul heard this, he began to wail and said, “You people, you are pagans! For many years now I have been ordained and have been a bishop. I was ordained by three bishops, according to the order prescribed by the canons. Why, then, am I now being deposed contrary to the canons and wickedly ordained again? If you are undoing my priesthood and ordaining me again, then first undo my baptism too, and baptize me again!”

They were not persuaded, but instead became filled with anger against him. They seized him tyrannically and forcibly, deposed him, and ordained him again. He struck his face, and his eyes grew dark and he became blind. From then on he wept, lamented, and wailed over himself, seeking a way to flee to the refuge of repentance. Thus the end of his life overtook him, and his old age went down to Sheol in anguish, sorrow, and misery. His case, however, remains reserved for the righteous Judge.

John's advisers took a written declaration and composed it as though it came from Paul himself. They put the following into it:

“I, Paul, who was formerly astray and lost, have come to understand the true faith. I have turned back and come willingly, of my own free choice, without compulsion or force, to the Church of God, to you yourself, my lord John, the ecumenical [?] patriarch. In this document I acknowledge that I accept the council of the six hundred and thirty holy fathers who assembled in the city of Chalcedon, and the letter of the holy and blessed pope of Rome, in accordance with the confession of Peter, chief of the apostles, until my last breath. [?] May I never again turn back or depart from it. I have acknowledged these things and confirmed them with my own hand.

“I, Paul, bishop, acknowledge that I agree with and accept everything written in this declaration.”

They then presented this to him for his signature, without allowing him to read it and discover what they had falsely and deceitfully written in his name, as though it came from him. And without fear of God, they bore false witness against him.

This Deuterius was hardworking and upright in his conduct. From the days of his youth until his old age, for a full thirty-five years, he labored with John, who was making disciples of the pagans in the regions of Asia, Caria, Phrygia, and Lydia. Together with him he established ninety-nine new churches and twelve monasteries. John relied on him and trusted him more than the others. He also appointed him bishop of the orthodox in the region of Caria and made him his successor, since he himself had grown old and advanced in years and had fallen into the struggle of persecution. He placed him over all the churches and monasteries, and Deuterius labored, visited them, and sustained them all until the end of his life, which took place in the imperial city. With the help of divine grace, Deuterius ran the course of the struggles of his ministry vigorously, diligently, and courageously. Although the supporters of the council pursued him to seize him, do to him what they had done to Paul, and appoint him in Paul's place in Antioch, the Lord did not deliver him into their hands. Thus he completed his struggle and departed in a good old age.

This congregation, then, consists of those who oppose the discourse that Theodosius of Alexandria composed while he was in the imperial city against the two heresies, namely those of the Tritheites and the Sabellians. They take offense at certain statements in it and suppose that he too introduces a numerical distinction between substances and natures. For this reason they separate themselves and assemble on their own, although they have neither a leader nor anyone to ordain priests for them. They have often sought to be united with the faithful, and discussions have indeed been held with them. Some of them were united—those who had the understanding to judge rightly. Others, however, without understanding, foolishly and without any valid reason, persisted in their cunning ways.

These Cappadocian monks, then, at the height of the persecution, as I also mentioned in the earlier account, were persecuted and driven out of the great and mighty monastery in Cappadocia called Gordison. They numbered no fewer than seventy men, venerable and zealous elders. They built and established many places, but were repeatedly driven from one place to another. They went and found a place that was good, secure, and suitable in every respect for their dwelling, called Kardonian. It was near the hot springs called Pythia, across the water to the south of the imperial city. A certain chamberlain who was a believer bought it for them, and they settled there. They planted a vineyard there and built a large church. That whole company of venerable elders died, and the younger men remained.

Eventually, when Emperor Justin, the empress, and the entire [?] senate were passing through on their way to the hot springs, they entered the monastery and stayed there. Through promises and gifts they brought the monks into submission. The emperor ordered that their former monastery, from which they had been driven, should also be given back to them, and that they should be granted exemption from public taxes. Thus they brought them into submission and drowned them, after they had struggled in the contests of persecution for twenty years. They divided: half of them returned and took possession of their former monastery, while half remained in that place. They were thrown into confusion and bewilderment, so that, one might say, their ship was wrecked at the entrance to the harbor. They turned away completely from all orthodoxy.

As for these convents of women, both large and small, some of their members were pressured and submitted, while others stood firm; or, even if they later returned, they remained in this condition [?]. Those who had submitted and those who had not submitted participated together in all their worship, except that they did not receive communion together. Even at the Eucharist celebrated by the clergy in each convent, at the invocation itself they stood together, took part in the service, and performed the entire order of worship; they could not separate themselves. Those who did not receive communion also had other, orthodox priests who celebrated the Eucharist and gave it to them. Because of the distress of the times, they could not act otherwise without immediately being driven out and scattered. The orthodox leaders were compelled to remain silent and overlook these things, so that orthodoxy would not disappear altogether.

It may happen, however, that some people are quick to resort to ridicule and take it as a joke that in these accounts we make use of the sign associated with misshapen animals, namely elephants. We bring this to mind neither casually nor, so to speak, contemptuously, but first for the glory of God, and secondly to rebuke and shame the pagans, the Jews, and the rest of those who go astray, who deny the cross and reject the saving work accomplished for us upon the standard of the cross.

For these elephants were taken from the accursed people of the Magi through the victory that God granted to the Christians, and were brought up to the imperial capital. They remained there a long time. Whenever they passed in front of churches, the first one, which went at their head, would turn toward the east, lower its head and trunk, and bow down. Immediately it would raise its trunk, curl it, and make the shape of a cross. Having made the sign, it would then pass on. The one behind it would follow and do the same, and the rest would follow one after another, however many there were. We saw this with our own eyes many times, marveling and giving thanks to God, who had imparted knowledge of Christianity even to speechless animals, to rebuke rational beings who neglect Christianity and deny the grace of the Savior of our race.

There was also another similar thing, equally deserving of wonder and great amazement, which these animals regularly did. Whenever there was a hippodrome event—that is, the customary horse race—these elephants would regularly enter [?], each with a man riding on it to guide it. They would stand in the middle of the hippodrome opposite the emperor. They would bend down as far as they could and as their nature allowed, and bow before him. Each of them would make the sign of the cross with its trunk, tracing it in front of the emperor. The crowds gathered there were astonished and amazed at how they made the sign of the cross perfectly, just like human beings. Then, after receiving gifts from the emperor, they would leave.

At the end of the reign of Tiberius and the beginning of that of Maurice, a disaster—that is, a great fire—occurred throughout the whole central part of the imperial capital. Many properties, large, medium, and small alike, were utterly destroyed and left in ruins. Even those who escaped were stripped and deprived of all their possessions and all their wealth, which, as they watched, became food for the flames in a single day.

Therefore, since it may happen that some people—[?]—some people sophisticated in learning who come across these histories while reading may heap criticisms upon the writer because the account of a single subject is sometimes presented in many chapters, intermingled and scattered about, let those who find fault with these things know this: most of these accounts were written during a time of persecution and the pressure of every kind of opposition. Out of necessity, the sheets on which these chapters were written, together with the other sheets and books, were hurried away to different places. Sometimes they remained hidden in various places for as long as two or three years.

It happened that matters arose which the writer wished to put on record, and some of them happened to have already been recorded in earlier chapters. But the earlier drafts were not at hand for him to read and discover whether these matters had been written down, nor did he remember that they had already been written. So he would give an account of them again afterward. For this reason, accounts of the very same subject are sometimes found in many chapters. Time did not even permit the subsequent comparison of them to be carried out readily and easily.

The pride in Patriarch Eutychius’s heart led him astray in many matters. From the beginning he had belonged to the heresy of the Sabbatians. When he became bishop, he wanted to conceal his heresy and please those who had appointed him, who held the Chalcedonian position. At first he stood up and vigorously championed the doctrine of two natures, and began persecuting harshly. When he was removed from his throne and went into exile, he composed a large book setting out the divisive teaching concerning two natures.

When he was recalled and returned to his throne after John’s death, as we have also explained in the preceding account, he began sending this book to the great households of senators, to men and women, especially those who recoiled from the confession of two natures. He wrote to them, “Read and learn that the church confesses two natures in Christ after the union.” But they laughed at his foolishness and sent his book back to him.

Then, after a short time had passed, he heard about the heresy of Athanasius. This man had been made the leader and founder of the heresy of those who count essences—that is, substances and natures—in the Holy Trinity. Following the error of John the Grammarian of Alexandria, he too went astray and said that these human bodies do not rise in the resurrection of the dead, but that other bodies come into being and come to the resurrection. Because of this madness of paganism and Manichaeism, a division arose among them, and they anathematized one another in writing.

When Patriarch Eutychius learned these things, he immediately joined them, became entangled with them, and became one of them. He began composing teaching on this subject and produced and published books, until his own bishops and clergy became agitated and stood against him. Much was said between them. Thus he was checked, fell silent, and put his book away, although he did not turn away from that position.

As he also informs us in another chapter, this excellent Eutychius zealously and vehemently opposed the words, “You were crucified for us.” He wrote everywhere and issued orders, urging the bishops to remove this confession from their churches and cities. From other bishops whom he newly appointed, he demanded written pledges that they would abolish this confession in their territories. As they strove to carry out their instructions, scandal and blasphemy arose in the cities and districts—that is, in the villages—and everywhere, especially in Syria, Asia, and Cappadocia, which had held to this confession from the beginning. Thus, in many villages and cities, people resisted and stood firm, saying, “Even if we are cut to pieces and burned, we will not deny God, who was crucified and suffered for us.” This dispute and conflict continued everywhere, even after the death of Eutychius.
The second book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished, containing fifty-two chapters.

Book Three of the Third Part of the Ecclesiastical History, concerning the histories of the church, and so forth.

Now, in our earlier account we have already dealt adequately with the events at the beginning of the reign of this later Justin, the victorious emperor: how at first he showed concern to bring about unity, and until the sixth year of his reign was peaceable and well disposed toward the whole party of the faithful; and how he finally turned to harsh and lawless persecution. In the two other books preceding this one, we briefly sketched a few of these many events. We also made brief, veiled references to the chastisement sent upon him from heaven, for his benefit, as it were, and to check the headlong course of his evil deeds. But we kept silent about the precise details, lest we should seem to have ventured openly to record and mention God’s merciful blow, which was justly sent upon him, in order to reproach or dishonor the exalted imperial office. For this reason we restrained ourselves at that time. But now, to inspire fear in those who will hereafter be invested with the great powers of government, and so that the judgment of God’s power that overtook Emperor Justin may be portrayed as a warning and imprinted on the hearts of all people, we have thought it right to commit a brief account of these things to writing as a memorial.

God, then, is merciful: he does not desire the destruction of what he has fashioned, and he cares for human lives. He saw that King Justin, exercising his royal authority, had plunged into excesses and practices foreign to the fear of God. To prevent the measure of his sins from becoming full and overwhelming him and destroying him completely, God acted. He saw that Justin had wrongfully shed innocent human blood and had plunged into plundering and seizing property, without consideration or restraint arising from the fear of God. He gathered and amassed the spoils of injustice beyond many who had preceded him. Besides these things, while sinfully committing every kind of evil and provoking God, he also turned to persecuting Christians, cruelly, ruthlessly, and without natural compassion. Through Bishop John, he overthrew the altars of the orthodox with bitter hatred and crushed the churches of the faithful everywhere. He seized priests and chief priests, oppressed and crushed them, and confined them in prisons, government headquarters, monasteries, and various harsh hospices—men who were old, advanced in years, and weak. Many of them perished under these afflictions and departed from this earthly life. Under oppression, torture, bonds, and bitter, harsh, and constricting imprisonment, they suffered torment and died.

There were also many other unspeakable evils that he committed unjustly, which we have no wish whatever to bring to remembrance or to bear witness about. God's justice does not forget the commission of these things and others like them. Yet it also took pity on him, so that he would not perish altogether, but would be disciplined and restrained from the violent onrush of his wicked deeds. God therefore sent upon him, as it is written, wrath, anger, and affliction, sending them through an evil angel. This angel suddenly entered him, took possession of him, and exercised cruel and terrifying power over him, exposing through him the foulness of his wickedness. Suddenly he lost his reason, his soul became confused and darkened, and his body was handed over to hidden and visible torments and severe agonies. He began making the sounds of animals: barking like a dog, sometimes bleating like a goat, sometimes crying like a cat, and at other times crowing like a rooster. He did many other such things beyond the bounds of human reason. All these things were brought about by the ruler of darkness to whom he had been handed over, who had darkened his understanding, taken him captive, and was working through him.

This spirit also drove him into trembling and agitation, so that he would flee from place to place in a savage frenzy, managing to get under his bed and hide among [?]. Then, whenever he became bewildered, he would rush out in an agitated, savage frenzy and run to the windows to throw himself down. Since people stood in awe of him as king, they would run and seize him to prevent him from throwing himself down and dying. The queen was therefore compelled to order carpenters to come up, put in panels, and board over all the palace windows throughout the wing where he lived.

Young, strong chamberlains were chosen to guard him. When, as described, they were forced to run and seize him, he would turn on them, since he was a strong man, seize them one by one, and bite and injure them with his teeth. He bit two of them on their necks, wounding them [?], and they were in a bad condition. The story even spread through the city that the king had eaten two chamberlains. Finally, as was reported, they repeatedly found themselves compelled even to bind him with ropes. He would shout and howl and speak words of madness. They would shout at him, 'Look, al-Harith son of Jabalah is coming for you! Be quiet!' Immediately he would flee inside and hide. If they named anyone at all to frighten him, he would likewise flee, become quiet, and hide under the bed.

Many other things, more disgraceful than these and contrary to decency, were recounted fearlessly by everyone throughout the city. We have now recorded some of them from what we heard from many people, for these things were continually being recounted. His ordeal and affliction lasted not merely a few days, but as long as five years. We have made use of only a few accounts of these things, although we were neither present nor eyewitnesses to them. But the entire senate and the whole city, those within as well as those outside, testify to their truth: they really and certainly happened, along with many other things that it is not fitting to put in writing.

Finally, when they wanted to give the king some diversion, collect his thoughts, and bring him back to himself, they made a little cart for him to sit in, with a chair mounted on it. They would seat him in it, and the chamberlains would pull it, running him back and forth for a long time. In this way he would become absorbed and dazed by the speed of the movement, and would stop much of his foolish talk.

They also distracted him with the sound of an organ. Close to the place where he was, an organ played night and day, with only short intervals, whether at night or during the day. Sometimes, as he listened to the sound and melodies of the organ, he would become quiet. But it also happened that he would suddenly become agitated, shout, and behave in disorderly ways.

For example, the patriarch once went in to visit him. When he approached him and bowed before him, he saw that he was confused and made the sign of the cross over him. But the king raised his hand and struck him on the neck, sending him sprawling onto a [?], a considerable distance away from him. He said to him, “You will come to a bad end unless you go and make the sign of the cross over yourself, so that your own demons may come out!” The patriarch then recovered himself, while others took hold of him and helped him up. For quite some time he remained dazed from the blow the king had struck him on the neck.

Later, however, since custom did not allow the patriarch to stay away from the palace, he again went in to see him, taking care and guarding himself against him. When the king saw him, he began laughing at him. He approached him, stretched out his hands, and took his mantle from his shoulder—that is, his episcopal stole. He spread it out and placed it over his head like a woman’s veil. He said to him, “How fine you would look now, my lord patriarch, if you put tassels on it, like the threads women wear on their heads!”

He would also look down toward the seashore and shout like the people who go around selling pots. Imitating them, he would cry out, “Who is selling pots?” There were many other things, beyond recounting or describing, that he did through the activity of the devil, to whom he had been handed over. In every city and village, in the houses, streets, and all the shops of the city, both outside and inside, and even along the roads, everyone talked about these things with great astonishment and amazement.

While the king was being chastised through all this humiliation and bitter trial, many people formed opinions and spoke about him, foremost among them his own wife, Queen Sophia. Not only did she fail to learn her lesson or become afraid [?] because of his affliction, trial, and chastisement, but she became still more arrogant, saying, “The kingdom was mine, and it came to me. This man was chastised and fell into this trial because of me, because he despised me and mistreated me.” This was not how anyone else understood it; rather, everyone regarded it as a wicked thing to say. We shall also record these matters later, in their proper place.

But what everyone believed to be the true explanation was this: they said that God had sent wrath upon him from heaven for no other reason than these three offenses: the innocent blood he had shed; his persecution of Christians, and the tortures, afflictions, chains, harsh imprisonments, and exiles he had made priests, bishops, and the rest of the faithful people, both men and women, endure; and, finally, his seizure and plundering of people’s property, since he would not allow orphans to inherit from their fathers. The cry of the orphans and widows, together with these other things, rose before the Lord, and he became angry with him and handed his kingdom over to another while he was still alive and could see it with his own eyes.

After Emperor Justin had remained in this affliction and the rest of his illnesses and other trials for five years, and had begun the sixth, still being chastened and afflicted by demonic activity, all business had come to a standstill, all the affairs of the entire state were in confusion, and attacks by barbarians were frequent on every side. The whole senate therefore consulted with the empress about advising the emperor to appoint a Caesar to succeed him, for the sake of the affairs of state. He himself was also receptive to their words. For there were times when his reason returned to him, though imperfectly, and during these he spoke coherently. After consulting with him at length, they chose Tiberius and appointed him Caesar. He had long been Emperor Justin’s secretary, even before Justin became emperor.

When Justin summoned him and had him stand before him to clothe him in the insignia and garments of imperial rule, an angel appeared to him, as he himself declared, standing beside him and telling him in his ear what he should say to Tiberius Caesar. The emperor began speaking astonishing and wonderful words, like someone whose reason had never been impaired. With weeping and choking tears he said:

“My son Tiberius, come, receive the empire of the wretched Justin, who angered God, and whom God has rejected and cast from his imperial office while he is still alive. Come, my son, enter and drive out the man who was unfaithful to his Creator, who had deemed him worthy of imperial rule, while his own eyes watch him being rejected and falling from his throne.”

He cried these things aloud before many thousands, so that bitter weeping and violent sobbing seized everyone who heard him. This was especially so when he turned around, waved his hand toward all the military units standing there, and said to them in a loud voice:

“My sons, open all the guarded gates of the imperial palace, of the empire [?], and let everyone enter, so that they may see the wretched Justin being stripped of his office and falling from his throne, because he angered and embittered that true King, whose kingdom never passes away, who made him emperor although he was unworthy.

“From now on, Tiberius, let me be a warning to you. Tremble and be afraid before the Lord, the eternal King. Be on your guard before him, and do not anger him by your evil deeds, as I angered him by all my deeds and conduct, so that all this harsh and terrible chastisement was sent upon me. Now, see, while I am still alive, I am being stripped of my office and rejected from imperial rule because I conducted myself unjustly in it. Take care that these imperial garments and insignia do not deceive you as they deceived me, lifting you up, leading you astray, and making you proud, so that wrath is sent upon you from heaven as it was upon me, and you too are stripped of your office and fall from your throne, as I do today.

“Look, my son, at the one standing beside me, speaking into my ears and teaching me all these things that I say to you, teaching, instructing, and warning you. Know, understand, and consider within yourself that these things I am now saying to you are not my own, but come from this angel of God. Although neither you nor anyone else sees him, he is standing beside me and teaching me these things that I am saying to you, so that you may tremble and be afraid of the terrible sentence of justice decreed and sent upon me, as you and everyone can now see. Because I did not keep his commandments, he is stripping me of my office and casting me out of imperial rule, and is now handing it over to you.

“Look at me now, my son, and take from me an example that will warn you and make your heart tremble at this sentence pronounced against me. Do not give yourself over to doing evil, evil such as I used to do, lest wrath be sent upon you too from heaven, as it is now upon me, and he reject you too from your imperial office.

“Take care not to let yourself be persuaded by evil people who give you evil advice and lead you astray, as they led me astray, and I angered God by all my deeds.”

These things, and many more than these, of which we have included only these few because of their great number, were spoken by the emperor with grief and weeping, in a loud voice before everyone. The illustrious Tiberius himself, completely stripped of his covering, threw himself face down on the ground at the emperor’s feet and bellowed like a bull, weeping bitterly and choking with sobs. The whole senate and the rest of the crowds standing around also cried out in great grief as they heard all these things and saw him surrendering his empire, and the man summoned to receive it. They were seized with cries of grief. When they lifted Tiberius up and made him stand, he fell on his face again, crying aloud.

Then all the crowds together cried aloud from their hearts with one mighty cry. No one could restrain or hold back his tears at what he heard from the emperor, who spoke while weeping over his humiliation. At last he gave orders, and they made Tiberius stand up. He continued speaking to him amid these things, with much sobbing. Then he clothed him in the robes, garments, and insignia of imperial rank, saying to him:

“From now on your name shall be called Constantine, since in you the empire of Constantine the Great has been renewed.”

And there were other words of boundless sobbing and grief spoken there, as many thousands wrote them down.

Tiberius became Caesar on the seventh day of the month of December, in the year eight hundred and eighty-six, on Friday morning.

It became known and was established for everyone that all these words had truly been spoken to him by an angel of God and had not originated with the emperor. Thus, afterward, when portraits of the two of them were put up, an angel was depicted between them, standing with his mouth placed beside Emperor Justin’s ear. In this way the account was accepted as trustworthy by everyone.

Everything he said was immediately taken down in shorthand by many people and committed to writing. For many secretaries and scribes were standing there, making accurate records and copies [?]. Because of their great number, we have left these out and passed over them.

After Emperor Justin had appointed Tiberius Caesar, he lived with him for four years. Both he and everyone else hoped for his recovery, especially because from time to time they would support him as he went up to the [?], in the morning only, so that all the people of the city could see him. Sometimes he would also sit and receive the homage of the senate. At other times he would distribute payments: they would put gold in his hand, and he would drop it into the hands of those receiving it. Then he would return to his affliction. Other pains and afflictions were added to his painful difficulty in urinating, which tormented him along with all the rest. His condition continually deteriorated. By then all affairs were being managed by the God-loving Caesar, especially the wars against the barbarians and the Persians. He would consult Justin, and whenever Justin was lucid and said something sensible, he would act on it.

But when the period mentioned above had passed, and the recovery that he and many others expected had not come about, but instead his pains and bitter sufferings kept increasing, he would often cry out and implore them, saying, “Bring a sword and kill me with it! Death would be far better for me than this life of torment and misery.” At other times he would cry out that all the palace gates should be opened, so that everyone could come in and see an emperor who asked for death and desired it more than life, yet was not granted it.

Later, when he was suffering still more from his painful difficulty in urinating and from the stones that were blocking his bowels, and was in great distress, the physicians came to operate on him. Being afraid, as physicians usually are, they persuaded him to take the surgical knife himself and hand it to them. He, however, implored them not to spare him, so that he might depart this life, saying, “Do not be afraid. You will be in no danger if I die.” Then he was cut severely in both groins, until all his [?] were [?]. It is said that even his sexual organ was [?] and cut off. As he suffered and wailed, he said in a loud voice, “Your judgments are just, O God! For already here, for every sin I committed and every evil I did with my body, I have openly received punishment in wrath in the very limbs with which I committed sin.”

When he had now given up hope of living and concluded that he was going to die, he summoned Caesar. He gave him many instructions and warnings, saying, “My son, I am dying. Come now, receive the imperial crown, and watch yourself. Do not engage in evil deeds and provoke God to anger. Take good care of the Roman Empire.”

Thus Tiberius received the crown on Monday, the twenty-sixth day of September, in the year eight hundred and ninety. After Justin had placed the crown on him, he lived with him for nine days. He departed this world on the fourth day of October of that same year.

After [?] the death of Emperor Justin, his wife, Empress Sophia, remained [?] in the palace with Emperor Tiberius, who promised her great honors, although she did not understand her own honor, as it is written. For before they made him Caesar, they demanded a written undertaking and many oaths from him that, if the emperor died, Caesar would keep Sophia in honor and do her no harm. He observed this very carefully, as is evident. When Emperor Justin died, he kept her with him in the palace in honor, saying to her, “You are my mother. Stay here and give orders, and command me to do whatever you wish.”

After he became emperor, he began pleading with her about his wife, asking that she might come and join him [?]. But Sophia was neither pleased nor content. Even while Justin was alive, he used to say to her, “Let Caesar’s wife come in to him, for he is a young man and cannot control his body.” But she turned on him and insulted him, saying, “You fool! Do you want me to act foolishly like you, who have clothed your servant in the insignia of your imperial office?” She declared on oath, “I will not give my imperial position and my insignia to another woman during my lifetime, and no other woman will enter here while I live.”

And so Caesar’s own wife remained where she was. During the four years before Justin’s death in which Tiberius held the position of Caesar, Sophia did not allow his wife to enter the palace. Eventually he was compelled to bring his wife and her two daughters and settle them in the House of Hormisdas, below the palace. From time to time he would go down and spend the night with them, returning early to the palace.

O women, how wicked you are! And, as the story was told, he was approached through another person and through the patriarch about Sophia herself or her daughter, who was also a widow: Caesar was to leave his wife and marry one of them. When he heard this, he was deeply distressed. According to what was reported, he answered those sent to him with great distress, saying, “Is it right in God’s sight and yours that I should leave the wife by whom I have three children, who shared her life with me and made me what I am when I had nothing? And now that God has raised me up, should I leave her and marry another?” Thus he would not be persuaded to agree to commit this injustice.

Caesar’s wife, whose name was Ino, had previously been married to another man, named John. He was a Roman, an adjutant in the Roman army, and she came from the fortress of Daphnudium. They had a daughter, whom they betrothed to Tiberius when he was still a private individual and an ordinary Roman. But the girl’s father died [?], and she too died before Tiberius married her. Take note. When she herself had died and her mother was left a widow—perhaps this too was an act of God’s providence—he married the girl’s mother, and he had three children by her.

When he sent for her and brought her to the House of Hormisdas, she lived in trembling and fear, uncertain whether her life was safe while she stayed there. No one dared to go to her and see her. For all the women of senatorial rank had gathered, but they were afraid to go and pay homage to her, lest the empress become angry with them. They therefore went in to consult Empress Sophia, asking whether she thought fit to authorize them to go and pay homage to Caesar’s wife, lest they later be blamed. When she heard this from them, she looked at them angrily and answered them harshly, saying, “Go away! Be quiet, be quiet! This is none of your business.”

After that, no one dared to go and see her. Consequently, she fled, left the city, and returned to Daphnudium. Then, when she also fell ill, Caesar himself was compelled to go out to her, see her, and return.

When Justin died, after Tiberius had received the imperial crown, as we explained above, Tiberius asked Empress Sophia to let him send for his wife, so that she too might come and reign. When Sophia heard this, she was neither pleased nor content, but she could not prevent it.

The praetorian prefect was sent to fetch her, together with the other senators, many warships, and a large military force. They set out with great ceremony to bring in the emperor’s wife so that she too might reign. When they reached Daphnudium and she learned of their arrival, she sent them this message: “Come in the morning—come, and we will enter together.” When they received this reply, lodgings were prepared for them, and they went in and stayed there.

But she immediately sent one of her trusted attendants, saying, “Go and prepare a warship for us. During the night I want to send you ahead with a message, without anyone knowing.” When the ship was ready, at midnight she took her two young girls [?] and one trusted attendant, went down, and boarded the ship with only them. She left the others behind to tell the prefect and the rest, “Do not remain here any longer. The woman you are seeking is in the city before daybreak.” When they learned this, they were greatly upset. They returned to the city, concealing the fact that they had come back empty-handed.

She was immediately taken to the palace. The bishop came in with the entire senate and the emperor, and they clothed her too in the imperial robes and all the imperial regalia. She went out in the imperial litter to go to church, accompanied by the senate and the chamberlains, while the factions stood ready. When they began shouting their acclamations to her, the Blues named her Anastasia, but the Greens named her Helena. The former kept shouting “Anastasia,” while the others shouted “Helena.” There was a great and frightening uproar, so that she and everyone with her were alarmed. She entered the church and worshiped, then returned to the palace and assumed imperial power.

It is not our business now to recount the many things that happened between them afterward. Indeed, we would have had no occasion to include even these things, except that we interweave accounts of the empire with those of the church, and because there had been a change of reign, and so that it might be known to everyone, to the glory of God.

Now after the death of Emperor Justin, Empress Sophia began preparing schemes of no small magnitude against Emperor Tiberius, who was also called Constantine, with bitter resentment and wicked plots. She was embittered at seeing him and his wife rise, take possession, and assume control of the empire, while she herself had now lost her imperial authority while still alive. She had not exercised that authority justly or in the fear of God. She had neither accepted correction nor taken heed through her husband’s trial and chastisement. It was as though she had not understood that she too ought to fear God, accept correction, and become like one of the righteous. Instead, as in the saying—the apostolic sayings addressed to such people—which says, “Because of your hardness of heart, which will not repent, you are storing up for yourself a treasure of wrath for the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, when he will repay everyone according to their deeds,” so this was fulfilled in her as well. Because of her hardness of heart and the arrogance of her thoughts, she did not repent or fear God, and she too fell from her imperial position. She had sworn with oaths that during her lifetime she would not give it to another woman. Yet before she was laid to rest, her imperial authority was taken from her and given to another woman, while she herself fell from it.

When her husband was at the point of death, as people said, she took many hundred-pound sums of gold out of the palace and brought them to her own house. Since we do not know the truth about these sums, we do not wish to record their number, for they were said to have been very numerous. Along with them she took many imperial possessions. When the emperor learned of this, he did not allow her to leave the palace, saying, “Stay and rest, and be at ease as our mother. Whatever you command, we will do.” So she remained in the palace, bitter, crushed, troubled, mourning and lamenting over her life [?], because she had been brought low, despised, and abandoned by everyone. Though still alive, she became as though she did not exist.

When Tiberius first took his place as Caesar, he began giving lavish gifts to everyone. Whenever he left the palace for prayer or anywhere else, he scattered gifts to right and left, as at a consul’s distribution. Even when he was at sea aboard a warship, boats would hurry up from every direction, and he would throw gifts to them all as at a consul’s distribution. He went so far that he received rebukes and reprimands from the imperial rulers for scattering so much. Eventually they sent and took the keys of the treasury from him, and allotted gold for his use. In this way they restrained him from giving such lavish and numerous gifts.

But after he became emperor and assumed power, and, as people say, saw the accumulated imperial treasures, he again began bringing out and scattering money extravagantly and freely. When he began to give his accession gift, which the Romans call the donative, consisting of nine gold coins—gold coins given when an emperor newly comes to the throne—he gave generously to all the troops. To those stationed in the East against the Persians, he sent eight hundred pounds of gold for their donative.

Again, wishing to pour out his gifts still more abundantly and lavishly, he did something that no emperor had ever done: he ordered the entire body of lawyers to come before him. Although they were very numerous, he gave each of them fifteen or twenty, ten or twelve, or more. Again he ordered all the physicians to come in, and all received generously. Then came the silversmiths and bankers. To some of these, if the thought occurred to him, he would give a pound of gold each, or fifty or sixty gold coins. Then came the imperial agents, the deans [?], and other groups in imperial service. He would say, “Why is all this gold hoarded here, while the whole world is being strangled by hunger?” So he brought it out and scattered it without stint.

In the end, however, once he had become emperor in the full sense, he closed his hand. He would grant no one any relief, nor would he admit anyone to an audience.

Now that God-loving Caesar was being pressed every day by John the patriarch about the Dissenters, that is, the orthodox. One day he made him swear by God to tell him whether they were heretics or not. Although John was very partial, once he had been put under oath he could not lie. Instead, he answered him, saying, “In truth, they are not heretics, and their faith is entirely sound. The trouble is that they keep away from us and from the church and are unwilling to share communion with us.” Then Caesar answered him, “If you yourself testify that they are believers and Christians, why, then, are you pressing me to become like Diocletian—a Diocletian persecuting Christians? Go, sit down, and be quiet. Our wars with the barbarians are enough for us. Do not bring us into wars with our own people.”

Now when Emperor Tiberius, who was also called Constantine, received the imperial crown, he immediately ordered a public procession to the church, to go and pray. Justin was still alive. When he entered the church, the whole city gathered, everyone without exception, to see him, together with the countless foreigners who were there. After acclaiming the emperor as usual, they began shouting, “Let the bones of the Arians be dug up! Let the bones of all the heretics be dug up! Likewise those of the pagans! May the Christian faith grow!”

When he heard these cries, together with the first cries [?] that they shouted to him about the Arians, he was deeply upset. He gave no sign of it there in the church, however, but prayed, presented the offering customary for new emperors, and returned to the palace. He immediately ordered an investigation and the arrest of those identified as having shouted to him in the church about the Arians. For he had taken it into his head that their shouting concerned him and was directed against him: they had supposed him to be secretly an Arian and had therefore shouted this at him. Indeed, many people privately entertained such a suspicion.

For a short time before, a large crowd of Goths had gathered, together with the wives of those who had gone down to fight the Persians. These women, too, were numerous and were Arians. They had called upon him to give them a church for their worship. Wishing not to upset them, he sent them this reply: “Go, and we will look into it and discuss it with the patriarch.” Thus, before he put on the crown, the rumor spread throughout the city that Caesar was an Arian. This was why those zealous for the churches had gathered and shouted these things to him.

When, at his command, they were arrested and brought before him, he received them with great anger, saying, “What have you seen in me that belongs to the Arians, that you have insulted me and shouted at me about the Arians?” Only after offering him many excuses were they finally released, with difficulty.

Then, because of this incident, he ordered an edict to be drawn up and posted in the city, directing that the Arians and all the Montanists, [?], and Sabbatians should be arrested, as will be related below. Many began to be arrested and imprisoned by people who had found pretexts for openly and fearlessly extorting money from others. They paid money lavishly to secure their safety. Many orthodox people were also arrested along with them and kept in distressing confinement for many days. They too were required to pay money, and only then were they released and allowed to leave, one by one.

In that same year, then, when King Tiberius assumed full royal power, he distributed a great consular largesse. According to what both he and everyone else said, he distributed seventy out of seventy-two hundredweights, apart from silver, garments of pure silk, and other things. He enriched the rich and the [?], but did nothing to benefit the poor. Sophia became angry with him and reproached him, saying, “What we gathered and stored up with such diligence and great care, you scatter to the winds as though with a winnowing fork.” But he said to her, “What you gathered through injustice, plunder, and robbery, I am determined to dispose of so that none of it remains in my palace.”

Even before this, he had ordered that a quarter of the public taxes should be remitted everywhere. Again, after he became emperor, because Justin had imposed a charge on those palace bread allowances established by Emperor Constantine—four gold coins for each loaf, which were being collected—King Tiberius ordered that the whole amount should be refunded to everyone who had paid it.

He also performed another act of mercy as soon as he became Caesar. A levy had been imposed on ships and all merchants, requiring them to give one measure from every [?]. This amounted to many hundredweights upon hundredweights, and everywhere they exacted it with oppression and great loss. When they had made it [?], he ordered that this too should be removed and abolished. So this too was discontinued. These were the things he did immediately at the beginning of his rule. Where his course would ultimately lead would become known at the end.

Another proof he gave of his Christianity was this: Justin had put an image on the coinage of his gold coins, which many people compared to Aphrodite. In its place, he ordered that there should be a cross on his own coinage. As he related, this had come to him in a revelation some time before.

At that time, then, persecution against the heresies was ordered and set in motion. In its onrush, as though from some mighty torrent, the congregations of the orthodox were also swept away. First they fell upon John, who was called “Over the Pagans,” the bishop of Ephesus, who had been living in the imperial capital for many years. They arrested him and everyone with him and took them away and confined them in the prison called the Cancella. This followed many imprisonments and other banishments that he had endured on numerous occasions.

They were imprisoned and afflicted during the days of the Nativity festivities. They were put in a chamber where water seeped in from all four sides. Even when the rain from the sky stopped, water continued dripping into it from every direction for two days, because it was an underground vaulted chamber. Thus they lived in it as though in a lake, constantly getting up and bailing out the water. They lay there in coffins of the sort in which the dead are buried, because they had nowhere to rest their heads.

Despite all this distress, every day, morning and evening, bishops, metropolitans, church advocates, and church advocates [?] were sent to dispute with them. But the grace that accompanied them would not let them give way. Instead, openly and fearlessly, they stood up for the truth of the orthodox faith and contested with their opponents. When those persecutors who upheld two natures were defeated, they resorted to insults and threats against them. Every day, for eighteen days, groups of bishops’ assistants, administrators, administrators [?], other clergy, and laypeople gathered against them. They spent in prison the consular celebration held by the emperor.

Since John would not do what they wanted, even merely in words, they sentenced him to leave the city. Thus they released them from prison, rejoicing and thanking God that they had been considered worthy, time after time, to suffer for his name. John also had a couch on which he used to sit because he suffered from trouble in his feet. The patriarch Eutychius sent men and seized even this from him. Many other things happened, of which we have included only a few as a record to preserve their memory.

After Bishop John and those with him were released from prison, on the following day a band [?] gathered—that is, the troop of persecutors, or perhaps it would be more fitting to call them a gang, a gang of robbers—at the church of the orthodox that used to assemble on Sundays in the great royal house of Marinus, of Marinus [?]. When the whole congregation had assembled, they entered, fell upon them, and arrested many. They entered like pagans, seized the altar, overturned it, and broke it. They spilled the consecrated elements that were on it and flung and scattered the offering.

After tearing apart and overturning the whole church, they dragged away the clergy and the other laypeople. They took down the images of the blessed Severus and Theodosius and carried them behind their heads in mockery as they went through the public streets. They took everyone away and confined them in the prison where the earlier prisoners had been held. As for the rest of the crowd whom they had seized, they stripped them and let them go. They snatched and stole everything that fell into their hands and went away.

Some days later, Eutychius sent for them and had them brought up to the bishop’s residence, where he disputed with them at length. He then released them on guarantees. In the end, when the merciful emperor learned of these things, he rebuked him, and he desisted for a little while.

Now concerning Eutychius, [?] the patriarch: when he was summoned and entered office after John’s death, people spoke highly of him, saying that he was righteous, performed miracles, and saw visions. He himself also used to put these things in writing and spread them abroad. But when he entered office, without a properly conducted inquiry into his deposition by John, who had expelled him, he went up and sat on the church’s throne, although his excommunication had neither been investigated nor lifted. Because of this, many broke away and withdrew from communion with him, as from an excommunicated man whose deposition had been carried out by the man who had died, and who in turn had deposed that man [?]. Yet in the end he entered and took his seat, accepting without examination or investigation that man’s ordinations and everything he had done, simply so that he might somehow secure the throne.

Then there was a second stumbling block that he caused the whole church [?] afterward. A few days had passed when he heard about certain people who had been caught up in an error derived from the teaching of John the Grammarian of Alexandria. As we also explained his position in the preceding book, he used to argue and say that these human bodies do not rise at the resurrection, but that other bodies come into being and rise in their place. Eutychius turned aside and fell into this error himself. He took the part of those who thus deny the resurrection and began to teach and argue that this was indeed the case: this body does not rise, but another comes into being and rises in its place.

When some of his bishops, along with clergy and others, disputed with him about these matters, he fought all the more insistently to maintain that it was so. He even composed a discourse setting out this opinion, had it written on scrolls, and sent it to prominent women for them to read and become his disciples. He said and did other things of this sort like a fool, so that many now regarded him as a deranged man who had lost his mind.

Indeed, as eventually became plainly evident in him, a demon would come upon him, throw him down, and crush him. Twice, while he was standing at the altar in the Great Church, it convulsed him in full view of the whole congregation, and they hastily picked him up and carried him out. This happened once more in the church of the blessed Mother of God in the Chalkoprateia. Again, as people reported, it also battered him many times in the episcopal residence.

Those who wanted to cover up for him said, ‘His extensive fasting and keeping vigil stir up a humor within him. This rises and gathers in his head, makes him dizzy, and throws him down. He does not have a demon.’ But many others replied to such people, ‘Does a humor really convulse and crush him, so that he foams and cries out?’ From then on, everything he did appeared to everyone to be the behavior of someone whose mind had been confused and darkened by an evil spirit. For he also used inappropriate language and indulged in laughter unbecoming to his position, along with other things of this kind.

He also produced a book in which, from beginning to end, he amassed material in support of the confession of two natures after the union. He criticized all the true fathers who would not join him in blaspheming by putting a quaternity in place of the Holy Trinity. He used to send this book around to households so that they might become his disciples. But everyone who read it laughed and mocked him as a man who had gone mad and lost his mind. Throughout the city they said, ‘This man, whom they used to say performed mighty works and miracles, has lost his senses.’

Now this Eutychius, Eutychus, after he had entered and taken possession of the episcopal throne of the church in the imperial city, became firmly established and enjoyed distinction at the beginning, as we have already related many things about him in the preceding, recent accounts. He was also received with honor by the merciful emperor Tiberius. But immediately arrogance, conceit, and boastfulness seized him, so that he even overstepped his position and spoke extravagant and foolish things. Consequently, everyone began to speak against him and laugh at him as a man lacking sense. He wrote a large book in defense of the two natures, as we have also related concerning it. Through this, the character of his foolishness became still more apparent to everyone. He began sending this book to the great households and urging women and men of senatorial rank, especially those opposed to the two natures, to read it and be persuaded by what was written in it, so that they would confidently confess two natures after the union. For, he said, anyone who did not confess this was a Eutychian heretic. Thus everyone, even his own people, mocked him and sent his book back to him.

Now, as this Eutychius again grew exceedingly conceited, he went further and displayed his zeal against the phrase, “You who were crucified for us.” He threatened and contended against anyone, he said, who dared to say, “You who were crucified for us.” There were well-known, large communities of nuns who had been driven out of Antioch at the beginning of the persecution and had since been living in various places in the imperial city. Following the customary Eastern tradition, they conducted their worship with the words, “You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.” For this reason he went to them in person with his clergy and began expounding and teaching them. He also threatened them. Now, in the days of the victorious Justin, when he had stirred up persecution against them and against everyone, some of them had submitted, while others had not been persuaded. They all assembled together, clothed themselves in courageous zeal, and stood against him, saying, “It is enough that you have forced us to change and destroy our faith. But we will never agree to deny God, who was crucified, suffered, and died for us, even if we face the sword, the cross, and fire.” As they all together vehemently and forcefully disputed with him and raised an uproar against him, his clergy saw their boldness and the intensity of their zeal, for they were saying these things to his face. They said to him, “Get up, my lord, and let us go. It is time for the liturgy.” So he got up and left there, without accomplishing what he wanted among them [?]. Finally, he wrote a long document, teaching, stirring up trouble, and threatening, and sent it to them. But they would not accept it, saying, “We are women and know nothing of disputation. But we will not depart from the tradition of the Eastern fathers, even unto death.” News of this dispute spread throughout the whole city and the palace and reached the emperor, and everyone found fault with him. Thus, as a result of this, he cooled down a little and kept quiet.

In the fourth year after Eutychius took office, just as at the beginning, he turned against the orthodox in bitter anger, sending men out, arresting, seizing, and imprisoning. He overturned altars everywhere and pulled down whatever images were found. Everything that could be found was seized and stolen, whether liturgical furnishings, vestments, curtains, books, Eucharistic bread, or vessels—in short, absolutely everything found wherever they went—by open robbery. In the same way they seized people, priests and bishops, and confined them in prison under bitter constraint for as long as they wished. There they were subjected to further extortion. Those who had nothing borrowed and paid. Even when they were then released and came out, they recovered absolutely nothing of what had previously been extorted from them. If, on the other hand, they had nothing to give, they were sent into exile and again confined in monasteries under severe constraint.

Meanwhile, the excellent Eutychius would go in to the merciful Tiberius and maliciously accuse the entire party of the faithful, without the restraint of any fear of God. All the heresies—the Arians, Macedonians, Sabbatians, who were his own people, Manichaeans, Marcionites, Marcionians, and followers of Montanus and Montius—were living quietly, with no one troubling them. Only the true believers were persecuted and plundered, and sent to various places of exile in distant cities and on various islands in the sea. They were subjected to every affliction of harsh bonds and oppressive imprisonment, to hunger, thirst, and every kind of trial. Had divine grace not visited and strengthened them, no one among them would have survived, as it is written concerning the affliction that is to come at the end.

While the victorious emperor was overwhelmed by the wars surrounding him on every side, Bishop Eutychius went in every day and kept troubling him about the Diacrinomeni. The emperor said to him, “Do not wear me out with these matters. The ordeal of the wars in which I am involved is enough for me. Go and do as you wish in the affairs of the church, at your own risk. You know best. I am free of guilt.”

Because of this, without fear of either God or the emperor, the persecution spread and grew—a persecution for the sake of plunder, not out of concern for the faith. So, to have people persecute as he did in every place and region, he did not hesitate to write to every region, every place, and every great city, urging them likewise to stir up a cruel persecution against all the Diacrinomeni everywhere. These people too, driven by the desire to seize and plunder property and to commit open robbery under the pretext of faith, joined with the rest of their party in setting persecution in motion in every place and region. Meanwhile, because of the ordeals of the wars surrounding him, the victorious emperor paid no attention and allowed no complaint or petition for redress to come before him.

Let this, then, be known to everyone who later encounters these chapters of the history: we write in this way because we adhere to the exact truth, and not because we consider ourselves opponents of the virtuous Patriarch Eutychius. Indeed, we have fallen short of the truth, even though we have told a hundredth part. We have not put these things on record out of eagerness to insult and ridicule. Nor, again, do we speak or write these things about the serene emperor in flattery. Rather, in everything we strive to be advocates of the truth. For when Emperor Tiberius was a young man, before even the first hairs of a beard had grown on him, he and I were constantly together, and we stood with the others before Justin of blessed memory. From that time onward I have been continually acquainted with his habits and conduct. Even now, when he has been deemed worthy to stand at the height of imperial power, he remains unchanged, maintaining the same generous and humble manner without wavering, as everyone now knows beyond dispute. He has not become conceited like a young boy who has gained imperial authority. He has ordered that no one be killed or plundered, as his predecessor did, staining himself and his hands with innocent blood. Instead, for the present he conducts himself generously and humbly, now into the third year of his reign, apart from the four years during which he was Caesar. Up to the present he has continued in this way, although many grumble about him, saying that he is quiet and meek and inspires no fear. But for the present he continues to conduct himself peacefully.

As for Emperor Tiberius himself, who was also called Constantine, while Justin was still alive and they were living in the great palace, the Authenticon, he was Caesar and lived in cramped quarters in one wing of the palace. Even after Justin died, his wife Sophia remained in that same palace, the Authenticon, and he could not get her to leave. Nor would she allow him to enter and live there. Because he was short of space after becoming sole emperor, especially after his wife came to join him with her two daughters, and because he did not wish to force or pressure Empress Sophia so that he could enter and live in the great imperial residence, he was obliged to pull down the entire northern wing of the palace and build a palace for himself. Thus he demolished many large buildings and vigorously undertook rebuilding. He also destroyed the beautiful garden in the middle of the palace, which had served as a place of recreation for the emperors, and planted massive buildings in it. He demolished on every side, enlarged the site, and built on a grand scale. He also built a substantial new bathhouse and substantial stables for horses up in the palace itself, along with many other things.

Now, after Emperor Justin had become deeply involved in persecution and the disruption of the church, and also in robbery and plunder, and that terrible chastisement had been sent upon him, other signs of wrath from heaven appeared in his case as well. For he wanted to turn his former house, which stood in the northwestern quarter of the city, at [?], into a palace. He himself demolished many houses, built and laid out a hippodrome, and carried out substantial construction and fortification. He planted gardens containing a mixture of every kind of plant, and so forth. Then he gave orders, and they erected statues of him and his wife—that is, large bronze images. Shortly after they had been erected and put in place, a powerful wind arose and knocked them down. They were found with their heads driven into the ground. Many people regarded this as a sign of wrath and downfall for them.

Afterward he again gave orders and began erecting a lighthouse for himself—that is, a massive tower—at Zeuxippus, on the seashore, on its eastern side, east of the city. He ordered it to be hollow, with stairs, so that people could ascend it by a broad and secure passage. It was built with courses of massive dressed stones—massive dressed stone reinforced with iron and firmly secured with lead. As it was being built, it rose to a great height and approached completion. While it was under construction, some of the city's inhabitants wrote a notice and attached it to a panel on it, as follows: “Build your tower, build! Raise it as high as you can. Go up and stand on top of it. Consider, look, and see the east and west, the north and south: look, they have been devastated and utterly ruined in your days!” But he died without completing it.

It was said that a dispute arose between Tiberius and Sophia when she told him, “Finish it.” He said, “I am not going to finish it. It is your responsibility to finish it.” She, thinking that he would have an image of himself made for it and would stand upon it, said, “If you are unwilling to do it for the man who built it, do it for yourself.” He became angry and swore, “I will stand neither on it nor on any other.”

But when he saw that the great masses of large stones in it would be useful for the construction he had begun in the palace, he gave orders, and it was demolished down to its foundations. He transported all its stones to the palace and to the Church of the Forty Martyrs, which he had been building for a long time. It was said that many hundredweights of gold had been spent on it.

Now, after the compassionate Tiberius had taken his seat as Caesar during the lifetime of Emperor Justin, because Justin himself had fallen under the affliction of various illnesses, the Caesar prepared for wars on every side. Above all, he faced the struggle against the Persians, together with all the other barbarian peoples who had risen against the mighty Roman Empire, and he was threatened on every side. After Justin's death they pressed him still harder, especially the accursed peoples of the Slavs and those with [?] hair who are called Avars. This happened especially after he became sole emperor. They gave him no respite, even for a short time, from the news and reports that poured in upon him from everywhere. Many people, both great and small, grieved for him, saying, “The empire has come to this man amid severe trials and evil days.” Day and night he was caught up in the struggle and anxiety of gathering armies from everywhere and sending them in every direction to fight the many wars.

For when Emperor Tiberius was compelled to assemble and bring barbarian peoples from the West, people who followed the teaching of the wicked Arius, to send them against the Persians, their wives and children remained in the imperial capital. They then asked Emperor Tiberius to set aside and give them one church in the city, where their wives and children and those of them who remained in the city could gather. As the emperor was trying to satisfy them, so that they too would exert all their strength on behalf of the Roman state and fight its enemies, he told them, “We will look into it and speak to the patriarch.” Because of this promise and the noncommittal answer he had given them, and because he had not sharply refused their request, everyone came to believe and say that the emperor was an Arian, that he shared the beliefs of those who had asked him for a church, and that he was concealing his convictions.

Thus, when he went to church for the festival, many people shouted, “May the bones of the Arians be overturned! May the bones of the [?] be dug up! May the bones of the Arians be dug up!” When he heard these cries, he realized that they were shouting against him, and he became deeply upset. On returning to the palace, he sent and arrested many of those who had shouted. He said to them, “What have you seen in me that is Arian, that you shouted against me and insulted me in church?” In their fear, they gave him some relief.

But because he wanted to free himself from this suspicion, he ordered the Arians to be persecuted. Then these church police, taking the command as their opportunity, rushed about like wolves. They attacked not only those against whom the order had been issued, but also those against whom no order had been issued: the Montanists, the [?], the Macedonians, the Sabbatians, and the rest. They even included the orthodox among them, falling upon everyone alike and openly plundering them, until the emperor heard about this, rebuked them, and threatened them severely.

In the second year after Emperor Tiberius became sole ruler, the wicked pagans of Baalbek, which is Heliopolis, who had openly been servants of Satan from the beginning, acted insolently toward the Christians. These Christians were few and poor among them, while the pagans all continually exulted arrogantly in their wealth and importance. Whenever they found an opportunity, they schemed to destroy the Christians and wipe out their memory from among them. They dared to mock Christ himself and those who believed in him, and they also dared to inflict many other evils on the Christians.

When the emperor learned of these things, he gave orders to a man who had previously been sent to the East by Justin because of the rebellion and uprising that the Jews and Samaritans had staged in Palestine. This man had gone down and subdued them, putting some to the sword, crucifying and destroying others, and subjecting them to harsh rule. His name was Theophilus. The emperor therefore gave him orders, and he went from Palestine to Heliopolis to act against the pagans. He arrested many of them and exacted punishment from them in proportion to their insolence, humiliating, crucifying, and killing them.

As he tortured them and demanded that they disclose the other pagans who shared their error, they gave him the names of many people like themselves in every region and city, throughout most of the cities of the East, and especially in Antioch the Great. He wrote and sent orders to the governors that the people named should be arrested and sent to him. Among those they named was a certain Rufinus Rufinianus [?], the chief priest in Antioch. Theophilus himself had also sent one of his own men to arrest him. He learned that the man was not there, but had gone to Edessa to see Anatolius, the governor and deputy prefect—that is, the man acting in the prefect’s place.

When the man who had gone to arrest him asked the governor and the bishop to give him an answer to take back, they gave him some of their own men, together with the church’s legal advocate, and sent him to Edessa, so that, if he found the man there, he could arrest him.

When those who had been sent reached Edessa, they learned that Rufinus was there. At night they went and surrounded the house to arrest him. It happened that the pagans there were celebrating a festival of Zeus, and they had gathered at Rufinus’s house to offer sacrifices. When they realized that the house was surrounded and that they were going to be arrested, they panicked and all fled. But when Rufinus realized that he had no way of escape, [?] he drew a knife and stabbed himself in the heart. He also slit open his belly [?], fell down, and died.

When they entered, they found there an old man afflicted with gout, who had been unable to escape, and an old woman, as well as Rufinus lying dead from his wounds, and all the sacrificial equipment. They arrested those they found and threatened them with death unless they told the truth about the identities of those who had gathered there. If they told the truth, they would live and not die. Out of fear, they identified everyone, including the governor and deputy prefect Anatolius, who had been with them.

He, however, thought he could devise schemes, though they would be of no help to him. He went and dressed himself in a traveling cloak [?], as though he had just come in from a journey. He put on leather leggings and traveling shoes [?], and went to [?] the bishop of the city. When the bishop heard that the governor had come, he was alarmed and said, ‘Why has the governor come now, at such an unusual hour?’

When he entered, he said to the bishop, ‘I have just come in from a journey. I was spending the night in such-and-such a village, and a dispute arose among us about the meaning of a certain passage of Scripture. That is why I have come to you before going to my residence, so that you can explain it to me.’

He did this as a trick, so that the bishop would testify that he had come to him straight from his journey. Thus, even if people said that he had been with those who offered sacrifices during the night, he could counter this with the excuse he had contrived. But as it is written, ‘The Lord is a God of knowledge, and schemes cannot stand before him,’ so this man’s schemes did not hold up.
