For immediately after he came down from the bishop’s house, those who had been sent met him and arrested him, saying, ‘Welcome, my lord prefect! We have had great need of Your Excellency. Kindly provide guarantors for a hundredweight [?], pledging that you will appear in Antioch within ten days.’

He began to protest, saying, ‘I have only just come in from a journey, and the bishop is my witness.’

They said to him, ‘Do not make excuses, my lord governor. Last night you performed a sacrifice to Zeus with Rufinus and the others who were with you, and here stand those who accuse you.’

When he began threatening them as though exercising his authority, saying, ‘You are obstructing public business,’ they told him, ‘Do not threaten us, my lord governor. No, by the life of Your Excellency, you will not leave here until you have provided guarantors.’

Thus, when he was pressed and realized that there was no escape, he agreed and provided guarantors that he would go up immediately to Antioch with them and with the officers of the law.

When, therefore, the records of what had happened in Edessa concerning those who had been discovered there also reached Antioch, he and his notary were summoned and arrested. They were questioned and offered false excuses. Finally, however, when his notary, whose name was Theodore, was subjected to torture and severe beatings, he made a deposition disclosing everything. As was reported, he also made a deposition against Gregory, the patriarch there, and Eulogius, who also came from there and later became patriarch in Alexandria. He stated that they had sacrificed a boy together with them at night in Daphne. They said that, when they sacrificed him, the whole city suddenly shook and trembled.

When these things were heard in the city, the whole city was shaken and thrown into turmoil. Various killings took place, and the church was shut. Gregory did not dare come down from the bishop’s residence, and no celebration of the liturgy was permitted in the church, nor the customary consecration of chrism on the Thursday of the Mysteries. People shouted confused cries. We ask to be excused from recording these or giving testimony concerning all these matters. For, according to what everyone was saying, records upon records concerning these things reached the emperor, and these matters were being discussed everywhere. Finally, it was thought that these things had been covered up out of regard for the Christian order, and so that the priesthood would not be disgraced and reviled.

Now Anatolius had placed an image of our Lord in his house, wishing to deceive people into thinking that he was a Christian by nature. He took many people with him and went to show it to them. But while he was showing it to them, the image turned around, with its back facing outward and its face inward toward the wall, so that trembling fell upon everyone who saw it. When Anatolius himself saw this, he turned it around and set it upright. Suddenly it turned around again, with its back facing outward. This happened three times. When they examined it closely, an image of Apollo was found inside it, behind its back, skillfully made so that it had not been recognizable or visible. The governor’s officers then threw him to the ground, kicked him, and dragged him by his hair to the governor’s headquarters, reporting all these things. As was reported, he too made a deposition concerning everything.

Theodore, his notary, died after exposing the bishops and the others, while he was being kept under guard [?]. Many people thought and said that he had been deliberately killed so that his deposition would be invalidated. We do not testify to this either. Many other things happened there that are beyond recounting and beyond the limits of this book.

When news of these events in Antioch, together with the records, reached the imperial city, the whole city, and even the merciful emperor himself, were shaken, disturbed, and moved to lamentation, along with the entire senate. These matters were being discussed in every part of the city.

Then those pagans were sent for and brought there. The emperor ordered some of the officials and lawyers to sit in judgment over them and investigate the truth of the affair. He strictly charged them and placed them under oath to judge without bias or favoritism. For many days they sat investigating the affair in the great imperial residence called that of Placidius. Everything they did was conducted in secret, and not one of these matters was made public. They took care that no one should learn of them, and nothing was disclosed outside. Everyone thought that bribery was at work and was concealing the truth.

Although many people were discovered to be adherents of paganism, the people of the city thought that the judges released whomever they wished—those who gave gold—and unjustly condemned whomever they wished. They thought that the investigation of the pagans had been relaxed and allowed to become corrupt, especially because the emperor himself had let the matter go and departed for Proconnesus, and the affair had not been investigated and disclosed for everyone to see.

There was much grumbling in the city, because people thought that the affair had been covered up with gold and passed over: now it had been dropped, the case against the pagans had been dismissed, and they themselves had been released. Then suddenly some men ran and gathered in the city's main street and began shouting, “Let the judges' bones be dug up! Let the pagans' bones be dug up! May the Christians' faith grow strong! Let the judges' bones be dug up!” They meant the judges who had been trying them, since they thought that these men had taken bribes and mishandled the case.

As they ran through the middle of the city shouting these cries, people came running from every quarter of the city and joined them. They became a vast crowd, fired with zeal for Christianity—more and more, for Christianity [?]—over a hundred thousand. The entire city was thrown into turmoil, and the shops were closed, along with all the silversmiths' shops—the silversmiths' shops [?]. Even Jews, Samaritans, and the other heretics came running from every direction and mingled with the crowd, preparing to burn the city and plunder other people's property.

The whole Christian populace rushed fiercely to the church against the bishop, insulting him with many different, shameful insults that are unfit to be recorded in writing. They thought that he was looking after the pagans' interests and that, because of the men of Antioch and Alexandria who had been spoken ill of in connection with paganism, he had gone in and pleaded for the affair to be covered up and passed over. For this reason they even threatened him with death. The bishop's residence was surrounded on every side, and the crowd was ready to burn it down, had they not been restrained out of concern for the church. The Jews and heretics were threatening to burn the church too, as they later admitted before the prefect.

One of the church's legal advocates who came out to confront them was thrown down and given a bitter beating. Then they all ran to Placidia, where the pagans were being tried, insulting the judges, who were patricians and magistrates, as well as the other clerks and advocates, and threatening to kill them too. When they reached Placidia—Placidia—they tore out doors and windows and smashed benches and chests. They entered the courtyard, raging over the pagans.

They broke open one chest and found it full of hundred-pound lots of gold. When they saw them, they drew back [?]. The man guarding them wanted to calm their fury and, thinking that they would immediately seize them, said to them, “My lords, my lord, do not make a disturbance! If you want gold, here is gold!” But the great crowd shouted as though with one mouth, “We are not robbers; we are Christians! We have gathered for Christ, and we want to exact vengeance on the pagans on behalf of Christianity. You look after your gold, because we will not touch it.”

They smashed everything they came across, even the statues—the statues—taking down and smashing every one they found, whoever it belonged to. In this way they found two of the pagans who were being held, a man and a woman. They seized them and ran to the seashore. They took a boat and seized the executioner who served the city, saying to him, “Set a fire and burn them!” But because he was afraid of the prefect, they themselves threw them into the boat and set it on fire. They threw the executioner in with them too. He managed to leap out of the fire and fall into the sea, and although he was badly burned, he did not die. The others, however, were burned and sank into the sea.

After this, the countless crowds that had gathered ran and broke into all the prisons. They broke down the doors and brought out everyone who was imprisoned, shouting, “The pagans are being released! Why are Christians being held?” Then they also ran to the praetor's headquarters, broke down the doors and chests and all the cases containing documents concerning Christians, brought them all out, tore them up, and threw them away. They also brought out everyone who was imprisoned there.

From there they ran again to the prefect's headquarters. When he heard, he came outside to meet them as they made a disturbance and shouted, “Let the pagans' bones be dug up!” Although he himself was widely said to be a pagan, he too began shouting with them, “Let the pagans' bones be dug up, and may the Christians' faith grow strong! Your zeal is good! Look, I too am shouting with you. You know that I was not the one who tried the pagans. I was not even entrusted with the case, nor were they tried in my headquarters. So do not make a disturbance.”

With these words he managed to restrain their fury, so that they did not lay hands on him and burn down his headquarters, as they were preparing to do. After this they turned to shouting at him again, “Come out with us to Prokensos [?] at once!” In his fear he said, “I will come out.” He hurried aboard his boat without the usual ceremony and without even putting on his official dress, trying to escape the fury of that boundless crowd. In this way he hurried out to the emperor.

He informed him of these events and said that more than twenty thousand of them had decided to come out there. While he was still speaking, they arrived, shouting various cries. Along with these they made accusations, saying, “Why was the investigation into the pagans mishandled and covered up? Why did bribery with gold—gold—go on and conceal the truth?” Alongside their shouting against the pagans, they also turned to shouting insults at the Arians, with a different aim. The whole palace was alarmed, and things were said that are unfit to be put in writing.

Then the emperor sent them an order: “Do not make a disturbance. Go back into the city. We ourselves will come in at once and do what you wish. We will not neglect the affair.” In this way the crowd was pacified, and the force of their savagery subsided. They returned to the city, and the riot died down, while they waited for the emperor's arrival and the matter's conclusion.

Then the emperor gave orders, and a substantial force of armed men was assembled, so that, if they rioted again, he could order the sword to be used against them. Afterward he entered the city and ordered a public audience [?]. That is, when the people assembled and came up and began shouting confused cries at him, he sent them this message: “Remain quiet and peaceful, knowing that everyone is repaid according to his deeds. So keep free of disturbance and disorder.”

Immediately upon entering, before these events, he dismissed Sebastian the prefect and appointed another prefect, [?] Dionysius, whose name was Julian. He ordered him to begin making arrests, subject them to torture, and investigate who the remaining people were. As soon as he began arresting and questioning them, he discovered that many of them were Jews, and others were Samaritans, Montanists, and others. The prefect, acting shrewdly so as not to stir up a conflict against himself arising from the Christians’ zeal, began arresting these people and questioning them under the lash: “Even if the Christians were stirred by zeal for the preservation of Christianity, you murderous Jews and misguided heretics—what zeal led you to riot and mingle with them?”

They all confessed to this: “When we saw a large crowd, we went in among them so that we might get something and seize some plunder.” They also confessed this: “We were preparing to burn the Christians’ churches, thinking that they would be arrested and subjected to torture, while we would remain unidentified,” along with other evil deeds that they confessed under the lash. Some of these he condemned to death by crucifixion; others he condemned to be put away [?]; and others he sent into various places of exile. As a result, no Christian could find anything to criticize or say about this, except: “These people are being repaid justly—indeed, justly.”

Then he began arresting Christians, treating them mercifully. They were taken around the city as though to frighten them. They were put on public display, and so that their backs would not be seen without wounds, he ordered red ochre to be rubbed on their backs, to make it appear that their backs had been flayed by blows. This was especially so with the little boys, of whom there were many among them. Some of them even laughed as they rode on mules and were taken around the city.

One of them was arrested and brought in to stand before the prefect. He said to him, “What is your occupation, and who are you?”

He said to him, “I am a Christian, a shopkeeper.”

He said to him, “Since you are a shopkeeper, why were you found in the riot instead of staying quietly in your own shop? For this reason we order you to be flogged.”

When they seized him to flog him, he said, “By the emperor’s head and life, if I am being flogged for Christ, you may not only subject me to lashes upon lashes and scraping combs, but afterward take my head as well—by the head of Emperor Tiberius!”

When the prefect heard this, he was alarmed and said, “This man wants to become a martyr at my hands! Who am I, then? Am I Trajan? Get him out!” And so he sent him out without his receiving a single blow.

He then went in and persuaded the emperor to decree a pardon for the Christians and order that Christians should no longer be arrested, since it was out of fervent zeal that they had assembled and shouted.

The merciful emperor ordered that their offense should be forgiven and that they should no longer be arrested. And so the Christians were pardoned. But Jews continued to be arrested and tried whenever they were found.

After all these things, the mild Emperor Tiberius wished to show that he had not neglected, and was not neglecting, matters concerning reverence for God. He therefore ordered all the officials and all the senators to assemble together—all the patricians, former consuls, illustrious dignitaries, former prefects, deputy prefects, and the rest of the entire senate. They were to assemble together in the prefect’s praetorium, and all the records of proceedings against the pagans, whether in the East or in the West, were to be read before them. He issued an order that anyone who failed to appear should be stripped of his belt of office. Thus, under this strict command, they all assembled together and sat the whole day, from morning until evening, fasting and exhausted. All the records of proceedings were read before them, and first they condemned to death Anatolius, whom the account mentioned above, who had formerly been governor and deputy prefect in Edessa. First, after tortures that brought him near death, he was thrown to the wild beasts. After being cruelly mauled by them, he was then taken away and crucified.

Before this, another man, his associate, whose name was Theodore—they had served demons together in all the practices of paganism—had undergone many bitter tortures and had himself confessed to many things. To keep him for further tortures and questioning about others, he was sent to be imprisoned and held in the praetor’s praetorium. That very night he died there. Many people thought that he had killed himself, because a sentence of death was about to be issued against him as well. Because he had sacrificed to demons after baptism, a judgment was issued against him that his corpse should be burned, even though he was dead. Others, however, out of natural compassion, neglected to do this. But he ordered that he should be given a donkey’s burial, dragged away and thrown outside.

This, then, was in addition to the two whom the crowd burned, a man and a woman. That man was the son of this Theodore. These people died in this way, besides many others who had been arrested and imprisoned and were being prepared for torture and interrogation. There were still others for whom men had been sent to Syria, Asia, and everywhere else, to arrest them and bring them to the imperial city.

Afterward, many others were named, and every day people were arrested and added to their number, until all the prisons were filled with them. Clergy of the churches were also named, arrested, and accused of many wicked pagan practices. A sentence was issued against them that they should be thrown to the wild beasts and afterward burned with fire. Thus they received here the punishment they deserved. As for there, however, only that fearsome Judge of righteousness knows the sentence awaiting them.

When so many people had been named and arrested, the judges appointed over them were overwhelmed by their numbers. Finally, they were removed from the praetorium of the city prefect, who was himself suspected of being one of them, and handed over to the praetor. From then on, the judges sat and conducted trials in his praetorium. Finally, they sat and conducted trials in the public hall, until the death of Emperor Tiberius. When Maurice succeeded him as emperor, he too displayed the same zeal and ordered that the pagans who presented themselves as Christians in name, but in practice served idols, should be tried and investigated. Thus every day they are brought to trial and receive repayment for their deeds, here and there.

An account of the suffering and distress of Eustochius, who was formerly bishop of Jerusalem. Because he stood against the pagans with fierce zeal and rebuked them, they devised schemes against him, unjust pretexts, and false accusations. When he was tried here in the imperial city by unjust judges, who were themselves secret pagans, they unjustly deposed him from the episcopate. After his deposition, he did not give himself over to wandering here and there. Instead, he immediately went and took a cell at the sanctuary of Saint Sergius in Hormisdas [?], and shut himself up there for eighteen years. The emperors themselves, the chamberlains, and the entire senatorial order, both men and women, regarded him as a righteous man and constantly went to pay him their respects. For he was an old man, dignified with gray hair, lucid in his speech and teaching, and well versed in the Holy Scriptures.

Now, in the third year of the reign of the victorious Tiberius, reckoned from his becoming emperor, Satan filled the heart of one of his servants during the night. He took a silver lampstand that was shining before Eustochius, raised it, and struck him with it, smashing his brain. As Eustochius cried out in pain and said, “Why do you do this, brother?” he turned and struck him again in the belly with its spike—with its spike—and tore it open, spilling out his intestines. He died immediately.

When the rest of his servants began shouting and wailing, the guards stationed below them heard and ran upstairs toward the sound. They reached out to seize the man, but he drew a knife and struck one of them. Another drew his sword and struck him on the shoulder, bringing him down. In this way they managed to overpower him.

Suddenly there was an uproar and shouting. A great crowd of people, groaning, ran from every direction to see that dreadful and sorrowful sight. News reached the emperor while he was outside the city at the [?] of the Hebdomon. Immediately, without delay, he ordered a [?] and came in. When he saw Eustochius dead, he wailed and wept like a woman over the husband of her youth, together with the others who saw him—a sight filled with bitter anguish.

He gave orders, and that murderous servant was handed over to the prefect to die a hideous and bitter death. The emperor then immediately departed. The servant was thrown to wild beasts. After they had bitten and mangled him, both his hands and both his feet were cut off. His trunk was then thrown into a boat together with his hands and feet, and it was burned and sunk in the sea. He received the reward for his deed, and what is written was fulfilled in him: “Woe to the wicked evildoer, for he will be repaid for what his hands have done.”

Now the conversion of the pagans took place in the days of Emperor Justinian, in the four regions of Asia, Caria, Phrygia, and Lydia. It began, with God’s help, in the mountainous district of Tralles in Asia. Many thousands within the jurisdiction of this city turned away from the error of idol worship, and he built twenty-four churches, while four monasteries were newly built among them.

The first was this great monastery, which is the subject our account has undertaken to describe. It was built in a village called Arira, in those rugged mountains, on the site of a large and famous pagan temple. According to what some of their old men told us, a thousand [?]—one thousand five hundred temples throughout all these provinces were under its authority. They said that every year they assembled there, received instruction, and obtained rules from it concerning how their priests and all the pagan peoples everywhere should conduct themselves.

Through a revelation from God, John, who was mentioned above, uprooted this temple down to its foundations and built firmly in its place this monastery called Arira. It stands in rugged, inaccessible mountains, among all these churches. He also built the other three monasteries, one above it in those mountains and two below it, placing them under its authority. He built the monastery itself solidly and spaciously, at great expense, with funds given to him by Emperor Justinian, together with funds for all these other churches and monasteries. The emperor issued a command and drew up three pragmatic decrees, so that this great monastery should have authority over all these churches and monasteries, instructing them, looking after them, and regulating all their activities.

From its very beginning, Satan was envious of this monastery and stirred up trials and fierce opposition against it from every direction. The demons that had long lived and rested there over the blood of the sacrifices offered to them there—on which they settled like flies on festering sores—openly appeared in this way, fighting and showing themselves.

At the very beginning of its construction, they lifted one of the builders, a certain cleric, up into the air and threw him down onto a cliff. From there another cliff below it, still steeper, received him. John stood with the others and watched him as he flew down headfirst, face downward, striking one cliff after another. He fell still farther and struck a rock in the river. The height from which he fell was no less than a thousand cubits.

As they watched him falling, they cried out, ‘Lord, have mercy!’ They thought his brains must have spilled out and been splashed over all the cliffs he had struck, and that all his entrails must have been spread across them. They ran down, wailing, to gather up at least the remains of his bones and bury them. But they found him sitting upright and looking at them. When they saw that he was alive, they were astonished and rejoiced. They gave thanks to God, who had rescued him from the bitter death contrived by the filthy demons. Christ had not even allowed him to suffer a wound, apart from a slight grazing of his nostrils. Everyone who saw and heard about the miracle that our Lord Jesus had performed was amazed.

After the year in which the construction of the monastery of Arira was completed, which was in the sixth year, the bishop of Tralles was stirred by envy against the monastery. He swore, saying, “I will make it an estate belonging to my church, and I will live in it throughout the summer.” He was also quarreling with John. So he went up to Emperor Justinian—Justin [?]—to lodge a complaint against him. He went in, explained the matter to him, and urged him to order that he himself should have authority and control over it, and that John should have nothing to do with it. But when the emperor heard these things from him, he said to him, “No, by Christ! You shall not enter your church or your city without John’s direction and permission. You could not even administer the church to which you were wrongfully appointed, yet you want to seize my monastery, which was built with my knowledge and by my command!” Then he ordered him not to leave the imperial city before John arrived. After some time John also came in, and the emperor told him everything the bishop had said to him and everything he himself had answered. He ordered John to go out and personally administer the city’s church and its hospice, and the bishop was to have no authority to do anything without his permission.

For he also stirred up many other trials and attacks against that monastery and against the twenty-four new churches that John himself had recently built and established around that monastery, among the pagans whom he had baptized and made Christians in the mountains of the city of Tralles. But God in his mercy brought all the evil one’s envy against them to nothing and has preserved them for the praise of his name to this very day.

Now while Eutychius the patriarch was full of deadly threats against the Orthodox party and was threatening them with harsh oaths, saying, “I will not leave a single one of them in this city, or its surroundings, or the other cities,” and while he was making these threats and menaces, his end suddenly overtook him, and he met with disgrace. On that day all his plans came to nothing and perished, along with all his threats and menaces. He had gone to great lengths in denying the resurrection of bodies and fighting against the words, “You were crucified for us.” There were very many things that deserved to be included in the accounts about him, but because of their great number we have left them all aside.

When Eutychius departed from this world on the fifth day of the month of Nisan, John the deacon was seized to succeed him. He had served as treasurer to John of Sirmium, who preceded Eutychius. He was an ascetic man, devoted to fasting and keeping vigil, who lived continually in seclusion in a cell within the Great Church itself. He was seized and entreated to agree to accept the primacy. While he was resisting, Emperor Tiberius ordered that he be taken to the palace and kept under guard there. The emperor and the whole senate pressed him, and with great difficulty they managed to persuade him. He solemnly declared, “I will not abandon my rule, and I will not meet with people until the ninth hour.” After much had happened, he was ordained. They used to say that he maintained this same discipline, receiving no one until the ninth hour, according to his former practice. People marveled at him, for they said that he lay on his face praying all day, though he was weak and as dry as a piece of wood.

Now those who, in the days of Eutychius, had been accustomed to attack orthodox people, and heretics as well, like robbers under the pretext of religion, and to seize their possessions, began as usual to ask him to give them permission, as his predecessor had done, to go and plunder people, drag them away, and bring them to be confined in prison. But when he learned of these things, he said to them, “Go, sit down, and keep quiet. I will not allow you to go and attack and plunder people, so that God and his holy Church are blasphemed.” They said to him, “Eutychius gave us these orders.” He said to them, “I order that there should be peace and tranquility in my days. But if you invoke Eutychius as your excuse, go to him now, and [?] do whatever he orders you.” There were many remarkable things that could have been written about him, but because of the length of the account, we have confined the stories about him to a few.

While Count Maurice was in the East in command of the armies, he and Mundhir, king of the Arabs, took counsel together about invading Persian territory jointly. After traveling for days, they reached the region opposite Beth Aramaye, where the Persian king’s city was, and found that the bridge ahead of them had been cut. They had expected to cross it and capture the royal city. Instead, they fell into a quarrel with one another, because Maurice suspected Mundhir of having sent word to the Persians so that they dismantled the bridge. Thus they returned without accomplishing anything, having become embroiled in hostility and strife with one another. From then on they began writing accusations against one another to Emperor Tiberius. The emperor made great efforts to reconcile them, but could not. Maurice then went up to the emperor and accused Mundhir bitterly and vehemently. The emperor accepted his accusations and became filled with fierce anger against Mundhir. He sought some means of outwitting him and arranging for him to be arrested and brought to the imperial capital.

Then Magnus the Syrian, the curator, wishing to win the emperor’s favor, said to him, “If you command it, I will bring him here to you in chains.” Magnus was Mundhir’s friend and patron, and Mundhir trusted him, since he acted as his representative before the emperor. The emperor was delighted and sent him off. He traveled down to the East by the imperial post, stage by stage, to his village called Huwwarin, which he had also made into a city, surrounding it with a wall and building a church in it. He had gone down on the pretext of consecrating this church. When he went down, he also took the patriarch of Antioch with him, to make it all the easier to deceive Mundhir into coming.

Then he deceitfully sent Mundhir this message: “Since I have come for the dedication of this church and am worn out from the journey—otherwise I would have come and paid my respects to you—and since I long to see you in good health, I ask you to come to me at once, without bringing a large body of troops with you. I want you to stay with me for some days so that we may rest together. Do not incur great expenses for a large army, but come yourself with only a few men.”

When Mundhir received the reply from Magnus, he rejoiced. Immediately, without hesitation and in confidence, he came to him as to a dear friend, without a large force, having no suspicion of him at all. Magnus, taking care not to reveal his wicked treachery, welcomed him warmly. He ordered a banquet to be prepared and said, “Dismiss those who came with you.” Mundhir said to him, “Look, as you ordered, I have not come with a large force. When I return, I cannot travel without a force, even a small one.” He said to him, “Dismiss them, and when you leave, send for them, and they will come.” But Mundhir, being a man of great understanding, was displeased by what was happening and began to grow suspicious. He sent word to his troops to withdraw a little and wait for him. When they had been dismissed, Magnus secretly ordered the troops with him to make ready, along with the duke who had been appointed to accompany Magnus.

In the evening he began to say to him, “My lord patrician, accusations have been brought against you before the emperor. He has ordered you to go up to him, set his mind at ease, and convince him that what has been said—said against you—is not true.” Then Mundhir answered him, saying, “After all these labors, I do not think it right that accusations against me should be accepted. For I am the emperor’s servant, and I do not refuse to go up. But at this time I cannot abandon my encampment and let the Persians’ Arabs come and take my wives and children captive and seize everything I possess.”

Then the armed Roman troops appeared. Magnus threatened him and said, “If you do not go up willingly, I will put you in irons, mount you on a donkey, and send you off that way.” When the treachery was revealed to Mundhir, and he saw that Magnus had stripped him of his troops, imprisoned him, and handed him over to the Roman troops to guard, he was brought low and subdued like a lion of the wilderness confined in a trap.

When his troops learned of this, they surrounded the fortress and prepared to burn it. But when they saw that the Romans had come out into the open and prepared for battle, they withdrew. As for Mundhir, the Romans surrounded him and led him out to go up under heavy guard. He reached the imperial city. When he entered, the emperor ordered him to lodge where he had lodged before. An allowance was assigned to him and those with him. So he remained, without being received in audience, with one of his wives, two of his sons, and one of his daughters with him.

Mundhir’s four sons, especially the eldest, whose name was Nu‘man—a man more cunning and better prepared for war than Mundhir himself—gathered their forces and attacked the fortress of Magnus, who had also gone up to the emperor. Without taking people captive, killing them, or burning anything, they plundered and carried off everything: gold and silver, bronze and iron, all articles of wool or linen, grain, wine, and oil. They seized all the herds of livestock of every kind that fell into their hands, all the herds of cattle, and all the flocks of sheep and goats. The Arab forces swept through and plundered all the villages of Arabia and the surrounding parts of Syria. They gathered possessions and vast quantities of booty beyond counting, then withdrew deep into the inner desert. There they established a large camp and divided the spoils, remaining alert and ready for battle and keeping watch on every side. They continued to go out, plunder, seize things, and bring them into the desert, until the whole eastern region, as far as the sea, trembled before them. People fled into the cities and did not dare to appear before them. When the rulers of the region and the commanders of the armies sent them a message asking, ‘Why are you doing all these things in this way?’ they sent back this reply: ‘Why did the emperor carry our father away like a captive, after all the labors, victories, and acts of valor in which he labored and fought on his behalf? He has cut off our allowances, and we have nothing to live on. This is why we are compelled to do these things. It is enough that we are not killing or burning.’ Finally, they went to the city of Bostra and surrounded it, saying to its inhabitants, ‘Give us our father’s weapons and the rest of the equipment of his royal office that is deposited with you. Otherwise, we will uproot, burn, and kill everything we can, both in your city and throughout its territory.’ When the military governor, a distinguished and well-known man, heard this, he became angry, gathered his army, and marched out, despising them as mere Arabs. They drew up their forces against him and overpowered him, killing him and many of his soldiers. When the inhabitants of the city saw this, they were terrified and sent them a message: ‘Stop fighting. We will give you what belongs to you. Take it in peace.’ So they brought out their father’s equipment to them. They took it and returned to their camp in the desert, but they did not stop plundering and seizing things for a long time.

When Tiberius heard these things about Mundhir’s sons, he was greatly embittered. He sent Magnus back again to make Mundhir’s brother king of the Arabs in his place, and, if he could, to subdue and capture Mundhir’s sons, whether through deceit, persuasion and disturbances, or battle. The governors of the cities and the military commanders were also ordered to accompany him with a large force, and so he went down with a great display of power. First he appointed Mundhir’s brother king; this man died twenty days later. Finally, [?] to them, to him, while [?] deceitfully.

As for [?] ordinations, he was responsible for them. Later, too, when Paul, who had become patriarch of Antioch, arrived, they managed these matters together. Thus, when Theodosius had grown old and very infirm and could no longer stand and celebrate the Eucharist, he instructed and authorized Longinus, who was still a priest, to stand in his place. Longinus celebrated on his behalf for the rest of his life. He also directed that Longinus should become bishop of the people who had become disciples and were called the Nobatae. We will also bring the account concerning them to mind in what follows.

In the communion of Pope Theodosius there was an elderly man named Julian, an exemplary priest. Now spiritual zeal for that erring people came upon this man, who was in the eastern border region of Thebes, farther inland than Egypt. That people was not even subject to the Roman Empire, but instead received tribute so that it would not invade Egypt and take its inhabitants captive.

Concerned for that people, the blessed Julian went in and spoke to Empress Theodora, of blessed memory, asking her to concern herself with their conversion. The empress, who burned with zeal for God, gladly welcomed this and promised to do everything necessary for that people to turn away from the error of idol worship. In her joy over this, she informed the victorious Emperor Justinian. She promised and was making arrangements to send the blessed Julian there.

But when the emperor heard that she intended to send someone from among the opponents of the council, he was not pleased. He devised a plan to write to his own bishops in Thebes, so that they would go in and make disciples of the people and establish the council’s name there. He too now became zealous, and hurriedly sent envoys ahead with gold, baptismal garments, and gifts of honor for the king of that people. He also sent letters to the duke of the Thebaid, instructing him to look after his envoy and convey him to that people.

When the empress learned of this, she too acted promptly and shrewdly, writing letters to the duke of the Thebaid and dispatching an imperial courier. She said: “Since the emperor and I have decided to send an envoy to the people of the Nobades, I too am sending a blessed man named Julian. I want this man of mine to reach that people before the emperor’s envoy. You must understand that if you allow his envoy to enter there before mine, and do not delay him with excuses until this blessed man of mine arrives and you convey him across and he enters, you will not remain alive. Instead, I will send someone there and have your head taken off.”

When the duke of the Thebaid had received these instructions, the emperor’s envoy also reached him. He lodged him, saying to him, “Be patient while we look for pack animals and get them ready, and prepare men who know the desert. Then you can take them and go in.” In this way he lodged him and delayed him until the envoys—the merciful empress’s own envoys—arrived. They found the pack animals and the men ready, and that very day, without delay, they took the animals as though by force and set out ahead of the others.

The duke sent word to the emperor’s envoy: “You should know that, after I had made preparations for you and was just about to send for you, the empress’s envoys arrived. They fell upon me by force, took the pack animals, and went on their way. You know better than I do how much the empress is to be feared. That is why I did not dare oppose them. But wait for me a little longer, until I make fresh preparations for you, so that you too can go in peace.”

When the envoy learned this, he tore his clothes, uttering many threats and hurling abuse. Then, after some days, he too set out and went after them, unaware of the trick that had been played on him.

For when the blessed Julian and the envoys accompanying him reached the country, they sent word to the king and the nobles to inform them. They sent troops out to meet them, welcomed them joyfully, and brought them into their country to their king. He too received them graciously. Julian also handed over the empress’s letters, which were read and their contents made known. They also received splendid gifts of honor, many baptismal robes, and everything else in abundance. Immediately, rejoicing, they committed themselves, renounced all the error of their ancestors, and confessed the God of the Christians, saying, “He is the one true God, and there is no other besides him.”

After instructing and teaching them at length, he informed them—and had informed them beforehand and taught them beforehand—of this also: “Certain disputes about the faith have arisen among the Christians. Because of this, when the blessed Theodosius was also required to accept it and would not consent, the emperor removed him from his throne. The empress, however, welcomed him and rejoiced in him, because he stood firm in the orthodox faith and left his throne for its sake. That is why she sent us to you, so that you too might follow Pope Theodosius, be baptized in his faith, and preserve his truth. The emperor has also sent envoys to you, and they are now coming behind us.” They taught them how to receive these envoys and what answer to give them.

When they had been firmly established in all these matters, the emperor’s envoy also arrived. He too entered and gave their king letters and gifts of honor. They also began to instruct them, as they had been commanded, saying, “Our emperor, the emperor of the Romans, sends you this message: ‘If you become Christians, join the church and those who hold to it. Do not go astray after those who have been expelled from the church.’”

When the king of the Nobades and his nobles heard this, they answered them, saying, “We accept the gifts of honor from the emperor of the Romans, and we too are sending him a gift of honor. But we do not accept his faith. Rather, if we are deemed worthy to become Christians, we will follow Pope Theodosius, whom the emperor drove out and removed from his church because he would not accept the emperor’s corrupt faith. If we are fleeing paganism and error, we will not agree to fall once more into corrupt faith.” Thus they dismissed the envoys, having put these very things in writing.

The blessed Julian remained with them for two years, suffering greatly from the burning heat. He used to relate that from the third hour until the tenth, stripped and wrapped in a linen cloth, he would go with all the people of the country into caves filled with water and sit there, with nothing out of the water except his nostrils. Nevertheless, he persevered, instructed the king, his nobles, and many of the people with him, and baptized them. He had also brought with him a bishop from the Thebaid, an elderly man named Theodore. After teaching them and setting things in order, he entrusted them to that bishop, departed from them, and reached Constantinople. In our presence and theirs, he was received by the empress with great honor. He related many remarkable things about that numerous people, which we have refrained from writing down because there were so many of them, and have confined ourselves to these few details alone.

On the day of his departure from this life, then, Pope Theodosius remembered that people, especially since the blessed Julian, who had made them disciples, had died a short time before, and Empress Theodora had also departed this life. He directed that the blessed Longinus should go there, as a zealous man capable of fully converting them and strengthening them in Christianity. Immediately after the pope’s death, Longinus became bishop for that place and prepared to leave. When he had put his belongings aboard a ship to depart, there were men whose teeth, as it is written, were spears and arrows, and whose tongue was like a sharp sword. They went in and said to the emperor, “You should know that Longinus has become a bishop, that he is an enemy of our palace, and that he has put his belongings aboard a ship to depart. If he goes—for he is an influential man—and enters among that people, he will immediately stir them up to wage war and take captives from the land of the Romans. Now give orders for him to be arrested.”

When the emperor learned this, he was stirred to anger and gave orders, and Longinus was arrested. They went up, and he took his belongings off the ship. Thus he was not allowed to leave. Three years passed after this, while he waited for an opportunity. Finally, realizing that he was being watched and would not be allowed to leave, he changed his appearance, putting a wig on his head, for he was very bald. Then, taking two young men with him, he escaped, and God delivered him. He went and entered that country, where he was received with great honor and great joy. He began again to make disciples of them all, enlightening and teaching them. He established a church there, appointed clergy, and taught them the order of worship and all the practices of Christianity.

When he escaped and the emperor learned of it, he became extremely angry. He ordered all the sea crossings to be secured and all the roads to be watched. Letters were sent to every region, but all these measures proved useless. Longinus himself persuaded the king of that people to send a chief ambassador to the emperor of the Romans with gifts and tokens of honor. When the ambassador was received and honored before our eyes, and so on, he expressed his gratitude to Longinus, saying, “Although we were Christians in name, we did not learn what Christianity was in practice until Longinus came among us.” While he recounted many great things about him, the emperor remained bitter toward him, though he said nothing.

When Longinus had spent about six years in that country, Satan, who envies good things, envied him and sought a way to drive him away and bring him out of there, and through him to cause scandal, division, and disruption in the church. He arranged for letters to be written to him by the head of the clergy of Alexandria, Theodosius the archpriest, and by Theodore, his sister’s son, the archdeacon. They summoned him to leave that country and come to the region around Alexandria, so that they could make him their pope and he could help the church. This was the beginning of the trouble and division.

When Longinus received these letters, he was stirred up and burned with fierce zeal. He disregarded all fear of death and began preparing to leave that country and carry out everything these letters instructed him to do. When the king and all his nobles learned of this, they gathered and tried to prevent him from leaving. But he showed them the letters, saying, “The business for which I have been instructed to leave concerns the whole church, and I cannot refuse to go.” They continued pleading with him, mourning and weeping, saying, “Once again, as we were until now, we are being left as orphans without a father.” And so, with sorrow and bitter mourning, they let him go and supplied him with provisions.

He left and came to Theodore, the elderly bishop of Philae in the Upper Thebaid, and showed him the letters. He consulted him about what had been written, asking whether it might be possible for him to accompany him. But because of his very advanced age, he could not. For it was nearly fifty years since he had been made bishop by Timothy, the predecessor of the blessed Theodosius. Nevertheless, he too agreed with the tenor of the letters and drew up a letter of authorization for Longinus to represent him and take his place, giving his assent to everything he would do.

So he left and came to Mareotis, to the place specified in the letters to him. He was considering what to do, trembling and afraid that his arrival in Roman territory after his escape might become known, and that he might be arrested and die a terrible death. Because of this, his heart trembled.

Now two bishops, John from the monastery of Saint Bassus and George the Urtian, who had been appointed at that time but was not yet permitted to exercise his episcopal office, were sent at that time by the eastern synod to Longinus and to Theodore of Philae, who was mentioned above. Their mission concerned the readmission of Paul of Antioch after his ordeal and his flight: whether they agreed to receive him and enter into communion with him.

As they were preparing to go to him in his own country, they learned that he had left his country and gone down to Egypt, and they followed him. Following reports of his whereabouts, they found him in Libya, outside Alexandria, at a place called Mareotis. He received them joyfully. When he read the letters, he was delighted with them and said, “God has brought you at a good time. Indeed, he has sent you now especially for this purpose: to lend us a hand in establishing the church. This is why I too, when I received a letter, set out and came from a distant country: so that there might be a patriarch in Alexandria.”

But they said, “How can we appoint a patriarch without instructions from our own patriarch? Rather, if this is what you want to do, let him also be present. He is not far away, and we will go and bring him.” After much discussion between them, they went and brought Patriarch Paul from nearby, as is reported, dressed in Roman clothing, to the region of Libya. They found Longinus traveling about, investigating and diligently searching for a man suitable for the office of chief priest. When they found him, they went together to the desert of the hermits, farther inland than the blessed Saint Menas, which is called Rhamnin. There they found the abbot of the monastery, a virtuous man named Theodore, who was Syrian by birth.

They began speaking to him, asking him to offer himself to become pope in Alexandria. When he heard this, he was alarmed, declined and tried to escape, even resorting to oaths and making declarations against himself. Eventually they bound him under an anathema if he should refuse this or speak against it. Thus they seized him by force, against his will, while he wept and wailed, and Longinus himself and these two bishops ordained him. Paul, as they swore, did not participate with them in his ordination, because he had not yet been released and received back after the lapse that had befallen him. In the end, however, although he was not found to have participated in his ordination, he agreed to the remaining proceedings, accepted him and entered into communion with him. It is reported that they even exchanged synodical letters as the patriarchs of Antioch and Alexandria.

Thus they all thought—and thought that all of them had performed a great deed—that they had acted and carried out the matter in accordance with the canons, bringing about the union and establishment of the church of Syria and Alexandria.

But because a bishop had been appointed for the Alexandrians without their knowledge, which was not right, the outcome was the opposite for them all. It brought trials, confusion, disputes, schisms and divisions upon the whole church in the East and throughout Egypt, and became the cause of many evils, both for each of those individuals personally and also for the fierce populace of Alexandria, causing them to descend into cunning and savage behavior without order or restraint.

When, therefore, the Alexandrians finally received the letters of Longinus and the bishops with him, as well as those of Theodore himself, concerning everything they had done, they learned that Theodore had become their patriarch. He himself had also addressed synodical letters to them, first setting out the truth of the faith and the other appropriate matters, writing to them henceforth as to his own church. He also spoke arrogantly: “It was for fear of those in authority,” he said, “and so that no disturbance would be stirred up, that we did not enter the city. Everything took place according to canonical order, with your approval and decree,” and much more besides.

When the leading clergy, those already mentioned above, and the others learned all this, they became agitated and disturbed and were roused to anger over everything that had happened. They also stirred up, inflamed, and disturbed all the rest of the clergy, bringing them into a frenzy and barbarous savagery against Longinus and Theodore, whom he had appointed, and against Paul, on whose account especially they had become so savagely inflamed, and against the others with them. They despised them, insulted them, and repudiated them, stirring up disturbances and quarrels against them in the church and the city. With disorderly cries and chants they said, “Let us all gather now, immediately, and without delay make ourselves a pope here, from among ourselves and by ourselves.” These men, in turn, were stirring up and agitating [?] so that they might appoint one of their own, the Andronicus mentioned above. Thus, as has been said, they themselves would henceforth exercise authority and leadership, controlling and holding all the administration of the church of Alexandria.

But they saw and learned that neither the clergy nor the citizens approved of him or wanted him, because shortly before, as was reported, a demon had even been seen manifesting itself in him. Then he indicated that he himself was now asking not to be appointed. When they saw that this plan had failed and that there was no longer any possibility of appointing one of themselves, they cunningly contrived to appoint an insignificant and inferior man. Their scheme was that he should possess only the name and outward appearance of the office, while, through ignorance and simplicity, he would remain excluded from all administration and everything appropriate to such leadership. In this way they themselves would command him, turn him this way and that, and administer affairs, while he would be unable to command them.

This they actually carried out and accomplished. They selected and brought forward an elderly deacon of middling rank, a simple and uneducated man named Peter. He had also been a companion of the blessed Theodosius during his exile. When they chose to appoint him, they had only one bishop available, whose name was John. Canonical accusations were also pending against him. So, in their haste, they rushed upon two visiting bishops who had previously been ordained by the blessed Jacob for Syria. Both had the same name, Antoninus and Antoninus. They seized them by force and made the aforementioned deacon Peter a second bishop at the same time, at [?], after they had received word that the synodical letters of the earlier bishop, Theodore, had been received.

They did not judge and examine the matter in an orderly and canonical way, to determine whether the earlier appointment had been made in due order and properly, according to the canons or contrary to them. Instead, they were stirred by bitter resentment and the bonds of wrongdoing. Anger commanded them, and brutal insolence—brutal insolence—directed them with barbarous impetuosity. They appointed, installed, and proclaimed a second bishop on the same throne, out of resentment against the first, bringing disturbance, confusion, division, and strife upon the whole church. This is indeed now established and visibly at work: it came about according to the pleasure and will of the Accuser, who brought these things about and accomplished them.

Like Pharaoh’s people and a people of foreign speech, they became puffed up and launched into all this confusion, disorder, and barbarity. They did not entertain even a single orderly intention, so as to judge and examine whether the first man, whose appointment they had learned of, had been appointed properly or improperly, as he supposed. Instead, they proceeded into all this barbarous savagery, so as to set up another over him. Nor did they restrain the impetuosity of their savagery with the restraints—with the restraints of their savagery [?]—of the fear of God, or reflect within themselves on the evils, divisions, quarrels, factions, conflicts, and disturbances that would arise from this in the church of God.

And indeed, as had been anticipated, this became manifest, happened, and was fulfilled. This evil, conflict, and warfare took hold between the two parties and has continued until now, some eight years, more or less, since that time. These years call for the lamentations of the sorrowful prophet Jeremiah, that lament may be made over them: over the wars that took place and the evils that sprang up; over the hatred that took hold; over the implacable hostility that darkened the hearts of many, so that they would not reflect on all these evils and cease their insults, abuse, and bitter oppression of one another.

Just as someone whose eyes are weak and dim cannot easily see clearly and gaze at the sun’s rays, and someone burning with a violent fever cannot perform any task as a healthy person can, so those carried away by the passion of anger and swept into the rush of furious zeal cannot judge and examine what is right before carrying out their actions. Likewise, those drunk with anger and confused by rage and hostile zeal cannot think or do anything sound at all. This is what actually happened to the wise Alexandrian clergy. They were not lacking in knowledge either, had the storm of anger not disturbed them and fury not confused them. They came to fit this saying of Scripture about those battered among the waves by winds and storms: “They reeled and staggered like drunken men, and all their wisdom perished.”

Such was the case with what they have now done hastily and savagely, contrary to ecclesiastical order. They received the synodical letter of the man who had become their bishop from among orthodox people who shared their communion. Even if, as they themselves complained, circumstances had not allowed his appointment to take place by their own decree [?]—for this was why they resorted to such utter savagery—they became confused by the rush of anger and sought to cover up their offense. They believed that they had been passed over in these matters, since the first man had been appointed without their decree. So they themselves, thinking themselves so very wise, rushed to appoint Peter as a second bishop at the same time and on the same throne.

If it was indeed right for them to do this, they should have done it without contention and appointed a bishop for themselves during the whole intervening period of ten years after the death of the blessed Theodosius. They should not have waited until they learned that Theodore had become their bishop first, and then issued a decree [?] of anger and, as though intent on contention, strife, and division in the Church, rushed to appoint that second man, Peter. Thus he would immediately be regarded by some as an adulterer who had gone in and committed adultery with his neighbor’s wife.

Again, at their urging, the man who had come into office unlawfully and contrary to canonical order, whom they had thus appointed as a second bishop contrary to ecclesiastical laws, was earnestly persuaded, as though to confirm his position, to proceed to appoint bishops himself—seventy in number, it is said. Even if someone had been looking for laborers to work the land, it would have been difficult for him to find and gather so many ready at one time.

What, then, are we to say about those chosen to shepherd Christ’s rational flock, which he commanded the blessed Peter to shepherd? Moreover, according to the apostolic command and teaching addressed to Timothy, even priests alone are to be appointed through selection, inquiry, and much examination. How much more must this be said of chief priests!

But just as the beginning of this undertaking was confused, disorderly, and entirely lacking in proper order, so was its end. Even then he was not restrained from the impetuous course of madness and savagery, nor did he put on the gentleness and humility of Christ. Instead, they cunningly urged him to hasten toward a division between the Church of Syria and that of Alexandria, and to carry out, unjustly and uncanonically, the deposition of Paul while he was far away. Paul had been made patriarch of Antioch at the command of the blessed Theodosius. Nor was this all: he also pursued accusations against Jacob, the bishop of Syria. He did these things not merely informally, but also put them into his own circular letter and sent it in every direction.

Because of their longstanding hostility and hatred toward Paul, he also included in it a document containing accusations of oppression, murder, and falsehood, alleging that Paul himself and others with him had drawn it up and presented it to the members of the synod. This document had also been anathematized by those who had suffered the wrong, in the very declaration they issued about this matter to the whole Church. They anathematized those who had drawn it up, those who had committed the wrong, and themselves as well, if they had done it, had knowledge of it, or had been involved in it in any way, secretly or openly.

Let none of those who encounter these records written by us, either now or later, suppose that our account of this utterly confused affair is written unjustly, with exaggeration upon exaggeration, or entirely without regard for the truth, or that we wish to vindicate one side and take pains to heap accusations on the other. Rather, we are recording, without additions, a little out of the many things that happened at this time—that is, in the year 886 of Alexander—and afterward. We do not, however, promise to leave nothing out. For great confusion, turmoil, and disorder arose through the activity of the murderer. We can make use of only a few brief examples of these things, setting them all down in a confused and disordered arrangement.

Now Theodore, who, as has been said, had first been made bishop in Alexandria by Longinus and the others against his will, learned that the Alexandrians had reached such a pitch of cunning and brutality that they would receive neither him nor his letters. Instead, they had made and installed Peter, who has been mentioned, after him and in his place, entirely outside canonical order. He therefore withdrew into seclusion and remained in the way of life he had originally followed. He was not at all disturbed by what had happened, but said, “Let there be neither schism nor contention on my account. For I have no concern except to remain in the quiet of my own soul, as I have done until now.”

For a time he remained like this, undisturbed. Eventually, however, many rallied to him, both in the city and in the deserts, in Egypt and in the Thebaid. In the Thebaid he also made [?] in his name and performed ordinations.

In the second book, then, we gave a full account of the lapse concerning the hope of unity that befell the blessed Paul and those with him. Now we must disclose and record the groundless supposition held by the Alexandrians, who in a brutal rush installed a second Peter on the throne of their church: namely, that he had entered the land of Libya with his bishops and had appointed Theodore together with Longinus. This is groundless and false. For Longinus himself, in one of his letters refuting this supposition, issued a declaration with many oaths that he had not been present at Theodore’s appointment, and that it had taken place neither at his direction nor with his knowledge.

For in that same brutal rush they had, they said, appointed Peter for this purpose: that he should brazenly carry out his deposition, without canonical procedure. Yet his own priesthood was still, according to the canons, open to objection, unstable, and unconfirmed. It had come about barbarously, through a furious rush, and not according to the order of the ecclesiastical canons. He had unlawfully taken his place on the throne as a second bishop after another had been appointed to it.

They also brought accusations against the blessed Jacob, and not merely in passing, but in written documents and letters—encyclical letters, that is, circular letters. They did this while the persons concerned were far away. Those persons had not been summoned according to the requirements of the canons and charged in person, but were nevertheless rejected, as the tenor of their proceedings shows. From this point onward, a schism and bitter contention arose between Syria and Alexandria, deliberately fostered and firmly established through cunning. A severe division resulted from the passion of their longstanding hostility and the bitter resentment they had long harbored toward Paul.

Concerning this elder Jacob. It was neither inappropriate nor far-fetched to apply to him, and to his simplicity and innocence, what is written about the brothers—that is, the holy disciples in the days of the blessed apostles—that they praised the Lord in sincerity of heart. Thus he too, along with his simplicity and innocence, was adorned with spiritual zeal and with struggles and labors for the church, from his youth to his old age. Yet he was pulled about by others: crafty and cunning men attached themselves to him and tried to turn him whichever way they wanted, so that through him and under his cover they could accomplish all their wishes. The elder himself, in his childlike innocence, was pulled this way and that by them, tugged about and turned around.

This also happened in the affair of Paul, whom he, together with the other bishops, had previously made patriarch in Antioch the Great—that is, their own patriarch and their superior. Afterward they acted freely, without his authorization, even after appointing him. Finally others reproached them, saying, “You ought not to do anything without the consent of your patriarch.” When many of them heard this, the statement greatly irritated them and was not at all welcome to them. Even so, they did not stop doing everything according to their own wishes.

These things continued in this way for some time. Afterward, ostensibly for the purpose of unity, Paul and the others were summoned to come to the imperial city. When they arrived, entered, and were received by the emperor, they held innumerable discussions, with many changes of position, over an extended period of more than two years. We have related some of the main points of these discussions in the second book, which precedes this one; for now we have decided to pass over the matter quickly.

In the end, Paul and three others with him relied on oaths and assurances from those in authority concerning unity. In the hope of unity, they were caught in the evil lapse of communion with the adherents of two natures. Many things, which have already been related, were said and done in the meantime, beyond counting, and they were all cast into exile. Then Paul, risking his life, escaped from the episcopal residence and got away from the hands of his enemies. He hastened to the regions of Syria and submitted to the eastern synod not just one but two written statements of repentance. He continued pleading for about three years, more or less. Then the blessed Jacob himself and his synod received him into communion by a formal decision and according to canonical procedure.

Jacob accordingly wrote many letters here to the imperial city, to Antioch, and to the other regions, saying, “You should know that we have received our blessed patriarch, Mar Paul, into spiritual communion, and we have shared communion together. Whoever receives him receives us, and whoever does not receive him does not receive us.”

But again, after a short time, through the working of the Evil One, various grounds for dispute arose among them, which, for the sake of propriety, we shall cover with silence.

Thus division and hatred persisted between the two parties for some time. Both parties were blamed for the confused and disorderly events in Alexandria, and especially the blessed Jacob. He wrote everywhere against Peter the Second, whom they had appointed there, saying, “He has become a new Gaianus in Alexandria, to the disturbance of the church.” He also wrote three letters on this very subject to our humble self, among many others.

As for Peter, certain people took him too, like a picture painted on a wall, so to speak, so that they could act through him and carry out their own wishes. They made him bishop of Alexandria after another man had already been appointed before him. Nor was it enough for them that, although his ordination was unlawful, precarious, and unconfirmed, he gathered people without number, young and old alike, and irregularly made a body of seventy bishops, besides the rest of the clergy. They also dragged him into another savage act: he rushed to divide the churches of Syria and Alexandria and tyrannically dared to undertake the deposition of Paul of Antioch, unlawfully and contrary to ecclesiastical regulations and canons, although his own position was unlawful. He was not restrained from this insolence. Rather, as though they intended to stir up unrest, hatred, and accusations against him, and a written indictment against him as well as against others for the false accusations he had fabricated, they urged him on. With such insolence, tyranny, and arrogance, he resembled a drunken man who had lost his understanding and did not know what he was doing. At the instigation of those who had set him up like an image for these purposes, he put these things into circular letters and sent them everywhere. These and the other similar things that he did produced divisions in the church and gave rise to many great disputes. Through deceit and savagery, endless turmoil arose between Syria and Alexandria.

For the guileless old man Jacob, as we explained above, was being pulled along by those zealous men who clung to him. They were devising ways to find a pretext and an outlet for their hatred, for their [?], which had arisen against Paul through the influence of the murderer. They were now drawing the old man toward Alexandria, ostensibly urging him to bring about unity between the Alexandrians and Syria, although they knew all along that the Alexandrians harbored an old hatred and implacable hostility toward Paul because of envy.

They succeeded in taking advantage of the old man's simplicity, drawing him away, and bringing him into Alexandria more or less secretly. Many who learned that he was preparing to go there wrote and solemnly warned him not to go to Alexandria alone and without due care. Otherwise, if he became embroiled in these men's hatred and was drawn into it, further divisions and disputes would arise between Egypt and Syria, and the growth of evil would gain strength.

But they would not listen. They drew him away and brought him into Alexandria, and he fell among a perverse people, as it is written. Then they compelled him to be swept into communion with Peter—the man whom he had reviled both in writing and orally, and whom he had called a new Cain who had arisen to disturb the church of God.

They further compelled and humbled him into preparing a written declaration in the form of a document of union and presenting it to the very man whom he had censured and reviled. He had said that this man was not even a bishop, but was like an adulterer who had seized his neighbor's wife and committed adultery with her, since another orthodox man had already been appointed and given the title; and among the orthodox there had been some before him and some after him [?].

These very people, because of their hatred of Paul and their desire to find a pretext to cut him off and remove him, shut their eyes to all these things—to everything—and turned to Peter, the new Cain whom they themselves had reviled in this way. As has been said, they trampled on every obligation. They assented to every violation of the canons with which they had previously charged Peter, agreed with him in everything, and endorsed every violation of canonical law that he had committed. This applied especially to the deposition of Paul, patriarch of Antioch, which Peter's party had carried out from a distance, insolently, tyrannically, and outside all canonical boundaries, before Jacob's party came to them.

When they heard of this, they received the news with satisfaction. Their passionate hatred found relief when it was put into action. Even though this had been done by others, it delighted them and pleased them greatly, for they thought that the yoke of their patriarch Paul had been lifted from their necks. They also put their names and seals to this deposition. But the old man Jacob made a plea that the deposition should take place without a sentence of anathema.

Now when the blessed Jacob and his companions had completed the confused affair in Alexandria, which became the cause of upheaval, disturbance, division, and strife for the whole church in Syria, and had agreed to and signed everything that came from Peter, then, as they were leaving, they asked him to have three of his bishops accompany them to Syria, as witnesses and confirmation of the change they had brought about. So they all departed together, and their arrival astonished and alarmed, so to speak, the whole of Syria. On their departure [?], when they began to describe the significance of what they had done and their deposition of Paul without the authority of the canons, great division, schism, and disruption immediately spread and took hold throughout the church of the faithful everywhere in Syria. Many accepted what the old man Jacob had done in Alexandria. One reason—[?] in Alexandria—was for his sake and because they had long been attached to him; another was that they thought a sound and complete union had been established in Alexandria.

Others, however, immediately broke away, turned against them, and repudiated everything they had done there, blaming Jacob and his party and complaining against them. First, because Jacob himself had previously found fault with Peter and reviled both him and those who had appointed him, calling him a new Gaianus whom the Alexandrians had appointed [?] to disturb the church. He had said that Peter's appointment was contrary to the canons, that he was of no account and had no right to the priesthood, and that he was an adulterer. Yet after all this, Jacob went in, accepted him, submitted to the very man whom he had rejected and reviled, and entered into communion with him. Nor did he do this simply, but he even presented him with a formal petition. The three bishops who accompanied him carried this document with them and secretly showed it to many, saying, “Look, this is the petition that Father Jacob drew up and presented to Pope Peter.” They did this secretly, since neither Jacob nor his companions thought that what they had drawn up was in the form of a petition. Rather, they said, “We drew up a document of union.” Were it not for the length of the account, we would also have set that document down here in its proper place.

Thus pain was again added to pain, and disaster to disaster. At this time too, in the year eight hundred and eighty-seven, it overtook the whole persecuted and harassed church of the faithful throughout all the regions mentioned above, through divisions, disputes, schisms, sufferings, and calamities. This division sprang up between Jacob and Paul, spread, and took hold like a bitter, spreading ulcer, without fear of God.

Bishops, clergy, large and small monastic communities, and the rest of the people belonging to the churches in the cities and villages throughout these regions attached themselves to each of them. Each faction rushed against the other to destroy and overthrow it, exchanging insults and abuse with unchecked, savage fury. They undermined one another, oppressed and divided the people, split the church against itself, and tore the congregations apart, so that each might wrench people away from the other, create divisions against him, and enlarge his own party. Through his own partisans, each did all he could to divide many people, make them stumble, split them off, and draw them to himself.

Thus both parties became so thoroughly filled and overwhelmed with a spirit of opposition that there was no order or judgment arising from the fear of God to make them turn away from these evils and stop dividing, disturbing, and throwing God's church into confusion. Instead, the one who asked to sift them like wheat piled them up in this state of murderous hatred, hostility, insults, and abuse against one another, and in mutual mockery and derision. Even the most savage and brutal person would not dare to speak and mock in this way against pagans, Jews, or heretics. And all this happened even though, in the matter of faith, there was no difference or deviation between them.

When, therefore, they had descended into all this deviousness and lawless brutality—not only these two individuals, Paul and Jacob, but also the parties following each of them—all Syria and the other regions became divided, split apart, confused, and bewildered. Some approved and accepted Jacob and everything he had done in Alexandria, while others joined Paul's party and rejected Jacob and everything he had done in Alexandria. They criticized him, saying that he had done everything contrary to canonical order. This was especially true of the great monasteries and the rest.

While these matters thus held sway everywhere in a savage, brutal, and disorderly fashion, Paul himself continually sent messages to Jacob through many people: “Why has all this turmoil arisen in the church of God? Let us meet together and examine the matters between us according to the canons and the law. If I am found guilty under the canons, for every single sentence and canonical penalty I will accept three. And if, instead, the guilt rests with you, I will likewise accept it in your place.”

But those surrounding the guileless old man Jacob would not let him yield at all and agree to see Paul and speak with him. For they knew that they could not stand against him, and they knew that with his very first words he would necessarily establish their guilt.

Jacob, however, used to say: “I have approved and accepted the Alexandrians, and I have entered into union with them in writing. I will not turn away from them. Without them, he will not see me, nor will I see him.”

For al-Mundhir son of al-Harith, king of the Arabs, a faithful, zealous, and diligent man, had also spent a long time making efforts and urging both parties to cease their anger and fighting, to meet together, to speak, and to make peace with one another. But Jacob's party would not listen to him. Paul himself, meanwhile, was urging both al-Mundhir and many others to have the matters stirred up between them by Satan investigated and examined.

For a long time, since the days of his father al-Harith, they had regarded the old man Jacob as a great man, and later Paul as well. But when they had descended into all this deviousness, brutality, and division against one another, and Jacob's party would not agree to relent, division then arose throughout all the Arab forces as well.
