Many of them were led to stumble: some followed Paul, and others followed Jacob.

Because of the strife and turmoil that had taken hold everywhere, especially throughout Syria, Longinus and his companions, together with Theodore, who had become their patriarch, went to Egypt. From there they went down to the eastern regions of Syria, to Paul’s party, so that together they might enter into discussions with Jacob’s party and, if possible, resolve the dispute and the evil that the Evil One had stirred up among them. Theodore remained quietly in the city of Tyre, while Longinus went down as far as Hira, in the territory of Harith son of Jabalah, to Mundhir son of Harith. He conversed with him and carefully explained the whole truth to him. King Mundhir again made efforts to bring them together and reconcile them, but Jacob’s party would not listen to him at all.

Eventually, however, they held a gathering at the monastery of Mar Hanina in the desert. A considerable crowd from Jacob’s party was there, and Jacob himself was with them. One of the bishops, a man named John, who belonged to that monastery and had come from it, deceitfully sent word to Longinus and his companions: “Since the elder Mar Jacob has come here and wishes to speak with you, set out quickly and come here. The three of us—you, he, and I—will be alone, and we will discuss how to resolve the dispute and put an end to the turmoil.”

When Longinus received a letter of this kind, he gladly got up and set out with others, and they arrived there. When they entered, they took him and brought him in, placing him in the middle of a considerable crowd of monks, laypeople, lawyers, legal officials, and their staffs, his own [?], and others. When Longinus saw the assembled faction, he said to John, the very man who had invited him, “What is this deceit you have practiced on me? You wrote me a lie, saying, ‘The elder is here alone. Come, so that the three of us can talk.’ Where is the elder, and what is this crowd?”

When he said this, one of the monks produced a document containing accusations against him and said, “Take this, read it, and give an answer to it.” But he replied, “Since I have now been summoned by deceit and lies, I will neither read it nor give an answer to anyone.” As he turned to leave, they laid hands on him and held him, saying, “You will not leave without reading it. Otherwise, we will read it, and you must listen.” When they began to read, he put his fingers in both ears so that he would not hear. When they began pulling him this way and that, he began shouting, “Help! I have a king! Why am I being murdered by treachery?”

An uproar broke out, a quarrel flared up, and a disorderly commotion arose there. The evil of murder very nearly occurred. Then, shouting for help, he tore himself free and got out from among them. He escaped from their hands and fled without having seen Jacob. And many such evils, arising from the manifest activity of demons, occurred everywhere among them, in every [?]

Against one another, without stopping or coming to their senses, he rejoiced and exulted, together with all the dark hordes of his demons, in the destruction and turmoil of the faithful. These things deserved lamentation and the bitter sorrow of mourning: things that had been stirred up at this time among the faithful in the church of God through the envy and activity of the Accuser, and that were being perpetrated unceasingly by both sides.

So these great and famous monasteries in the West and the East became divided, split apart, and thrown into turmoil, and became embroiled in battles and struggles against one another. They would become so embroiled that boundless evil would be practiced among them, murders would occur, and many would be arrested by the judges. Bound in irons and fettered with chains, they would be led to Antioch the Great and thrown into prison. The venerable monastic habit, which had not been preserved with due honor, would be dishonored and mocked by pagans, Jews, and heretics, as they were bound in irons, fettered with chains, led to court, and made to give statements [?] like murderers: elderly monks with long beards and trailing hems, put into collars, standing before judges and being questioned about murders. Who would not shudder, lament, and wail over these calamities, mourning like a jackal and lamenting like a jackal’s young, over the salt that had not only lost its flavor but had also gone bad and become repulsive, and so was thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people? As for the others who had divided against one another, one faction in each case remained in the monasteries themselves, while the other faction, which left, went and took possession of a place. They named the place they occupied after the monastery from which they had departed, and they prepared themselves for deadly opposition to one another, without restraint or consideration.

There was also a great assembly of many abbots, besides the many other assemblies that had previously taken place in various locations. This later assembly also took counsel and prepared to oppose Paul’s party. They appointed three men from among themselves who were unrestrained and ready for battle. Some of them drew up a letter for them and sent them to the elder Jacob and the others with him, stirring them up, preparing them, and urging them on through the document they had drawn up. We would have included this document too, were it not for its length. It demanded that they act energetically and appoint a patriarch for themselves in place of Paul. They also asked them what they decided concerning the ordinations Paul had performed, and concerning the Tritheists and the other matters. The elder adopted this course as well, and at his command an assembly was held at the monastery of Mar Hanina. When they began to discuss the matters, some of the bishops would not agree. They said, “Paul the patriarch is alive and has not been condemned under the canons. How, then, can we now appoint another patriarch while he is alive, behaving like senseless fools, and bring ourselves under canonical punishment?” Thus, since they did not agree, it was called off, and the assembly dispersed.

After they had been prevented from appointing a patriarch, the blessed Jacob suddenly became troubled in his thoughts. Taking bishops and other companions with him, eight in number, he set off in great haste for Alexandria. Many people formed various opinions about him. Some thought that he was going there to appoint a patriarch together with Damian, who was there. Others said that he was going to establish unity with Paul’s party. Since he concealed his intentions from everyone, the purpose of his efforts was not known for certain.

But God, from whose eyes nothing is hidden, watches over the welfare of his creation. While they were traveling, they reached the great monastery on the border of Egypt called the monastery of Cassian. There, as is reported, one of the bishops accompanying him suddenly died. He had been abbot of the monastery of Qartmin. The old man arose and offered the Eucharist in his memory. Then his personal attendant Sergius, who was said to have become a bishop himself, suddenly fell ill and died. Afterward the old man himself fell ill for three days and died. Then, after him, his deacon also died. All these died suddenly, one after another, within twelve days, leaving people in astonishment, great uncertainty, and conflicting thoughts.

When this became known to the Alexandrians, Damian and the others hurried there after the old man’s death. They wanted to take his body away, but the monks of that monastery would not allow it. Astonishment and amazement seized them over everything that had happened: how the blessed Jacob and his companions had suddenly been snatched away. Many pondered within themselves whether perhaps he had been stirring up something alien and still greater turmoil for the church, or had been planning to appoint a patriarch, and God had spared him so that the soul of that man of God would not be lost.

Because the death of the blessed Jacob and his companions had been so sudden, those who had no concern for the harm done to their own souls did not fail to say, “Some of Paul’s party went out at his command, ambushed Father Jacob on the road, beat them with clubs, and pelted them with stones. Thus he went on to Egypt and died.” This was not only false but thoroughly wicked. As though eager to add to the harm done to their own souls and to increase the scandal, they spread the story everywhere, so as to unsettle many and cause them to stumble, and to wound the consciences of the faithful. They supposed that in this way they would cause others to stumble and enlarge their own party. They were neither disturbed nor grieved at the loss and ruin of their own souls, displaying themselves as entirely without the fear of God through such murderous slanders.

At this same time there were three envoys: Theodore the patrician, and John and Peter, the consuls. These supported Patriarch Paul more than anyone else and fought on his behalf—that is, the consuls did. They were so zealous that, one might say, they devoted more effort to gathering assemblies every day and speaking on his behalf than to the affairs of the entire state. Father Jacob himself therefore went to them with many others, and things were said between them that exceed the bounds of narration and the scope of this book. Neither party could persuade the other to agree. So the two parties broke off in bitterness and withdrew from one another.

Moreover, in every city they entered, they raised the same issue. But throughout almost all the regions east of the Euphrates, and even as far as Persia, people supported the blessed Jacob more strongly than Paul. They were not persuaded at all and would not submit to the envoys. So the envoys came up and arrived here in the imperial city, frustrated and reviling all the people of the East.

Now all the tribes of the Arabs had been attached to the blessed Jacob from the beginning. Moreover, even during the lifetime of the elder Harith, Paul used to go there and take refuge with them, and they were also edified by him because of his discipline, humility, and teaching. This was especially so after Harith’s death, when the two parties met among them and received one another lovingly. There, at Hirah of the Arabs, they were all attached to both Paul and Jacob.

But afterward, when Satan stirred up dissension between them, all the Arabs were distressed, especially their king Mundhir, together with his brothers, his sons, and the others. They implored the elder Jacob himself that the two should draw near to one another and unite. But he would not be persuaded to receive Paul and unite with him, making the Alexandrians his excuse: “If they do not receive him,” he said, “neither will I receive him.” Thus all the Arabs were troubled and distressed. Whenever Paul went to them, they received him and took communion from him; and whenever Jacob came, they did likewise, until Jacob forbade them to take communion from Paul. They all remained in this state, troubled, distressed, and bewildered, until the death of the elder Jacob. After his death, most of them followed him, while some followed Paul’s party, and others continued to receive both. All alike were anxious and distressed over this alien division and quarrel that had arisen among them, and especially—especially Mundhir their king, who continually implored both parties to make peace with one another. But the envy, hatred, and hostility that came from Satan, and from those who advised both parties according to his will, did not allow them to find relief and make peace, even until death. Thus, while the elder Jacob was still engaged in this struggle and had directed his journey toward Alexandria, God, who knows everything and foresaw what would benefit him, decreed that his life should end on the road, as we have already related many times above.

Again, when John the Synodite, bishop of Alexandria, brought accusations against the orthodox clergy through numerous letters, an order was issued, and they were arrested and brought up to the imperial city. They arrived in the month of May in the year eight hundred and ninety. When they went to Eutychius the patriarch, he treated them arrogantly and sent word to them outside: “Since, on that previous occasion when I released you, you promised me that you would take communion, go in now and take communion. Then you may come in to me and see me.” When they heard this, they sent word to him: “We did not promise you that we would take communion unless the Council of Chalcedon was rejected.” Then he became angry with them and gave orders, and they were taken away, separated, and confined in monasteries.

Theodosius, the head of the church of Alexandria, was confined in the monastery of the Silentiarius. After his imprisonment, he fell ill and died at a good old age. All the Alexandrians grieved deeply for him, especially those who were imprisoned. This happened after they had once been summoned and had gone in for a discussion with Eutychius the patriarch. They told him, “We will not speak with you without the emperor or the senate as mediators.” After much had taken place, they were sent back to the monasteries, each to the place where he had been confined. While they were still waiting to be summoned again and to enter into discussion, their leader died, as has been said. Even now they are all confined in those monasteries and carefully guarded.

So the furnace of the Babylonians was being heated ever more fiercely and blazing between these two parties, the followers of Paul and the followers of Jacob. This arose from worthless pretexts, empty suppositions, and the urgings of certain people who, moved by envy and longstanding hatred, were disturbing the peaceful and hardworking soul of the aged Jacob, so that he would enter into opposition against Paul. Insults and abuse, beyond every proper limit and rule, were poured out against one another by both parties, without restraint and without the constraints of the fear of God. This happened not only during the aged Jacob’s lifetime, but also after God’s will had been fulfilled concerning him, and he had departed from this troubled and afflicted life and left the world. They continued savagely stirring up and preparing the very same things, with further additions and mutual anathemas, in every place, every region, and every province, in the East and the West. It reached the point that, as it is written, we became a reproach to our neighbors, an object of mockery and scorn to those around us.

For when the illustrious patrician Mundhir was summoned, went up to the emperor, and was received with great distinction, he armed himself with courageous zeal and the fear of God against all these evils that he saw being committed against one another by people who shared the same faith and communion. Then he brought both parties together and began rebuking, admonishing, and reproaching them for all these evils, divisions, and disputes that had arisen among them. He advised them to put an end to their divisions, to stop fighting and quarreling, and to make peace with one another, especially since they shared the same faith. Indeed, from the very beginning he had been working, counseling, and pleading with Paul and Jacob personally to make peace with one another and live in love.

This journey of the illustrious Mundhir took place in the year eight hundred and ninety-one, on the eighth day of the month of February. He was received with great ceremony and boundless honor by the merciful emperor Tiberius, who honored him with distinctions, magnificent gifts, and royal presents. He did for him everything he wanted and gave him everything he requested. He also took both his sons into his service alongside him, and even deemed him worthy of the royal crown.

After the illustrious Mundhir had accomplished everything he wanted with the emperor, he convened an assembly of prominent men from both sides, together with the Alexandrians, on the second day of the month of March that year. He urged them to make peace with one another and to put an end to and extinguish everything Satan had stirred up among them. Many matters too numerous to recount were raised and discussed among them, now not by two parties but by three: the followers of Jacob, the followers of Paul, and also the Alexandrians, addressing one another. Our humble self was also with them.

There were many discerning men on both sides, and they were deeply distressed by everything being done cunningly and savagely by the troublemakers among these three parties just mentioned [?]. They welcomed peace and the ending of all these evils. They all yielded together and gave pledges that there would be unity among them. Arrangements began to be made for all the disputes Satan had stirred up among them to be quieted, examined, and brought to an end. Everyone agreed to this, and a document was drawn up among them concerning their union and the abolition and annulment of all the divisions and disputes that had arisen among them. All the archbishops, bishops, clergy, monks of all the monasteries, and laypeople who had been divided were to accept one another, and all were to come together in unity with one another, without dispute.

Thus a prayer for union was offered by the priests of both sides and also by the Alexandrians. Unity was established, and everyone thanked God for having driven the Evil One out from among them, together with everything belonging to him and originating from him [?]. Everyone pledged to take care to bring all the members of his own party who were physically absent into this union that had been established.

There were, however, some troublemakers and agitators who, filled with the filth of wrongdoing, were very angry and did not rejoice at the peace that had come about. The gathering with King Mundhir had been an assembly of leaders and prominent men, and it had not involved the entire body of the people. Particularly because the whole body had not been taken into account and summoned, some turned to opposition and to undoing and nullifying what had been accomplished. They gathered, made [?], wrote, and stirred up trouble throughout Syria and in Alexandria. They incited many to take a partisan stand, not to yield, and not to accept what had been accomplished. This delighted Satan and all his black demons.

The assembly, however, dispersed in peace and joy, with everyone expressing gratitude to God and also to the illustrious Mundhir.

Before the events we have just related, Damian, who had irregularly become pope in Alexandria after Peter, who himself had caused strife, division, and contention, also acted in such a way as to show himself like his predecessor, outside every rule of church order, undisciplined and lacking understanding. He conceived an empty and senseless plan and went to Syria to appoint and install a patriarch in Antioch in place of Paul, while Paul was still alive, in violation of all the limits laid down by the canons.

For he and his predecessor had themselves come into office after another man had already been appointed before them and recognized by name, namely Theodore, who had written synodical letters to Alexandria. But the Alexandrians became insolent and were stirred by a furious surge of anger, behaving savagely and barbarously. They appointed Peter, a certain deacon, a simple and uneducated man, and used his name to do as they pleased. Thus there were now two patriarchs on one throne at the same time. Consequently, many called Peter and Damian, his successor, adulterers who had entered another man's marriage and committed adultery with his wife.

So Damian, intending to conceal his disgrace from everyone—the disgrace that he and his predecessor had come into office while Theodore, who preceded Peter, was still alive—devised this scheme: he would also appoint another man over Paul in Syria while Paul was still alive, so that there would be something to match their own disgrace.

When he went there, summoned the bishops of Syria, and urged them to agree with him and appoint a patriarch in Antioch, some of the bishops raised an objection on canonical grounds, saying, ‘We will not consent to appoint another man over Paul unless Paul has been summoned, tried, convicted of wrongdoing, condemned, and canonically deposed. Otherwise we would not only incur condemnation under the canons but would also be excommunicated.’ Other bishops, however, sided with Damian and agreed with him to appoint another patriarch. When they pressed one or two men to accept appointment, these men likewise objected, each saying, ‘While the man is alive and has not been canonically summoned, tried, condemned, and deposed, I will not take office and be elevated above him. It may happen that in the end I too will be deposed.’

Finally, they found a certain reckless man like themselves, named Severus. Damian took him along with two other bishops, and they entered Antioch by night. They secretly sent word to the caretaker of the church called Cassian's and promised to give him eighteen darics if he would open it for them, so that they could enter by night and ordain him there. The caretaker accepted the arrangement and gave them his word. Confident of this, they prepared to enter at night and carry out their wishes. But some people learned of the scheme they were preparing to carry out. They immediately went and informed the patriarch of the city, who at once sent men to arrest them.

They surrounded the house on every side, entered it, and arrested three monks from their company. Damian took fright, and he, the bishops, and the rest of his companions went down into the hollow beneath the house, that is, into the sewer. They went out through an opening at the sewer's outlet, beneath the baskets. Thus, with their whole bodies and all their clothing soaked, smeared, and befouled with all the filth of that sewer, and dragging themselves along, they came out, escaped, and fled without being arrested: Damian; Sergius Anphitor, that is, the [?]; George Sarcabinus; the bishops with him; and the man they had been preparing to ordain, together with the rest. They were more ashamed of being smeared with excrement than of the failure of their schemes.

The monks who had been arrested were brought to the patriarch. At his command they were hung up and subjected to severe torture. They confessed everything they had been preparing to do. When they confessed about Damian and his companions, orders were sent in every direction for their arrest, but they escaped and were not caught. Those who had been arrested also confessed about the caretaker. He was brought in and confessed. He suffered even more torture than they did, and his possessions were seized.

After Damian escaped, he secretly went up to Constantinople, before the assembly for unity took place. Through the efforts of people who wanted peace, he came by night to the illustrious Mundhir, and they spoke with one another. He promised to work for peace, to seek it, and to agree to it. After showing himself to only a few people, he fled and departed for Alexandria. For, as has been related, he also ordained bishops in the imperial city.

Now, after the assembly had been held and dissolved, the illustrious al-Mundhir went in and petitioned the merciful Emperor Tiberius on behalf of the Alexandrian clergy, who were being detained by order in the imperial city, together with certain well-known laymen, over the matter of the faith. The emperor released them, and an order was issued for them. He also did great things for them in recognition of the unity they had achieved. Thus they departed joyfully, boarded a ship, and went to their city.

After this, the illustrious al-Mundhir asked that he too be allowed to leave. He also petitioned the merciful emperor about peace for the church and an end to the persecution of Christians. The emperor promised him under oath that, if he gained a respite from the wars, he would immediately establish peace. With this promise he sent him away with great honors and royal gifts: much gold and silver, splendid clothes, many golden saddles and [?], and armor. Along with all these things, he also bestowed a royal crown on him. This had never happened before, nor had such a crown been given to any of the kings of the Arabs before him. They had only been permitted to wear a diadem.

Thus he was sent away and departed with pomp and great joy. When he reached Antioch, he was welcomed there too. Relying on the emperor’s wishes, promises, and oaths concerning the unity of the church, he informed the patriarch of the city and the others that the emperor had ordered the persecution to stop. The patriarch immediately gave orders, and letters were written to all the provinces, saying that no one should dare to carry out persecution, because the emperor had commanded this and wished to establish peace. Thus the persecution stopped for a short time.

When the supporters of the two natures in the imperial city heard this, they were stirred to great anger against al-Mundhir. Without delay they went in and vehemently accused him before the emperor. But the God-loving emperor did not listen to them.

While al-Mundhir was on the road, his enemies, the Arabs allied with the Persians, supposed that he was spending a long time in the imperial city. Seeing that he was far away, the Arabs and Persians gathered and headed toward his country and territory, against his sons and brothers, intending to fall upon them, ravage their land, and take them captive. When the two sides had prepared to face one another, al-Mundhir suddenly arrived. Immediately, while the enemy were not expecting it, he marched out against them, fell upon them, and slaughtered them until he had destroyed them. Only a few of them fled and escaped his sword. Thus he returned rejoicing and brought back all their captured possessions. He was greatly acclaimed by everyone, and his name was highly praised.

But that zealous Damian the Syrian, who had at that time come to be in Alexandria—the same man mentioned above—when he reached Alexandria and was reproached by some people concerning Paul, then acted as someone intent on pleasing people, not on pleasing God or striving for the peace of the church. He went back on his word and broke his promise to the illustrious al-Mundhir and to the other believers from both sides who had appealed to him. He turned against Paul and wrote anathemas, insults, and harsh abuse against him. Not content to employ these things himself alone, he also wrote them all in an encyclical letter—that is, a circular—and sent it to Syria and everywhere within his jurisdiction and outside it. His letters were delivered especially to disruptive and savage people, those who are yoked to Satan and run and work with him. They did not gather with Christ, but, running in the opposite direction, thoroughly scattered. These people eagerly stirred up agitation and disorder, created divisions, provoked disputes, and produced quarrels, strife, abuse, and everything that pleases the devil, more than before.

He also induced the clergy who had been present at that assembly for union held in the imperial city to perform these deeds of his—and perhaps it is not improper to call them Satan’s deeds as well. Thus they too, along with him, would lie to the Holy Spirit and go back on their word after they had obtained relief, been released, and escaped their affliction through al-Mundhir’s care. For they had promised unity before him and before a large gathering, and had entered into union. They had also put this in writing under their own names, and it was on this account that they had been released and had come out of custody and prison. Yet they turned back and proved false like their fathers—that is, like their father Damian, who was worthy of them, and they of him.

So when King al-Mundhir returned from war against his enemies and learned of their change and their turning from truth to boundless falsehood, he was grieved and distressed. Along with this, he was astonished and bewildered, especially by Damian’s encyclical letters, which were not far removed from every kind of wickedness. Al-Mundhir therefore did not neglect to write to each of them by name, reminding them and reproaching them for their falsehood toward God, toward himself, and toward the whole church. But in their shame and denial they could neither receive his writings nor make a written reply to him. And so he took offense, while, especially because of these circumstances, the furnace of wrath was being kindled, blazing and flaring up against the whole church of the believers. There was also an even greater increase in divisions, disputes, insults, abuse, and strife, which continually blazed fiercely between the two sides, without restraint and without fear of the judgment of righteousness.

Thus, while the letters of the mighty Damian of Alexandria were circulating in the East and giving disruptive people an opportunity, some presumed to appoint a second patriarch in the name of Antioch, contrary to the proper order. Although the first had not been shown to have been canonically condemned, they would set another over him. This made the affair a matter of laughter and mockery for scoffers, who said, “It was necessary for two men to be called patriarchs in Antioch, just as there are three in Alexandria besides the one belonging to the adherents of the Council, so that they would not reproach one another!” Thus, in a debased and confused fashion, everything among the believers was being conducted perversely and without order because of the disputes.

For in the year eight hundred and ninety and eighty and two [?], after the death of the blessed Jacob, his bishops, abbots, and clergy reached this decision: they appointed and installed as patriarch a young layman named Peter, the son of Paul, from the city of Callinicus. While he was alive, the blessed Jacob himself had twice wanted to appoint this man. Others, too, after the blessed man’s death, had again wanted to appoint him, but he would not be persuaded and did not consent. He said, “I will not agree to take the place of a man who has not been canonically summoned, condemned, and lawfully deposed.” In the end, he was anathematized and expelled from the church. And now, at last, Peter was persuaded. As is reported, he went to Alexandria and was ordained by Damian and the others. He was named patriarch of Antioch in place of Paul, while Paul was still alive and had not been condemned and deposed by a synod. Thus the church of the faithful was in this state of ruin and confusion, entirely brought about by the Accuser and pleasing to him.

After this, all the abbots who had consented to this action took counsel together and assembled. They all drew up letters bearing their signatures to John, bishop of Ephesus, who was residing in the imperial city. They invited him to unity and communion with themselves and with the patriarch they had appointed, without even openly telling him his name or who he was. John stood between the two parties and was reproached by both alike. He mourned and grieved over the breach that had arisen between them because of the envy and hatred of the Alexandrians, and over the divisions and disputes throughout the whole church of the faithful. He advised and admonished them and solemnly warned them, absolutely refusing to be drawn into taking one side and fighting against the other.

When he received these letters, he was moved to tears and bitter sorrow over this further increase in the ruin and confusion of the church of the faithful. He was not even disposed to write. A year earlier, they had also sent him other letters inviting him to stand with them in battle, as it were, against the other party, and he had declined to send them a reply. Since they also reproached him for this in their letter, he was compelled to write them a reply containing a stern rebuke: since they themselves had acted entirely outside all canonical order in what they had done, how could they invite him to union and communion? Were it not for their great length and the bulk of their wording, we would have included here both the letters they all sent him and his reply to them.

Let this, then, be known to both parties, who have been stirred up against one another through the working of a spirit of opposition, and to everyone else: we have written these accounts, composed by our humble self concerning what was set in motion and took place between them and brought by us into the record of these memoirs, to bring accusations on behalf of the truth and to administer an equal rebuke to both parties. We have not written these things to favor certain persons against others, even though in various places we appear to direct reproaches and accusations against each of the parties. These concern the opposition and disorder that they have displayed toward one another in a savage and unlawful way. We mourn and grieve over these things, and our eyes stream with tears over the offenses, destruction, schisms, quarrels, divisions, disputes, insults, and abuse that have arisen and been practiced among us to the satisfaction of the murderer. We ourselves have also been compelled by the distress of our hearts to bring accusations concerning these matters, grieving that, although we are companions and share one another’s faith, we have been driven by certain unworthy causes to plunge into all these evils thoughtlessly and without restraint.

From the beginning we had also written these things personally to the individuals themselves, and especially to the hardworking elder Jacob, until the day of his death, as follows: “I, humble as I am, follow the laws of the church, and since I see no offense against the faith, I withdraw neither from communion with you nor from communion with Paul, because you are engaged in conflict with one another over accusations under the canons, whether true or false. But as for the other things that have been or are being done among you without order or propriety and beyond the boundaries of the church—whether you have employed excommunication and uncanonical deposition against Paul’s party, or Paul himself has done so against you or against the Alexandrians, or the Alexandrians have acted against you or against Paul outside the order or limits of the canons—I have no part or fellowship whatsoever in all these unlawful acts, until they have all been judged and examined by canonical judgment and lawful investigation before a synod, and it becomes known which things follow and conform to the laws of the church and which are remote from and foreign to proper order.”

These things are found written personally to the blessed Jacob during his lifetime in more than ten of my letters, as well as to the others. Although I have great sorrow over these matters and pain that never leaves my heart, I have endured accusation and opposition from both parties. I call as witness the one who examines the innermost thoughts and the heart: without joining one party against the other, I have remained in the middle until now, troubled, groaning, and grieving over all these evils that have taken place through the working of the one who asked to sift us like wheat.

But Paul himself, the patriarch of these evil days, when he saw that storm waves were rising on every side, went away and settled in hiding in a cave, reportedly in the rugged mountains of Isauria. He has remained there until now, a period of four years. He has shown himself to no one except the few who attend to his affairs. He neither writes to anyone nor receives letters from anyone. Consequently, many have grumbled against him and reproached him for hiding in this way and disregarding all this conflict that has arisen everywhere on his account. Even when zealous men in Syria appointed another in his place, he neither appeared nor spoke. Instead, up to this very hour, he remains in seclusion and hiding.

Now Theodore, whom we mentioned above as having been made patriarch of Alexandria by Longinus and the others, continued, as was his custom, to live quietly and openly in Alexandria itself, since he had been a monk from early on. He occupied a monastery and lived there, and many people gathered around him. Because of his humility and quietness, no one harassed him or drove him out of the city, even though he was an opponent of Damian, who succeeded Peter. Instead, they left him alone because of his gentleness and quietness, and because he used to say, “For my part, I have no claim to press. Let there be no disturbance or division in the church on my account.”

After some time, however, he became resentful toward Paul and Longinus and their associates, because Paul had gone into hiding and was neglecting everything. Longinus, meanwhile, had been driven farther inland, beyond the people of the Nobadians, among whom he had been living, to another great people many stages farther inland. The Greeks call them Alodians, and they are thought to be Ethiopians. God helped him, and he spoke to their king, all his nobles, and all the peoples under his rule. We shall also set down the accounts of these events in their proper order.

But now let us bring the narrative back to its original subject, the account of Theodore that we began to write. Let us return to it, since, in trying to show what occupied Paul and Longinus, the narrative strayed and went off onto another subject.

Theodore, then, was resentful and distressed with them, saying, “They came and plunged me into this trial and brought me out of the desert. Now they have abandoned me and neglected me, and have not even asked whether I am alive or dead.” He consequently wrote many letters of complaint to Syria, to us as well, and to many people in the imperial city. These were full of accusations, grumbling, and complaints. He sent them through a certain blessed stylite, a virtuous man who had been with him in the desert, and through another man who accompanied him, a priest named George.

We received these men with their letters and gave them much reassurance, and we also wrote to Paul and his associates, reproaching them on their account. But then a fierce persecution overtook us, and we were seized. They left the city, and we never saw them again. Later he wrote us this same complaint again. We did not think it right to bring the reasons for it into the written record, but rather to cover them in silence and pass them over.

Now, through the coming of the blessed Julian—who, as we have already explained above, had previously been sent through the efforts of the late Empress Theodora to the great people called the Nobades—their king, his nobles, and the greater part of the peoples under his rule had been made disciples within two years. Julian had then left there, entrusting that entire people to a certain Bishop Theodore, a very elderly man who lived in the city called Philae. This city is in the Upper Thebaid, on the border of the country just mentioned. This bishop would go in to visit and exhort them, and then return to his city. They continued in this way for about eighteen years.

Then Longinus changed his appearance and went in among them. He again made disciples, exhorted and taught them, and baptized the rest of those among them who remained unbaptized. He spent six years with them. Envoys were also sent by their king and came to the imperial capital. We spoke with them on many occasions, and they praised, exalted, and expressed very great gratitude to Longinus.

For when the people of the Alodians learned of the conversion of these peoples, the Nobades, their king sent word to the king of the Nobades, asking him to send the bishop who had taught and baptized them, so that he might also make disciples of these people and baptize them. But when Longinus received letters from the Alexandrians, he quickly left for Roman territory and encountered all the trials recorded above, one after another. Then afterward, with much labor and great difficulty, the king there finally managed to send envoys, who took him and brought him in among them.

The Alexandrians, through Satan’s envy, also sought to stir up that king and all his people and turn them against him, so that they would not receive him. They even sent him the decree deposing Longinus, which they had drawn up unjustly, contrary to the requirements of the canons. But they paid them no attention and did not accept them, saying, ‘We will receive no one except our spiritual father, who gave us a new, spiritual birth. We consider everything his enemies say against him to be lies.’ Thus they sent them back and did not receive them.

When the Alexandrians learned that the king of the Alodians had twice sent an embassy to the king of the Nobades, asking him to send Longinus to instruct them, they sent messengers to that people out of envy, not zeal, to discredit Longinus and induce them to accept instruction in the corruption and violation of the Church’s law that they themselves had committed. They diligently and carefully composed a letter to them against Longinus, without fearing God or giving any thought to righteousness. Drunk with envy and hatred, they conceived this in their hearts. It is not godly to send a misguided, pagan people, who have asked to turn to Christianity and learn the fear of God, written accusations and insults from Christians against Christians, bringing corruption and a stumbling block immediately, before everything they needed for their instruction. But, as has been said, their minds were darkened and their understanding blinded, so that they did not comprehend. Instead of teaching the fear of God, they eagerly sought first to lay for these people a foundation of hostility and stumbling. They thoroughly filled their letters against Longinus with hateful accusations and sent them with two bishops whom they had ordained contrary to the Church’s laws, and some others. They wrote: ‘Because we have learned that Longinus—Longinus, whom we have learned [?], who is among the Nobades, in [?]—has been requested by you to be sent to baptize you, we have therefore sent two bishops and the others to inform you that you must not be baptized by him. He is a heretic, and sentence of deposition has been passed against him. He is not permitted to exercise the priestly office or to baptize anyone.’ Along with many other things, they wrote to them what would corrupt them rather than offer the admonition needed for instruction.

But the Lord turned Nabal’s recompense back upon his own head. As it is written, ‘The nations who did not know the law of righteousness attained the law of righteousness, and they became a law to themselves; but Israel, which pursued righteousness, did not attain it.’ Thus this was fulfilled in their case: they were rebuked and repudiated by a pagan people and were not received, but returned humiliated and ashamed. For the people said to them: ‘We do not know who you are. We will not receive you, and we will not be baptized by you. Rather, we will receive the man who baptized the people of the Nobades, and we will be baptized by him. We do not accept what you say against him, for we see that you are his enemies and that you say these things against him out of envy. Go away and leave our country, lest you meet a terrible death.’

So they left that place, neither they nor anything they had said having been accepted at all. This was through the action of God, who saw their crooked intention and their hostile zeal.

Now when the king of the people of the Alodians [?] sent envoys to the king of the Nobades, asking him to send Bishop Longinus to instruct and baptize him and his people, it became clear that, by God's grace, arrangements were being made for that people's conversion. The Lord stirred Longinus's spirit to go and enter their country. Although they were distressed at his departure from them [?], the king, his nobles, and his leaders sent him with men who knew the desert. But he and his companions became ill. As he reports in his letter, seventeen of the camels accompanying him through the desert also died from the desert's scorching heat, besides the others.

In addition to these difficulties, there was another people [?] and another kingdom between these two kingdoms, whose inhabitants are called the Makurites. When their king learned that Longinus had set out on his journey, Satan, in his envy, stirred him to post guards at all the crossings of his kingdom, on every road, in all the mountains and plains, as far as the Red Sea, to seize Longinus and obstruct the salvation of that great people, the Alodians [?]. But God concealed him and blinded the eyes of those who were trying to seize him. He passed through their midst and went on, and they did not see him.

When he reached the borders of the kingdom to which he was traveling, and the king learned of it, he sent one of his nobles to meet him, as Longinus reports in his letter. His name was Eutychius. He welcomed him and escorted him through the country with honor and great ceremony. When he arrived, the king himself came out to meet him and welcomed him with great joy. He went in and spoke the word of God to him and all his nobles, and they opened their minds and received it joyfully. Within a few days they were instructed, and the king and all his nobles were baptized, followed afterward by many of the people. And so, rejoicing and glad [?], the king wrote a letter of thanks to the king of the Nobades [?], which reads as follows.

Your love is remembered, my lord and brother Orfiulus, for you have now shown yourself to be my true kinsman, not only physically but also spiritually. You sent our common spiritual father here to me, and he showed me the way of truth and the true light of Christ our God. He baptized me, my nobles, and all my people. In every respect the work of Christ is growing. I trust in the holy God that I too will take care to do what gives you peace, and I will drive your enemies from your country. For the enemy is not yours alone, but mine as well. Your country is also mine, and your people are my people. So do not lose heart, but be brave and strong, for I am not neglecting you or your country, especially now that I have become a Christian through the hands of my holy father, Father Longinus.

Since we need them, prepare church furnishings for us. I expect you to send these to me with care [?], and I will carry out your instructions [?]. I did not wish to write the day on which I celebrate the feast, lest my letters fall [?]. But you must be free of anxiety, and be brave and strong, because Christ is with us.

These things, then, were written by that new confessor, the king of the Alodians, to the king of the Nobades. And now also a short portion from the letter of the blessed Longinus, which he wrote from that country itself and sent to the king of the Nobades, asking him to send it to Alexandria [?]. This he did. The passage from the letter reads as follows.

But so that I do not recount distressing things to you and make the letter longer, I have left all these matters aside. Instead, I write to tell you the second matter, which brings joy to all of you who are truly Christians and firmly orthodox. I rejoice and share in the joy of you all. You too, then, rejoice in the same thing, and rejoice again with me. For he who desires everyone to live, and does not desire the death of a sinner like me, forgot all my sins, remembered his own mercy and grace, opened the door of his mercy to me, and rescued me from those who were hunting for my life. He brought me through their midst and blinded their eyes, so that they did not see me.

Yet we too were not beyond his love for humanity and his discipline. For everyone who was with my weak self fell ill, from the greatest to the least, and my insignificant self was the first to become ill. Indeed, it was right that I should be disciplined first, since I am responsible for many sins and for the transgressions into which I have fallen. Not only did we fall ill and despair of our deliverance, but the animals with us were also dying, unable to endure the burning heat and thirst of the mountains and the foulness of the water. Seventeen of our camels died.

When the king of the Alodians learned about me, that I had committed myself to going to him, he sent one of his chiefs, whose name was Itiqā. With a great escort, he brought me into his country. When we reached the riverbank, we boarded a boat. When the king heard, he rejoiced and came out himself to meet us, receiving us with great joy. By the grace of God, we instructed and baptized him, his nobles, and all his people. The work of God grows every day. Moreover, there were people from Axum who had fallen into the sickness of Julian’s doctrine of an illusory body, and who said that Christ suffered in a body that was neither subject to suffering nor mortal. We taught them the true faith and required them to condemn the heresy in writing, and we received them on the basis of a written declaration.

And again, after other matters:

So that all the provinces may learn of this and, rejoicing spiritually with you, offer thanksgiving and praise to our God, who loves humanity, for all these indescribable gifts of his; and so that the fathers may take care to send bishops here who can labor and minister in this divine work, which is pleasing to God and to people who place their trust in it, and which is progressing well. For there are a thousand thousands here who are hastening toward salvation, to the glory of Christ, the Savior of us all. Believe me when I say that a little while ago a human thought arose in me: that I should not write to anyone. But when I considered the danger faced by those who treat these spiritual gifts carelessly, I undertook this humble letter to your spiritual love. For I have coveted neither silver nor gold nor clothing. God is my witness, he who examines human hearts and knows my circumstances: I lack daily bread, and I even long to see a leaf of greens with my own eyes. It is enough for me to make this much known.

These things were written by the reverend Longinus himself. He also copied out extracts from them and sent them from the country of the Alodians to the king of the Nobadians, writing to ask him to send them to Alexandria. When the king eventually received them, he sent Longinus’s letters to Alexandria, to Theodore, the patriarch who had appointed Longinus. The king himself also wrote him a letter explaining the whole course of Longinus’s journey, the remoteness of the country, the trials and obstacles that had confronted him, and the help that had come to him through the grace of God. He wrote of the other things too, as matters of wonder. His words are as follows.

Letter of the King of the Nobadians to Theodore of Alexandria

Before everything else, I most warmly greet you in Christ, blessed fathers. Furthermore, I wish you to know this: seven months ago, the king of the great people of the Alodians—that is, Ethiopia [?]—sent here and fetched my holy father, Bishop Longinus, to baptize him. This did indeed happen, as the king and that same holy father of mine have written to me.

When I first spoke to my father here about this matter, he immediately accepted it readily and willingly, and his blessedness promised to undertake it. Every day he urged me on, saying, ‘We must not neglect this undertaking, because it belongs to God.’ Because of the wicked schemes of the one between us—that is, the king of the Makurians—I sent my reverend father to the king of the Blemmyes, so that he might send him there by routes farther inland. But the aforementioned Makurian also learned of it and stationed his guards along every border of his kingdom, in the mountains and on the plains, and as far as the Red Sea. He sought to seize my father in order to stop that good work of God, as my father wrote to me here.

He endured great hardship and bitter trials, both spiritual and bodily, in the country of the Blemmyes [?]. Added to these were great distress and deprivation. Yet even so, the wicked schemes of his opponent could not prevent my reverend father’s readiness to do God’s work. Rather, the Lord our God himself made straight the roads and paths of my reverend father, enabling him to pass along the great roads and through the strict guard posts. Although his baggage train of camels and other animals was lost, God nevertheless helped him, and he escaped and reached the country. He was joyfully received by the king and all the people, and he instructed and baptized the king and everyone with him, as is related in the letter he sent here.

Know this also: how closely God, the Lord of all, accompanied my father, and how he entered with him, so that you may marvel at the great wonder he performed for him. When my uncle the king and his fathers, the kings, used to send an embassy to that kingdom, the envoy would be away for eight or ten years before returning here. But after my reverend father entered that country, within two hundred days he sent us an embassy from that king, although many of our earlier envoys have never returned here at all.

So that I do not make the account in this letter longer, my father has sent me letters here for me to forward to you. Now I have sent them by his envoy. They contain everything that happened to him and everything he did, which his letter makes known, so that you too may learn of it there. For it is not fitting for your blessedness to conceal and neglect all these matters. It is especially fitting for your reverence to help my reverend father through your holy prayers.

We place this extract from the letter of the king of the Nobadians here to confirm the account, since in it he bears witness to the whole divine undertaking. He also wrote two other letters on the same subject, which we have refrained from including because of the length of the account.

Since the significance of this whole undertaking and this divine activity is made known to everyone who reads these two letters, those of the bishop and the king, we therefore thought it best not to expand the account of these matters further in our own words. Rather, with thanksgiving and wonder, let us recall, in connection with these events too, the words of our Savior, who says, ‘Truly I tell you, this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed among all nations, and then the end will come.’

With God’s help, these things happened in this way in the year eight hundred and ninety-one, and we have set them down as a record.

We have already mentioned Paul’s hiding, according to what was believed at the time, since many thought that he was hiding in a cave in the mountains of Isauria. But now, as the events that took place at the end reveal and teach us, those who wish to investigate say that during these four years when he was not seen, and was thought to be hiding in the mountains of Isauria, he was hiding in the hills of the imperial capital. Although we were living there, this was not known or revealed to us until the very end of his life. His confidants thought that this had been concealed from us, or from most people, and that his burial had been disclosed to only three individuals. These misguided people had forgotten the Lord’s saying: “There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed.”

Theodore, who had been made bishop in Alexandria by Longinus, had received no communication at all from Paul during these four years. Although he had written to him many times, he had not even received an answer to his letters. Moreover, Longinus had gone to those peoples who had become Christians in the interior of Cush. Theodore was left without consolation on any side, until he felt obliged to consider writing a circular letter to Paul’s entire party, complaining and protesting against him for neglecting and treating him with such contempt. He sent it through two of his own priests, and they reached the imperial capital. When this became known to everyone, and especially when they heard the complaint and protest from these priests, many were distressed and reproached him. They wrote to him at the place where he was thought to be, but he could not be found. So, with much reassurance and consolation, the priests were sent to the island of Cyprus, where some of his bishops were staying. They then returned and went back to Theodore, having achieved nothing. As a result, he became still more distressed, and finally set out himself and went to Cyprus.

For when Pope Theodore saw that he was receiving no reply either through his letters or through the people he sent, he finally boarded a ship and went to the island of Cyprus, but did not find Paul. He did, however, find some of Paul’s bishops. After many things had happened and disputes had arisen between them, and Paul had still not revealed himself to him, two bishops were assigned to accompany him to Alexandria. Thus he returned in distress, because he did not believe that Paul was anywhere other than there or in Cilicia, yet Paul had not appeared to him. But, as eventually became known, throughout those four years when he was not seen, while reports were being circulated that he was hiding in caves in the mountains of Cilicia and Isauria, Paul was secretly hiding in the imperial capital. This was known and disclosed to only a few. There his end overtook him, and we are also giving a separate account of it.

For during these four years, as we indicated above, when Paul was thought to be hiding in the eastern regions, he was on the hill of the imperial city. This was revealed and became known to everyone at his death. Those concerned for him tried to conceal even his death, so that it would not become known, even though he was mortal.

For, as was said and also became known, he had come up to the city with the knowledge of some of his supporters, and had remained hidden with some of them throughout the entire period mentioned. Suddenly he fell seriously ill, and shortly afterward he died. Great consternation and intense, overwhelming fear fell upon those with whom he had been hiding, or who had known about it, lest the authorities hear of it and they themselves be put in danger on his account. So they sent for just three of the priests who accepted him. They demanded solemn oaths from them that they would not tell anyone that this was Patriarch Paul. Instead, they instructed them that, if the matter attracted attention, they should say, ‘A stranger named Christopher came to this city and died.’

These three did just that. They took him, covered up, by night and brought him to a convent of women for burial. When the nuns heard about this, they became alarmed and said, ‘We will not receive a dead man at night, in the dark, without knowing who he is. Perhaps he is someone who has been murdered, and we will be put in danger.’ But the men pleaded with them at length, saying, ‘He is a great and righteous man, and a stranger. Do not be afraid.’ When they had been persuaded to receive him, the men brought him in with his face covered. As they hurried in agitation to lower him into the pit, the nuns began to object, saying, ‘If things really are as you say, and your words are true, that this is a great and righteous man, let us perform the service over him according to the proper order. Uncover his face so that we may see him, approach him, and receive a blessing from him. Then you may lower him into the grave.’

But they hurriedly bound him up and buried him, saying, ‘Let us lower him now and be on our way, for we are in a hurry.’ Thus they buried him in confusion, with the burial of a donkey, and left. This threw the nuns, who numbered more than a hundred and fifty, into great agitation.

From them spread reports full of doubts and many conjectures, not only in the city itself and in Syria, but also in Alexandria and everywhere else, as the matter became known. Paul’s death was being discussed everywhere, while these men still brazenly insisted and swore, ‘It was someone else who died, not our patriarch, Mar Paul.’

Among all the orthodox in the city who accepted him, there was much grumbling and distress because the secret of his death had been revealed to three of them and concealed from the rest. In the end, many did not remember him affectionately either, especially when they learned that his arrival, his residence in the city, and his death had been concealed from them and revealed to only three of their number. Meanwhile, his confidants continued to swear with practiced deceit that Paul had not died, but was alive. They did this, as they reasoned to themselves, so that his opponents would not rejoice.

Thus this dispute continued for an entire year, and his name was proclaimed as that of a living man in the diptychs of the living, supposedly to prevent his death from becoming known and being confirmed, although it had become known to everyone.

Now, if anyone considers the end and departure of these two blessed men—I mean Jacob and Paul—whose quarrel and struggle with one another caused a great breach and bitter division in the persecuted church of the faithful, he is left in great astonishment and helpless perplexity: how lamentably, suddenly, and obscurely they were taken from this life and departed from this world. First, the blessed Jacob, in the very heat of their quarrel and dispute, took two other bishops and a company of monks with him, and they set out in great haste for Alexandria. The reason for his journey was concealed from many, and many people had numerous opinions and all sorts of thoughts about it. But perhaps he alone who cares for the welfare of his creation saw and knew that Jacob’s journey would benefit neither the church nor Jacob himself, and so checked, obstructed, and prevented his arrival. Some reported concerning him and everyone with him that, after they put out to sea and began their voyage, a violent storm came upon them, their ship sank, and they all died at sea; their bodies were not found. This was not clearly established for anyone. Others, however, who were anxious to speak on his behalf, say that a storm did indeed come upon them, but their ship did not sink. Instead, they were driven ashore and landed in the territory of Egypt, and entered a monastery in the desert called the Monastery of Cassian. They say that within three days of their entering that monastery, first the two bishops died, and then Mar Jacob himself and one other of his attendants: all four together, one after another. Which of these accounts is true, God knows. We have not learned the facts of these matters with certainty.

Then, after an interval of about two or three years, Paul’s departure also took place in a confused manner, entirely outside every rule of proper order, in keeping with all the things of which we gave a brief account, out of much material, in the preceding chapter. These things were done secretly—or so those who did them supposed. What, then, should we think or write about these things, except to cry out to God with the prophet in sorrow and groaning, and say: ‘Though our sins testify against us, Lord, have mercy for your name’s sake, for your grace is great, and we have sinned against you.’

After the deaths of Jacob and Paul, the factions that had arisen around each of them began to discuss unity with one another. They did not, however, assemble to talk together in a proper manner, with a purpose of humility and fear of God, but arrogantly and deceitfully. Each faction thought that it was the head and the other the tail, and that it was exalted, superior, pure, and free from every reproach; each sought to subdue and subject the other. Each faction cast the blame for all these evils, breaches, and divisions upon the other, and each exalted itself over the other. Each was eager to receive the other as though it were coming to it in repentance, and to subject it to itself, following the teaching and deceit of the Accuser, who had acted deceitfully and set them against one another. And so their undertaking did not succeed.

This Peter, who had been irregularly installed by certain people and had become patriarch in Syria while Paul was still alive, was reproached first by his own conscience and then by many others for having uncanonically occupied another man’s throne while that man was still physically alive. When at last the two parties began discussing union with one another, the whole party of Paul opposed Peter because he had taken a position above Paul while Paul was still alive. Whether in pretense or in truth, or with deceitful cunning, he began to say: “Let there be no dispute on my account. I will withdraw and go and live in retirement. Let the parties unite with one another, and let them appoint someone else who is acceptable to both parties, so that there may be unity between them.”

Many approved of what he was saying, since his words bore the appearance of humility and peace. Others, however, reproached him, even rebuking him to his face, saying: “You say these things deceitfully and cunningly, not sincerely from a pure heart. Rather, you say them because you know that your supporters, who installed you, will not let you go. Besides, you use Alexandria as an excuse.”

When he had heard these things and much else from many people, he set out, took some of his supporters with him, and went to Alexandria, to show that he was indeed eager for unity. His professed purpose was to urge them toward unity, together with Damian, whom they too had appointed as their head. Many matters were raised and discussed between them. In keeping with the apostolic saying quoted above, “whether in pretense or in truth,” he was seen to speak and argue at length about unity. But they opposed him and would not accept what he said. Thus, as it appeared, he left there amid ridicule. Some thought that this had been done artfully and cunningly. For God, who examines the mind and heart, knows the truth of these things.

Because they left there on friendly terms with one another, it was suspected that he had gone there and come away playing an assumed role. For even afterward he persisted in the dispute, saying: “I will do nothing without the Alexandrians.”

After all these things, then, the assemblies of both parties—that is, the bishops, monks, and the rest—continued for a considerable time, about a whole year, disputing and meeting in various places. They went back and forth, sent messages to one another, and made burdensome and harsh demands on one another. As we explained above, they made these demands arrogantly and imperiously, not fraternally and lovingly: first through individuals from each side, and afterward through writings directed against one another. Once the dispute had begun and become established, contentious troublemakers appeared from among their own ranks and in their midst, as well as others who obstructed peace. They stirred up strife between the parties, and they turned to outright opposition against one another. They tore up the documents that had previously passed between them and began circulating writings against one another to the imperial capital, the East, and the West. Each party placed itself on the side of the innocent, while hurling insults at the other and bringing forward everything that tended toward condemnation, together with abuse and fabricated falsehoods. They all employed hostile writings against one another and harsh accusations, so that these were sent even to us and to many people in the imperial capital in the form of official proceedings. Not only did they fail to agree to act as messengers of peace toward one another, but they persisted at that time in complete division, schism, contention, and mutual hostility, and in all this turmoil that delights Satan, who asked to sift us like wheat. Thus, through the recklessness and disorderliness of both parties, who did not approach one another with the discernment that comes from the fear of God, he gained strength. And now he leaps and rejoices with all the hordes and [?] of his demons, taking pleasure in what passes between the two parties. These things have continued from their beginning until the present, the year eight hundred and ninety-six. In this year a little has been recorded out of the boundless extent of all these boundless troubles.
The fourth book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished. It contains sixty-one chapters.

The chapters of the fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History. First, concerning those who proclaim gods like the pagans, and related matters. After twelve chapters concerning these things, there follows an account of the reign of the victorious Emperor Maurice. This should have been placed at the beginning of the book, but that was not possible.
1. First chapter: Concerning how the Tritheites began to perform ordinations.
2. Second chapter: Concerning Nisha.
3. Third chapter: Concerning the party of Conon and Eugenius, the leaders of the heresies.
4. Fourth chapter: Concerning Conon's release from exile.
5. Fifth chapter: Concerning the division of the Tritheites into two heresies.
6. Sixth chapter: Concerning the journey of the two of them to the region of Pamphylia to lead people astray, and concerning the death of Eugenius there.
7. Seventh chapter: Concerning what was sent to Conon by John of Asia.
8. Eighth chapter: Concerning the proposal of the Tritheites, who deceitfully and cunningly make a show of wanting to be united, but not sincerely.
9. Ninth chapter: Concerning how they did the very same things both in Alexandria and in Syria.
10. Tenth chapter: Concerning the great book of disputations that the Tritheites produced.
11. Eleventh chapter: Concerning the assembly of the bishops and the bishops of the Tritheites.
12. Twelfth chapter: Concerning one of the Tritheite bishops who returned to orthodoxy.
13. Thirteenth chapter: Concerning the reign of the victorious Maurice, which, in the proper order, ought to have been described at the beginning of the book, had matters not turned out this way.
14. Fourteenth chapter: Concerning Emperor Maurice and the wedding feast he held for himself, and concerning the son whom he afterward fathered in the palace, and related matters.

15. Fifteenth chapter: Concerning those who habitually attacked people under the pretext of religion, robbing and stealing the possessions of others, and who did not cease stirring up [?] the emperor against the orthodox.
16. Sixteenth chapter: Concerning the persecution of the church of the Arians.
17. Seventeenth chapter: Concerning Gregory, bishop of Antioch, his journey up to the imperial capital, and his interrogation by the emperor.

18. Chapter eighteen: Concerning his parents, brothers, sisters, and very numerous relatives, whom Emperor Maurice sent for and brought to him in the imperial capital, and whom he enriched and raised to high rank.
19. Chapter nineteen: Concerning Domitian, metropolitan of the city of Melitene, a relative of the emperor.
20. Chapter twenty: Concerning how Maurice, when he became emperor, found the palace treasuries empty and fell into distress and anxiety.
21. Chapter twenty-one: Concerning the troublemakers, persecutors, and oppressors of others who continually troubled the hearing [?] of Emperor Maurice and the rest of his household.
22. Chapter twenty-two: Concerning the rebuilding of Arabissus, a ruined city in Cappadocia, from which Emperor Maurice's family came.
23. Chapter twenty-three: Concerning the destruction of the city of Arabissus by an earthquake roughly two years after its rebuilding.
The fifth book of the third part of the Ecclesiastical History, concerning the histories of the church, and the rest.

At first there were two bishops from Cilicia, Conon and Eugenius, who were the leaders of the heresy [?]. When their heresy was exposed and became known, they were repeatedly reproached and admonished about many things, but they did not turn back. Consequently, sentence was passed against them and they were deposed. They and Athanasius, the son of Empress Theodora's daughter—the man who fostered and enlarged the heresy through the large amounts of gold he distributed—jointly devised ways to obtain three bishops, as required by the canon, so that they could ordain bishops. They began showing honor to and importuning John of Ephesus, who lived in the imperial capital and had authority over the administration of all the congregations of the faithful there and everywhere else. They tried to win him over with presents and gifts, so that he would yield to them, join them, and ordain bishops with them. But he did not yield to them. Instead, he repeatedly reproached them on many points and argued with them, showing that they were heretics and that the Arians, Macedonians, Nestorians, and the other heresies were far less heretical than they were. When they could not make a fool of him and lead him astray, a certain Theonas happened to come to the city. He had been made a bishop by order of Patriarch Theodosius, but later a charge had been established against him, and Theodosius had deposed him. Thus he wandered about without an office. They approached this man, and when they had led him astray with gifts, the two of them, Conon and Eugenius, took him and, together with him, ordained many bishops. They sent them in every direction to spread their heresy.

For, in defiance of church order and the ecclesiastical canons, the party of Conon and Eugenius, the chief leaders of the heresy of many gods, began appointing bishops with the help of a man who had been deposed from the episcopate. They did so indiscriminately with anyone who came their way, whether young or old, uneducated or learned. Practically every last one of their disciples and notaries, and everyone who presented himself, they made a bishop and dispatched to different regions and countries. They went so far as to establish congregations in Rome, Corinth, Athens, and Africa, and in Africa, and to lead whole populations astray after them. They even tried to lead astray the patrician Narses in Rome, taking with them chosen men from among their number, two brothers born of the same mother, Phocas and Theodosius. Despite their considerable efforts, he turned his face away from them and would not receive them. They did, however, lead astray some of his chamberlains and officials, as well as some generals.

The followers of Conon and Eugenius, the leaders of the heresy, persisted in the imperial city even after they had been excommunicated. They were [?], debating and leading people astray. They also troubled many people and went in to complain to the emperor as though they had been mistreated and wronged. The emperor issued an order to the patriarch of the city to assemble both parties before him, and to have them argue their cases against one another before him and his synod, all of whom were their enemies. We have given an account of all these matters in other books. These things continued until Emperor Justin launched a severe persecution and, through Photius, sent them—that is, Conon and Eugenius—into exile in Palestine. Meanwhile, all the others were traveling about outside the capital, throughout Syria, Cilicia, Isauria, and Cappadocia, leading people astray and ordaining priests and deacons in churches, monasteries, towns, and villages. Eventually they led many regions astray and spread their heresy far and wide.

Now many people remained attached to Conon, as they had been before, since his house was below the palace. They would go down in their court shoes and secretly receive communion, then go back up and stand before the emperor without being discovered. Because of this, and because he presented himself as humble and righteous, many people gathered and pleaded on his behalf. He was released and left the monastery where he had been confined, and went to a village called Aulas. There he lived in a convent of women. From then on, all of them, especially the people of Cilicia and Isauria who adhered to their error, flocked to him as though he were one of the apostles. They glorified him and followed him still further into error. In the end, however, they split into two heresies and turned against one another.

We have briefly described in the preceding books the error and division of those who proclaim gods, and the causes that brought them to this point. We have also described the destructive writings expressing the error of John the Grammarian of Alexandria. One of these, the first, led them all astray and overwhelmed them. They all adhered to it together, carried it around like the Gospel, and boasted of it. Many things happened in the meantime, some of which have been set down in the accounts. The rest, because of their overwhelming number, have not been set out and recorded. For the second book by John the Grammarian, which reached them later, teaches that these bodies do not rise, but that other bodies come into being, and that those bodies rise from the dead. This led them still further astray and divided them into two heresies, each outdoing the other in impurity. Some of them did not accept that second book, but argued against it, reviled it, and anathematized it. Others accepted it even more readily than the writings—the writings of the prophets and apostles. Thus they argued and rose against one another, divided and separated, anathematized one another, and repeatedly exposed one another in writing. Both heresies remain locked in opposition to one another.

Now this region of Pamphylia had belonged to the orthodox from the beginning. It contained many large villages with churches, and many monasteries for men and women. At the time of the schism of those called Acephali—that is, the Headless—many of them had broken away and gone into the region. Through the zeal and diligence of the orthodox there, however, they had all been won back and had come to orthodoxy. Thus they all alike embraced zeal for the true faith. Orthodox bishops were frequently sent there, coming to visit them and putting church affairs in order: that is, consecrating altars and the new churches and monasteries established there. They also ordained many priests and attended to the other things that needed to be done. Thus, twice to our own knowledge, this very wretched Eugene—wretched Eugene, who fell into heresy—was sent to that region, as were other bishops. Eventually both Conon and Eugene became eager to go to that region, lead it astray, and add it to their heresy. This they also diligently undertook. While they were staying there, Eugene met his end and died there. Conon, however, returned to the imperial city.

Now before the heresy of the Tritheists split in two—that is, the party of Athanasius separating from the party of Conon—Athanasius had made a will concerning his property and had named the emperor and empress as heirs. He freed his slaves and left a legacy to each of them and to many others. He also left a substantial amount of gold to Conon, all of which was to be distributed through his hands. For Conon himself, however, he left ten pounds, to be received from his estate one at a time. Besides these, he was to receive two pounds every year for as long as he lived. Athanasius himself sealed this will and kept it, before the division arose between them.
