When it did arise, and they anathematized one another and eventually even published writings full of abuse against one another, Athanasius was considering changing the will and excluding Conon, but suddenly died. When the will was opened, Conon was found receiving what had been specified in it, even while anathematizing the man who had left it to him. It was for this reason that he had come to the imperial city. While John of Asia—that is, of Ephesus—was there, he wrote to him, solemnly warning him: “How long will you fail to take to heart, O wise man, that you are mortal, and that you must stand with your neck exposed before that fearful judgment seat of justice? You will be required to give an account for being called ‘Rabbi’ and having your hands kissed at the cost of dividing the church of the living God, who gave himself up for her. Why have you persisted in such complete insensitivity, when you know that all those who belonged to our two parties, ours and yours, have gone to God? Here, until now, only you and my humble self have remained alive in the body. Let us turn away from all the cunning that comes from Satan, put on the gentleness and humility of Christ our God, and both draw near to one another in love. Let us bring this dispute and division to an end. Just as it came about so disastrously in our days and in our midst, so now, while we are still in the body, let us take measures to dismantle the barrier of hostility, so that this ruin does not remain in the church of God.” When Conon heard this, he said, “I too desire it.” But he gave no further answer. Instead, he took the gold that had been left to him and departed for Cilicia. There he revels like a drunken man in his heresy.

So, when those who proclaimed essences, natures, and divinities were being reproached by everyone and were despised even by their own hearts, they often appeared in sheep’s clothing, pleading to be united with the church of the orthodox. They had gone out from that church, but they had not belonged to it; for if they had belonged to it, they would have remained in it. Concealing the deceit in their hearts, they would say that they wanted to be united. But when they came to discuss this and were required to turn back and stop speaking of substances and natures in the Trinity, so that a multiplicity of gods and divinities, like that of the pagans, might not thereby enter Christianity, they immediately fled and refused, saying, “We cannot refrain from speaking of a number of essences and natures.” But this reply was made to them: “The faith of the church confesses one God, known in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Three persons, three names, one divinity, one essence, one nature, one lordship, and one power, will, kingdom, authority, and dominion in heaven and on earth. One is three, and three are one, without division and without confusion. How is it that you, while speaking of a number of essences and natures—even if you do not acknowledge it openly—wish thereby to introduce swarms of gods into the catholic church, like the pagans? You seek union in appearance and not in truth, and you scheme and plot deceitfully to mislead the whole church and draw it into your heresy.” And so they would depart, refuted and put to shame. They did this many times in the imperial city and in other places, deceitfully and not sincerely.

For they repeatedly did these very same things in Alexandria and Syria as well. When they saw that they had been unable to make fools of those in the imperial city, they went into Alexandria and drew up a petition. They skillfully set out their confession in it and presented it to Damian, who had succeeded Peter there. When he too required them to abandon the enumeration of multiple natures and essences, and also to anathematize John the Grammarian and both his books, which had led them astray, they indicated that they would anathematize the latter book, concerning bodies not rising again. But they would not agree to reject or anathematize the former book, concerning the multiplicity of gods. He, for his part, anathematized and expelled them. They also did this many times in Syria. Finally, when they saw that their schemes were not succeeding, they remained in the corruption of their heresy, and they remain there even now.

So those among the Tritheists who considered themselves philosophers tore a large book out of the living body of the writings of the holy fathers: passages which, through their own heresy, they imagine establish and confirm that heresy. These are the things concerning which God’s law commanded, “You shall not eat flesh torn from animals.” In the same way, they too tore off dead limbs from the proofs of the holy fathers, intending, as they suppose, to show that all the fathers, like themselves, introduce and teach a number of many natures and substances—substances, that is, many essences. Through this, even if they did not think so, they stand convicted of also teaching and proclaiming a number of many divinities and gods, like the pagans.

For those who teach a plurality of gods, the followers of Conon and Eugenius, also appointed many bishops and sent them in every direction to promote and establish their heresy. Many of them remained even in the imperial city and opened large meeting places, since John of the imperial city had supported them from the beginning. A large crowd gathered around them openly and without fear. When John died and Eutychius succeeded him, Eutychius sent men against those who had broken away from the members of his heresy, those who deny the resurrection of bodies. He arrested everyone he found there, seized all their liturgical equipment, and uprooted and demolished their altars. He arrested their bishops and the others and confined them in monasteries, where they remained for a long time.

One of these well-known bishops whom the followers of Conon had appointed in the region of Cilicia recognized and understood the error of their heresy and turned away from them. He submitted a written declaration to the orthodox, anathematized the followers of Conon and their heresy, and joined the company of the faithful.

After the death of Emperor Justinian, which took place on November 14 in the year 876, after he had reigned for thirty-nine years, Justin, his sister’s son, succeeded him and reigned for thirteen years less forty days. During this time, when a severe illness of chastisement overtook him, he appointed Tiberius Caesar on December 7 in the year 886. Justin himself granted him the imperial crown during his own lifetime, when he saw that death was pressing upon him. He installed him as emperor while he himself was still alive, lying in the depths of death. He lived alongside him for nine days after Tiberius became emperor, and then died.

After Tiberius had held the position of Caesar for four years, and then, after being proclaimed sole emperor, had reigned for another four years less thirty-one days, he became gravely ill with a fatal illness. When his condition became critical, he too appointed a Caesar: Count Maurice the Cappadocian, on August [?] 5 in the year 893. Maurice had arrived only a few days earlier from the eastern region, where he had been appointed chief and commander over all the commanders of the Roman armies, as we are told in the earlier chapters concerning these matters. He also gave him the name Tiberius. He made his younger daughter, whose name was Augusta, reign alongside him, and also gave her the name Constantina. He immediately gave her to Maurice as his wife. He lived alongside them for eight days. When he saw that his condition was critical, one day before his death he placed the imperial crown on Maurice. He departed this world at the [?] of the Hebdomon. They then brought him into the city, to the palace, and he was buried according to the custom of emperors.

Now when the God-loving emperor Maurice had taken his seat on the imperial throne and had been publicly recognized and acknowledged as sovereign, he began administering the affairs appropriate to the empire. Some time later, when the mourning for Emperor Tiberius had ended, he made great preparations and arranged imperial festivities, with many splendid displays befitting the reign of emperors. It would not be easy to describe these without considerable labor. Nor does the purpose we have set ourselves call for us to occupy ourselves with such things, except to mention particular details connected with the history of the church, which is the subject of our account.

After the royal wedding celebration had ended, she enjoyed many gifts and royal pleasures. Afterward she conceived, and in due time a son was born to them in the purple, on the fourth day of the month of Ab [?], in the year 894. They named him Theodosius, apparently with Theodosius the Younger in mind. From the time of Constantine onward, he alone had been born in the purple. He himself did not father another child in the purple, nor did the emperors who came after him: Marcian, Leo, Zeno, Anastasius, Justin, Justinian, the other Justin, and Tiberius, down to Maurice himself.

Thus, when a son was born to Maurice, many rejoiced over him, especially because other individuals, who were utterly unfit, had set their sights on the throne and were scheming to seize the empire by force. On the day of this child's birth, their plans were extinguished and brought to nothing. Indeed, even in the Hippodrome, the people of the city praised him and shouted an acclamation to him, saying, “God has graciously given you, and you have freed us from subjection to many.”

Immediately, offerings, gifts, and many presents were brought to this child by all the great men and women, the senate, and the rest. Everyone was devising ways and striving to surpass his neighbor in the magnificence of the gifts he presented with great reverence.

From the very beginning of the reign of the God-loving Maurice, the troublemakers and thieves mentioned above never stopped stirring him up and agitating him against the orthodox, accusing them of many evil deeds and bringing false charges against them. Yet he himself did not know what beliefs they held or why they were divided against one another. As they continually stirred him up and agitated him, he became angry, summoned the patriarch, and ordered him to send men to seize and imprison them so that they could not assemble.

Now John the patriarch was distressed and mourning over the affair of the pagans. Through what seemed to be the action of God, they had been exposed, revealed, identified, and informed against by one another, and records of proceedings had been drawn up against them all—not only those in the imperial capital, but those in every region and city, as we explained at length in the preceding chapters. Most of the senate had been implicated in these matters. Even the emperor himself was alarmed that these things had happened at the very beginning of his reign, and that he might be deprived [?] of his leading men and kill and destroy his entire senate. So he kept quiet and let the matter drop on this account, and covered up the affair [?]. Only a few of them were put to death, while others went into exile. The rest remained as they were, left in their positions of leadership and authority.

This was why the patriarch was mourning inconsolably. Consequently, when the emperor ordered him to persecute and arrest the orthodox, he answered him with a cry: “Even God groans at this! After their paganism had been exposed and become known to everyone, we acquitted the pagans, set them free, and let them go. Now that we have declared these people innocent, are we instead to persecute, condemn, and kill Christians? Are these the laws of justice? What do the Dissenters say or do that we should persecute them? Let Your Majesty know that, when the pagans were acquitted and released, not one of them was even removed from his position of authority. How, then, can I persecute these Christians, whose Christianity is beyond reproach and who consider themselves more faithful than we are?” In this way he put a stop to the persecution at that time.

A short time afterward, these troublemakers, who had repeatedly asked to attack the gatherings of the faithful without obtaining his consent, fabricated pretexts and multiplied accusations against the gatherings of the Arians. Their entire band assembled and went to attack the Arian church, which met outside the city in the queen’s courtyard. They fell upon them while they were assembled and offering the Eucharist. They overturned their altar, threw their offering onto the ground, and took all their liturgical equipment, their books, and anything else that fell into their hands. They dragged them away, brought them in, and imprisoned them in the church’s chancel.

The saying of our Lord applies both to these people and to the others imprisoned there: “Truly I tell you, you will not come out of there until you have paid the last penny.” These people too are required to pay the last penny of their livelihood before they can come out of there.

Now, when the prosecution of the pagans took place in the imperial city, in Antioch, and everywhere else, various allegations were also made against the blessed Gregory of Antioch. As a result, the whole city rose against him, wanting to burn him, and shouted, “This man to the fire! A Christian patriarch for the city!” along with many other things. But the whole affair was covered up, corrupted, and brought to nothing everywhere because of great and prominent people, and so it was hushed up. He too remained in office, although all the people were thoroughly aroused against him and took offense at him.

After some time, he prepared to go up to the emperor. He assembled a great store of gold and silver, many splendid garments of every kind, and other things suitable as gifts and marks of honor for the dignitaries of the senate. These preparations were such that, as was reported, his journey cost many hundred-pound sums of gold. When he reached the imperial city, he lavished his gifts on the entire senate, on the great men and the great ladies. He also pacified and soothed with his gifts all the members of the church who were angry with him because of the reports of paganism. Along with these, he won over all the associates of the patriarch, who, on hearing that he was coming up, had decided not to enter into communion with him. Since the patriarch himself would not accept a bribe, those around him were persuaded, and they persuaded him, and he received Gregory.

The emperor and the entire senate also received him with honor, and they all took his side. Although many had expected that proceedings would be brought against him and that he would not return to his see, he was received. He accomplished everything he wanted and was dismissed with great honor.

Having resolved to appease and please the people of his city, he asked the emperor to authorize him to build them a hippodrome. He granted him this too, even giving him funds for the construction of this church of Satan, in which Satan was to fulfill all his will and pleasure. Indeed, as was reported, he went so far as to take mime actors with him and bring them down from the imperial city. To some people this became a matter for laughter, mockery, and ridicule, but to others it brought mourning and sorrow. They all said, “Look, in this man our Lord’s saying is fulfilled: ‘If salt loses its taste, with what will it be salted?’” and the rest.

Although he had been made head of the church of Christ, he showed himself instead to be the builder and founder of the church of Satan in Antioch, after all these generations had passed. He persisted diligently and supervised its construction without flagging—as was said derisively and mockingly.

Immediately, then, at the beginning of his reign, the emperor sent and brought to him his father, an elderly man named Paul, his mother, his brother named Peter, and his two sisters, one a widow and the other married to a man named Philippicus. He first appointed this man count of the Excubitors. Later he put him in his own former position, giving him authority over all the commanders of the Roman armies throughout the East, and sent him to prepare the armies for war against the Persians. He also made his own father head of all the patricians, above the entire senate. He immediately granted him and his son Peter, the emperor’s own brother, the entire estate of the great patrician Marcellus, the brother of Emperor Justin. It was not much smaller than the imperial estate. This included his houses, country estates, gold, silver, wardrobe, and absolutely everything he possessed everywhere. He also gave his father and mother another house near the church and the palace. To his sister and his brother-in-law Philippicus he also gave a large, substantial house on the western side of the city, in the place called Zeugma. The house itself was known as the house of Elras [?]. To his other sister, the widow, he also gave a large, new, substantial house, which had likewise belonged to the patrician Peter, who was called Barsymes. He had recently built it, and it contained as much as a whole city. He also granted the rest of his relatives other large and well-known houses belonging to the imperial estate. He eagerly gave to them, advanced them, enriched them, and strengthened their position. Along with others, he also promoted them to great and distinguished offices close to the imperial throne, appointing them, securing their positions, and giving them authority. Since these people are not the subject of our account, we have refrained from saying more about them.

As for this excellent Domitian, Emperor Maurice himself, while he was still a count and had been sent to the East by Tiberius, had made him bishop of Melitene in Cappadocia. After Maurice had spent a short time in the East, about two years, more or less, and had gone up and become emperor, Domitian immediately hurried to him. He became his adviser and intimate companion, closer to him than anyone else. He advised and comforted him in the harsh and bitter trials brought on by the wars, both those against the pagan people of the Persian Magi and those against the barbarous and savage peoples who had come from the far reaches of the world, called Avars, and the other peoples, the Slavs, who surrounded Emperor Maurice on every side. In all these matters the bishop of Melitene comforted and advised the emperor, although he was still young. He was, however, thoroughly steeped in the Chalcedonian beliefs of Leo’s party. The many important matters brought to him from every direction he himself presented to the emperor, persuading him and settling them as he wished, even on the spot.

Now Emperor Tiberius, who appointed Emperor Maurice to succeed him, recklessly squandered all the treasures of Emperor Justin. When he took charge of the empire and appeared as its ruler, he found in Justin’s treasuries a great quantity of gold that had been unjustly amassed and stored away in his vaults. It was Justin who had appointed Tiberius himself to succeed him. When Tiberius saw these hoards, it was as though some spirit of zeal entered him: he began bringing the gold out, scattering it, and distributing it—sometimes compassionately for [?], sometimes for the soldiers’ pay, as was customary. Sometimes he spent without order or calculation, scattering it as though with a winnowing shovel, until Justin’s treasuries were exhausted. This happened especially through the largesse he distributed during his consulship. As he himself used to say, he distributed seventy-five hundred-pound weights of gold, besides silver and the other customary imperial expenditures, until he was compelled to open Emperor Anastasius’s vaults, bring out their contents, and distribute them.

But when he departed this world, having appointed Emperor Maurice to succeed him, Maurice found the palace swept clean, as though with a broom. He was compelled to hold on to whatever gold could still be found, or whatever came to him from the taxes, and to tighten his grip. He also withheld and retained a portion of the army’s pay, saying, “I am not scattering and squandering it; rather, I am gathering it and setting it aside so that I can spend it to secure peace for the state.”

With this intention he tightened his grip and stopped many customary payments, to the point that many people laughed at him, mocked him, and even abused him in many ways. They called him tightfisted, a skinflint, and a miser, saying that he had found ways to promote, advance, and enrich only his own relatives. There were many other things of this kind which, were it not for a reason, it would not have been fitting for us to include in the records of church history.

While the emperor was engrossed in the troubles and concerns of the wars that surrounded him on every side, these troublemakers were driven not by zeal for the faith but by this motive: they were eagerly intent on plundering houses and taking other people’s possessions. They schemed to obtain permission and authority to do these things by force. They never stopped wearing out the ears of the patriarch and the emperor, persistently and zealously denouncing and accusing people, especially those who rejected the Council of Chalcedon, as well as many others. They said, “Look, all these people gather large congregations and celebrate the Eucharist and perform baptisms, more than the catholic church and all the heretical groups—the Arians, Sabbatians, Tetradites, Montanists, Marcionites, and the rest of those like them. They disturb and overturn the whole church. Give us authority over them, so that we may seize them, imprison them, torture them, and uproot all their meeting places.”

But the patriarch, being a peaceable and merciful man, knew their deceitfulness and that they were intent on plunder and robbery. He rebuked them, saying, “If you were showing genuine zeal in what you are eager to do, or were concerned to bring these people to the right path, your zeal would be good. But we know what concerns you: you are intent on stealing, plundering, and seizing other people’s possessions. Go and keep quiet. We will not allow persecution to take place in our days. Instead, we teach and admonish as far as we can.”

These people were not only from the ranks of the clergy but also from the laity. Nor was that all: among them were people who were not sound in their Christianity, physicians and pagans. Besides their eagerness for plunder, they also wanted to present themselves as people who, like Christians, were zealous for the Christian faith. When they saw that the bishop would not be drawn into their recklessness, they did not stop wearing out the ears of the merciful emperor himself. Some of them were, in fact, imperial physicians. But the emperor, whose whole activity and all whose thoughts were taken up with the wars against the barbarians, would not turn toward them or even lend them a hearing. He said, “Are the foreign wars surrounding us not enough for us, that you also want to embroil us in internal wars?” In this way their onslaught was checked, and their plans were thwarted and hindered.

When the God-loving Maurice came to the throne, Tiberius had ordered that he too should be called Tiberius, after his own name. But Maurice did not like to change the original name he had received from his ancestors. He even ordered that Maurice should be inscribed on the dies for his gold coinage, and that was the inscription on all the gold coins minted.

He was eager, above all else, to build up his own city, Arabissus, to establish and elevate it and make it famous. He sent imperial agents in every direction, and gathered and brought in craftsmen skilled in stonework, stonecutters and masons, builders, carpenters, architects, smiths, engineers, and practitioners of all the other crafts. He stationed a military unit there so that they would all remain constantly at the work, assisting all the craftsmen in every task.

First he ordered that the church there should be taken down and made much more spacious and extensive. He sent an abundant supply of gold and silver furnishings and splendid vessels for the altar, and lavishly provided for the adornment and furnishing of the whole church. He also ordered a large canopy, like those in the other churches of the imperial capital, to be made here out of bronze, and sent it to be installed there.

He further ordered that there should be a large guesthouse there, with lofty buildings. Along with these, in keeping with the city's status, there were also to be a large public bath, long and spacious colonnades, large basilicas, a palace, and a strong wall. Because of these things, many people spoke against him and grumbled bitterly, saying, ‘To the Roman troops who labor and fight for the state he cries out every day, “I have no gold to distribute to them.” And now, when so many strong cities in the east and west have been conquered and devastated by the barbarians, he cries, “There is no gold for me to give.” How, then, are so many hundred-pound sums of gold being lavished here, as people say?’

Since we ourselves do not know precisely whether things are as many people say, we do not attest them and enter them into the records of our history as established facts. For they were saying, ‘He has sent all these hundred-pound sums of gold to build and establish a city that has never been renowned or contributed anything to the Roman state.’

For while the city of Arabissus was being built with great care and diligence, and while construction was still continuing, suddenly a great, terrifying, and violent earthquake, in the second year of its construction, which was the third indiction, overturned places throughout the east. As though in some act of wrath, it overturned the whole of Arabissus. According to the report, it brought down all the buildings in it, both new and old, so that everyone was astonished.

Emperor Maurice himself was deeply shaken and distressed, since the overthrow of his city seemed to have come from God through a hidden command. Nevertheless, he did not refrain from building and establishing it again a second time. All the craftsmen who had been gathered for its construction remained there once more under the previous arrangements, to build and establish it and raise it up anew.

The fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished. It contains twenty-three chapters.

Book Six of the Third Part of the Ecclesiastical History: On accounts of wars, briefly recorded.

We therefore did not consider it improper or out of place to append to the ecclesiastical histories a brief account of the wars, conflicts, devastation, and bloodshed that occurred in our days. For the knowledge of those who come after us—if indeed the world still continues—we will record and make these things known as far as we can, according to what we understand and receive by report. Through these things we recall the life-giving word and teaching of our Savior, which instructs us, warns us, and bears witness to us concerning the final time, the end of the world, and the time of his coming, saying: “When you see all these things happening, know that it has reached the door.” In our own days, we see that all these things have happened and have been fulfilled. From now on, therefore, we ought at all times to await that fearful coming, with great power and abundant glory.

We are making a few brief records of the events that have recently taken place in the eastern regions. Let us begin our historical account with the illustrious patrician Marcian, a relative of Emperor Justin, who was one of the commanders sent to the East at that time. Burning with zeal for the Christian state, he assembled his army, went down, and encamped against the city of Nisibis, which the Persians still hold. He pressed the attack vigorously to capture it and built siege works all around it. Since he also had engineers with him, he erected siege engines against it, with high towers and strong siege frames [?]. The city was in distress. Its inhabitants, together with the Persian troops stationed there, despaired of their lives, seeing that it was now virtually conquered by the Romans. While those inside were in dismay, those outside were preparing to capture and destroy the city.

While all the Romans were expecting and preparing to enter it, there appeared a brutal man named Acacius Archelaus, sent by Emperor Justin against Marcian, without any regard for what was right, to remove him from his command, cut off his military belt, and send him away from the eastern regions. He arrived and presented the order while Marcian and his army were fighting against Nisibis and expecting to enter and capture the city the following day. The entire army was shaken and lost heart.

The illustrious Marcian had been working and preparing, and was close to capturing Nisibis. When he heard the order, he said to Acacius, “You have seen how much trouble we have endured to capture this city. Now restrain yourself and grant us just two days, and then immediately carry out what you have been ordered to do. The emperor has the authority to have his orders carried out.”

But Acacius became angry with him, insulted him, and flew into a rage. He seized him in front of all his troops, tugged him this way and that, pulled off and cut his military belt, and subjected him to insults. It was even said that he struck him on the cheek. Thus the whole army was in an uproar, and the entire force lost heart. Cursing at the injustice they had witnessed, they took his standard, lowered it, and turned it backward. Immediately the whole army broke camp and fled. They turned back and withdrew from the city, mourning and grieving over what had happened to their commander, a good and faithful man. They grieved also because, just when they had expected to enter and take the city, they had turned back without any of their enemies pursuing them, becoming an object of laughter and mockery to those who hated them.

When the Persian force inside the city saw these things—the Romans’ sudden confusion and retreat, and the turning back of Marcian’s standard—they were astonished. They took courage, armed themselves, and pursued them. They fell upon the infantry troops who had been left at the rear, slaughtering and striking down many of them. Then they returned to their city, laughing and jeering at the things the Romans had brought upon themselves through their own actions. Immediately they wrote and informed their king of all this, saying, “Hurry to cross into Roman territory at once, because the great gods, the Sun and Fire, have cast them down. By their own emperor’s command they have turned against one another in this way, removed Marcian in disgrace, and all fled away from our city.”

Now, in keeping with the purpose and sequence of these successive accounts, let us explain clearly and truthfully the cause of Emperor Justin’s anger, first against Mundhir son of Harith, and then against Marcian on his account. He became angry and issued orders against them both unjustly and without a fair judgment, under we know not what influence. His anger against Mundhir arose for the following reason.

Harith, king of the Arabs under Roman rule, had held all the Arabs under Persian rule in great fear and dread of him. When they saw that he had died, they despised and belittled all his sons, his nobles, and his army, and thought that his entire encampment had now been delivered into their hands. Then they gathered, came, and encamped in the territory of Harith’s family, where all their livestock were, and drove off all their herds of camels. When Mundhir learned of this, he was deeply embittered and seethed with fierce zeal. He took all his brothers, his sons, his nobles, and his entire army, and they fell upon them suddenly, when the others did not imagine at all that they would dare stand against them. They slaughtered and destroyed them. When their king Qabus saw the fury of the slaughter inflicted by Mundhir and his army, who had attacked, gained the upper hand, and already slaughtered his whole army, he mounted and fled with a few others, escaping stripped of everything.

Mundhir entered and sat in his tent. He carried off his entire camp, his baggage, and all his camel herds. He also captured and bound members of his family and some of his nobles. The rest he slaughtered and plundered. He went on and pitched his own tent in Qabus’s territory, three stages farther on, where all the livestock and all the wealth of the Arabs under Persian rule were. He remained encamped there for a long time. When Qabus’s raiding parties came and saw the tent pitched in Qabus’s own territory, they thought that their king Qabus himself was in it. They would confidently enter and plunge into Mundhir’s camp, where they were captured and killed, while the prominent men among them were bound. Thus, after remaining there for a considerable time, as long as they wished, they returned from there with a great quantity of captured horses, many herds of camels, weapons, and other things.

After some time, Qabus went and gathered a large army for himself. He sent word to Mundhir: “Prepare for battle, for we are coming against you. Although you fell upon us like a raiding band and imagined that you had defeated us, now we are coming against you openly in battle.” But Mundhir sent word to them: “Why are you troubling yourselves? I am coming.” He accepted the challenge, made preparations, and matched his words with action. He encountered them suddenly in the desert, when they were not expecting it. He fell upon them, threw them into confusion, and slaughtered most of them, and once again they fled before him.

We have already mentioned these events earlier in other accounts. But now our purpose is to explain what happened unjustly, without proper examination, and what plot was devised against him after these great successes and this immense victory in the two battles. Mundhir, expecting to be favorably received and praised by the emperor, wrote to him about everything he had done and about the whole extent of his victory. After this, he wrote asking him to send him gold so that he could hire an army, since he thought that they would certainly gather against him again. When Emperor Justin heard that he had written asking him to send gold, he became angry and exceedingly furious. He insulted him, threatened him harshly, and resolved in his heart to have him killed secretly by treachery.

Then Emperor Justin, as though filled with some hostile spirit, wrote a letter to the patrician Marcian, intending, as he thought, to have Mundhir killed secretly. He wrote as follows: “I have written to Mundhir the Arab to come to you. See to it that, as soon as he comes, you take his head without delay, and write to us.” To Mundhir, however, he wrote: “Because of certain urgent matters, I have written to the patrician, the patrician Marcian, to speak with you. Go to him immediately, without delay, and discuss the matter.”

As everyone eventually learned, through what seemed to be an act of God, the arrangement was reversed. Mundhir’s own name was written on the order addressed to Marcian to take Mundhir’s head, while Marcian’s name was written on the one addressed to Mundhir, as though by mistake. Thus an imperial courier received both orders, went out, and delivered them to the two men according to their written addresses. Mundhir consequently received the order addressed to Marcian for taking his head, while Marcian received Mundhir’s, which said: “Go to Marcian, for I have written to him to speak with you.”

When Mundhir received this and read it, he was deeply shaken. He said, “In return for my labors and hardships on behalf of Roman territory, I am being repaid by having my head taken off! Is this what I deserved?” He was filled with anger, assembled his entire army, and instructed them to guard him, saying: “If you see anyone sent to me by the Roman emperor, then, if they are few, seize them and keep them under guard outside the camp. But if they are many, immediately meet them fiercely in battle. Do not let yourselves be persuaded by anything they say to you, and do not let them come anywhere near the perimeter of your camp.”

Thus all the Arab divisions remained assembled, armed and ready, night and day, keeping watch and preparing to fight any Romans who might come to them. When the Persians and their Arabs heard this, they knew that they no longer had anything to fear from Mundhir and that he would not throw himself into battle on behalf of the Romans, who had sought to kill him. They therefore confidently prepared to invade Roman territory, both the Persians and their Arabs. They devastated and burned it—“and burned” [?]—and advanced as far as the region of Antioch. They took an immense number of captives, destroyed, uprooted, and burned large, strong villages resembling towns in the region of Antioch and elsewhere. They plundered and completely devastated all these districts, and returned to their own country with great spoils.

Mundhir himself was grieved and mourned over the plot against him and over the devastation the enemies had caused, enriching themselves from Roman territory. He took his army, went out, and settled in the desert. Everyone who heard of the unjust order issued against him, though he had committed no offense, was deeply distressed. People voiced their disapproval and blamed those who had issued these orders without thought or a just judgment.

When the emperor heard these things from every side, and also learned that Mundhir had freed himself from all responsibility for Roman affairs, he sent word to the governors and military commanders in the East to go to him, persuade him, and reconcile him. But when many sent him messages proposing to visit him, he sent each one this reply: “You should know that, if any man from anywhere in Roman territory comes to me, I will meet him in battle. Either he will kill me or I will kill him. Far be it from me ever again to entrust my life to a man from Roman territory! As far as you and your emperor are concerned, my head has already been taken off. Was this, then, what I owed the Romans?” Thus, for a period of two or three years, many appeals were written to him, but he would allow no one near, sending out the order and making it known to everyone.

Anger fell upon Marcian because Mundhir had survived and escaped, because the secret had been exposed and revealed, and because the plan had not been carried out. It also became clear to everyone that this death sentence had been issued against him unjustly and maliciously, without any regard for the fear of God.

So King Mundhir remained on his guard with his entire army, taking every precaution and being wary of all the nobles and armies of the Roman Empire—“of the Romans of the empire” [?]—for roughly three years, more or less. Yet, as a Christian man, he grieved for Roman territory and was filled with anger against the Persian Arabs because they had dared to cross the border with the Persian army, devastating, burning, and taking captives as far as Antioch, and had returned to their country with great spoils and countless captives. He therefore resolved to make peace and fight on behalf of the Roman state.

Letters from the emperor were constantly being sent to him through many nobles. The emperor denied responsibility, saying that the order for his death had been written without his knowledge. But Mundhir remained wary and would not consent to receive either the letters or any of those sent to him. He kept his sword ready against anyone who dared approach the perimeter of his camp. Finally, however, he sent a message to the patrician Justinian, son of Germanus, who was the chief commander, above all the commanders of the Roman armies throughout the East. He wrote to him as follows:

“From the beginning I had heard of the Romans’ treachery and knew of it. But now, through experience as well, I have learned the truth through this deadly plot devised against me in return for my labors. From now on I will never agree to entrust my life to any Roman leader. But as for you, because I know you to be a Christian man of noble birth who fears God, if you come to the shrine of the blessed Saint Sergius at Resafa and send word to me, I will come there with my army, armed for battle. If I am met with peace, and you speak truthfully with me, I will return in peace, and so will you. But if I find treachery, I trust in the God in whom I believe that I will not weaken or let my hands go slack.”

When the patrician Justinian received this, he was exceedingly glad. He sent word to him: “Have no doubts about me, for the God of the Christians stands between us. Come on such-and-such a day to the shrine of Saint Sergius, and you will find me there. Do not put your army to trouble, for I trust in God that we will part from one another in peace, harmony, and love.”

When Mundhir received this reply, he relaxed and changed his mind. He immediately set out with a few men and went to him. When the two stood together before the resting place of the bones of Saint Sergius, many things were discussed between them, too many to put in writing. They requested and received assurances from one another as they wished, and then, trusting one another and reconciled, they parted with great joy. When Emperor Justin and the rest of the senate learned of this, they too rejoiced greatly that Mundhir had been persuaded and reconciled. Afterward, letters of peace and reconciliation passed between the two sides.

A short time later, the brave and mighty King Mundhir, filled with anger at the insolence of the Persian Arabs and anxious to go and rescue the captives they had taken from Roman territory, quietly assembled his brothers, all his relatives, their sons, and all their troops. He instructed them to make ready at once, quickly, with weapons and provisions, and all to assemble before him on Monday. When they had assembled and were fully prepared, he revealed the secret to them, saying: “Immediately, without a single man scattering or going far from us, let us all together fall upon Nu‘man’s Hira in Persian territory. Because of their arrogance and the violence of their insolence against the Christians, God will deliver them into our hands.”

They all set out swiftly, reached Hira, and fell upon it suddenly, while its inhabitants were at ease and unsuspecting, to their utter astonishment. They destroyed and wiped out the entire army they found there. Mundhir devastated, demolished, and burned the whole city, except for the churches. He pitched his tent in its center and remained there for five days. He seized and bound all the Arabs he captured. He took away all the captives of Hira, together with all the captives they had seized and brought out of Roman territory, all their horses, and all their possessions. He led them away and returned to his own country in great triumph and overwhelming victory.

This added still further to his glory and wealth. He distributed that wealth, giving generously to all the monasteries and churches of the orthodox and to the poor. He won exceptional renown among everyone. Even the two empires were astonished and marveled at the vigor of the man’s heroism and at the victories he had won.

Now the king of the Persians, with his powerful armies, as soon as he learned that Marcian had fallen and that the army had fled from the city of Nisibis, immediately arrived and found all the siege machines and all the engines that Marcian the patrician had made for use against it. He immediately went and laid siege to Dara, taking with him all Marcian’s siege equipment that had been used against Nisibis. He brought it and set it up against the city of Dara, having also brought craftsmen of every kind with him.

First of all, he brought in stonecutters and others to cut through the eastern mountain outside the aqueduct and divert it away from the city. As is reported, they encountered hard rock. They would light a fire against it and afterward pour vinegar on it, and in this way they made it crumble. He set up against the city all the engines that Marcian had made for use against Nisibis. He remained besieging it, varying the methods of warfare he used against it in order to capture it, for a period of six months. He also built two siege mounds against it. But the Romans devised means of setting them on fire and burned them while the city remained closed.

Among the commanders in it were John the general, the son of Timostratus, a fighting man, and Sergius son of Saphani, who was also a general, and others. Sergius, however, as people reported, was struck by an arrow and died.

Finally, the king of the Persians went up and pitched his tent on the northern mountain above the city. Sitting there, he could watch everything that was being done inside it. He therefore ordered a siege mound to be built up there as well, against the great tower that was higher than all the other towers, which they called Heracles. Those inside had no means of doing anything against it. Outside, however, they strengthened the siege mound and took up their positions, confident of capturing the city.

Even before this, when he saw how much effort he had expended without shaking the city, he had also ordered a brick wall to be built around the outside of the city wall, so that, if the people of the city happened to come out, it would hold them back. When he saw that all his devices had been frustrated, as has been related, he became sick and so distressed that he nearly died. He sent word to the city that they should send someone to speak with him.

There was there a well-known and renowned man, an interpreter for the Romans and the Persians, whose name was Comitas. The people of the city sent this man to him. After speaking at length with him, the king told him to tell the people of the city to give him five hundredweights as the city’s ransom, and he would withdraw from it. Although Comitas eventually promised him that he would do so, he was confident that the city could not be captured and did not tell them this.

When the king saw that days had passed, that they had disregarded him, and that they had given him no answer, he became still more enraged and was filled with great fury. He again pressed his attack against the city and reinforced and strengthened the siege mound that he had built last. By then the Romans despised him and mocked him, saying, ‘He will be put to shame with this one just as with the others.’ In this way they became careless about fighting on the wall. All the more so because the cold was severe and intense. They came down from the wall and went inside to eat and drink in their houses.

When the Persians saw that the wall had been emptied of Roman troops, and that the siege mound they had built rose above the wall, they devised a plan: they lashed timbers together and rested them against the wall. The troops crossed over and filled that entire section of the wall, then came down into the city. Suddenly a cry arose: ‘The city has been captured!’ The Persian army overwhelmed the Romans, who were astonished, shaken, and thrown into confusion. They all ran together to the city gates to escape from them. When the Persians saw how numerous they were, they too became frightened and alarmed. They held back and let the Romans flee, rather than stand and face them.

The Romans ran to all the gates, shouting for the keys. A search was made, but the keys could not be found, because the commanders had hidden them. When the Romans saw that the Persian army had gained strength and had already filled the city, while they themselves were hemmed in and held back on every side and could not escape, they gathered their courage, whether for death or for life, and hurled themselves against the Persian army. They cut them down and threw them to the ground like reapers cutting ears of grain. The others, in turn, did the same to them. Fierce fighting took place inside the city, and they slaughtered one another while the city remained closed for seven days, until the city was filled with corpses and stank. Out of necessity, they dragged the bodies away and threw them into the river and into the cisterns.

When the Persians saw that they were being slaughtered and could not enter and gain possession of the city’s plunder, and were themselves alarmed by the Romans, they fled and went up onto the wall. They decided to deal deceitfully with them. They sent a treacherous message to the Romans, saying, ‘Why are we slaughtering and destroying one another like this? Come, let us give one another our word, and let both sides lay down their weapons and make peace with one another.’

By then the Roman troops were anxious for their lives and saw that they were trapped in desperate circumstances. They agreed, gave their word and received the others’ word, and laid down their weapons. They now approached one another trustingly, as though at peace. The Romans relied on the pledge and were no longer afraid. The powerful Persian army entered in confidence, and the two sides mingled with one another as though at peace. But when both sides began plundering the city, the Persians’ fraud and treachery were revealed. They turned against them and broke their word, seized the Romans, and slaughtered a great many of them. They bound the rest one by one and brought them out to the king, together with all the freeborn men and women and the city’s leaders. He gave orders, and they were all branded.

He also ordered everyone who possessed gold to bring it to him, and that wherever gold or silver was found, it should be brought to him. So a great amount of gold was gathered. It is said that more than one hundred or two hundred hundredweights were collected before him.

But since we have no certain knowledge of these matters, we do not wish to make a false assertion. Rather, we pass over in silence those things about which we have no certain knowledge.

The king, it is said, when he saw all that gold, summoned the leading men of the city and said to them, ‘May the great God of heaven hold you responsible for all these lives that have been lost, both yours and ours. [?] I wanted only one hundredth of all this gold now piled up here, for you to give as the ransom of your city, and I would have withdrawn from it. I even sent you this message through Comitas, but you paid no attention to me.’

When they heard this, they swore to him, ‘We have never heard this message.’ He summoned Comitas to confront them and said to him, ‘Was it not through you that I sent them this message?’ He said, ‘Yes, my lord.’ He said, ‘And did you tell them?’ He replied, ‘My lord, I did not tell them, because I was afraid.’ In his anger the king sentenced him to death, but then said to him, ‘Because you have worked on behalf of both states, I will not kill you.’ He gave orders, and both his eyes were blinded.

Thus he plundered the city, taking an indescribably great amount of booty. He took its people captive and emptied it of all its inhabitants. He left a force of his own in it and returned to his country with an immense and boundless haul: the silver and gold of the city’s people, of the churches, and of the others. He brought out of it a great quantity of plunder and a multitude of captives.

As for its capture and its surrender into the hands of the Assyrians, the time from its foundation under Emperor Anastasius until its capture is reckoned at approximately seventy-two years.

While the Persian king was still besieging Dara, the city of Dara, and saw that no one was opposing him, he immediately sent a marzban named Adarmahan against the city of Apamea with a large army. He too captured fortresses, destroyed and burned large, fortified villages, and went on until he reached Apamea.

Previously, when the Persian had captured Antioch, he had encamped against Apamea and put it under pressure. Apamea too had surrendered to him after obtaining his promise, and the king himself had entered it and watched horse races there. He had not destroyed or burned anything in it. For this reason they trusted him, believing that the man who was now coming would likewise do them no harm. With this confidence, the city's leading men and the bishop went out to meet him and brought him gifts of honor. But he deceitfully told them, “Since the city belongs to us, open the gates for me so that I can enter and see it.” Trusting him and not expecting him to do anything harmful, they opened the gates for him, and he entered the city.

Immediately he seized the gates and began arresting and binding the men and women and plundering the city. They brought out all the booty and the entire population and placed them outside the city. When they had plundered the whole city of Apamea, which was full of wealth accumulated over many years and was far more prosperous than many other cities, and had brought out its entire population and all its booty, including the bishop along with them, they set fire to it and burned it completely. Thus they took all the captives and all the booty from it and from the other places and went down to the king while he was besieging Dara. The captives brought down from Apamea and the other places were counted before the king: two hundred and ninety-two thousand. They were then divided up and taken into Persian territory.

After the king had captured Dara and plundered it, he found limitless wealth there too, for people from the other cities and from everywhere had been fleeing to it as to an impregnable fortress. They brought out its entire captive population, a number beyond counting, and he departed and returned to his own country.

Now the Persian king was drunk with pride, and his mind was carried away by the great quantity of plunder and captives he had taken from Roman territory. He ordered that two thousand young women, perfect in stature and beauty, be selected from among the captives. In stature and beauty—when these women had been selected according to his command and brought before him, he ordered that they be adorned in every way like brides, with splendid, expensive clothing, gold and silver, jewels and pearls. They were to be sent as a gift of honor to the barbarians beyond his country, who are called Turks and Avars, so that he might win their favor and please them, and thus enlist their services.

When everything had been done as he commanded and they had been magnificently adorned, he assigned an armed force to accompany them, together with two marzbans. He ordered luxurious [?] for them, fine and luxurious [?], and sent them away. He commanded that they should not be hurried along the road, but should travel at ease and be given rest, so that, as he said, they would not waste away and become ugly.

These young women were tormented not only by their separation from their fathers, their brothers, and all their relatives, but also over their souls, which were being lost to Christianity, and over their bodies, which were being delivered into the hands of the bestial savagery of their barbarian enemies. With weeping and lamentations, and bitter lamentations again, they spoke together in their own language, now treating one another as sisters. All of them together asked for death rather than life.

They made all these things known and disclosed them secretly to other Syrian captives, men from their own country who were with the marzbans and the others appointed to escort and attend them, confiding in them as fellow countrymen. Thus, in the end, these things became known to everyone, and were learned from those who shared their country and language.

When they came within five stages of those barbarian peoples to whom they were being sent, and learned that they were approaching the places to which they were being sent, they happened to come upon a large river with an exceedingly strong current. It was, they said, very difficult to cross. Since those who were conducting them had been commanded to give them rest and not hurry them, they camped beside that river for one day.

Then all the women took counsel together. Among them all arose this one strong and courageous resolve: to make light of death. They all hurried to one another, consulted among themselves, and said to one another:

“Let us all consider this together: after we have all defiled ourselves with paganism and with the unclean foods of animals, of creatures that have died and creatures that have been strangled, among the barbarians, and have lost our Christianity, in the end we shall all be handed over to death. And afterward we shall come to judgment and torment. Now we are all sisters, Christian women and daughters of Christians. Let us not be divided against one another. Instead, from now on let us all have one will, one soul, one purpose, and one mind—all of us. Before our bodies are defiled by the barbarians and our souls polluted, and death finally overtakes us, let us now, while our bodies are pure and our souls preserved from pollution and uncleanness, offer him our souls and bodies in purity, for the sake of the name and in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us surrender ourselves to death now, so that we may be delivered from our enemies and live a life that lasts forever and ever, in exchange for the brief suffering of our souls for our Christianity and for preserving the purity of our souls and bodies.”

Thus they all bound themselves together with one agreement, one secret, and one promise, and swore oaths to one another. All together, as one, they threw themselves into that river. All together, as one, they drowned and did not fall into the hands of the barbarians. This resolve pleased them all equally, and they chose it.

While those guarding them were watching them closely, they secretly worked out their plan and waited for the right moment. Their guards remained constantly beside them. The women said to them, “If you give us permission, we would like to bathe along the banks of this river.” Since the guards wanted to give them comfort, as they had been commanded, they allowed them to bathe. But the women said to them, “We are ashamed to bathe while you stand beside us and look at us. Move a little way away from us, and then we shall bathe.”

So they left them and moved away. The women all strengthened and encouraged one another, and all signed themselves in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Then all together they flung themselves with a sudden rush into that river and drowned.

When their guards looked into the river, they saw some of them floating and being carried down the river like driftwood, while others were sinking. They ran to the place where the women had asked to bathe and saw that not a single one of them was alive. They all wailed bitterly, running this way and that to rescue one of them, but they could not. Nor could they find a way to escape.

But these weak women, who had become strong in Christ, thus surrendered their souls into the hands of God for the sake of their Christianity. In spirit and body they were delivered from the uncleanness and bestial savagery of the barbarians.

After [?], after all these events, it was agreed that there should be peace in the territory of Syria for three years. In return, three hundredweights were also given for these three years. In Armenia, however, there was to be war between the two sides. As for the beginning of the affair—the submission of the Armenians under Persian rule to the Romans—we have already given brief accounts in the preceding portions of the Ecclesiastical History. Now let us turn—let us turn our account—to what happened afterward.

The Persian king was carried away by pride because he had captured Dara, and the arrogance of his heart led him astray. Now confident that he faced no war in the territories of Syria, he gathered his army and confidently went out, setting out for Armenia. He had set his sights on Theodosiopolis, on the frontier of his Armenian territory, on Caesarea in Cappadocia, and on the other cities. He was so confident that, when Theodore the silentiary had been sent to him as an envoy and he decided to go out to war, he took Theodore with him. When Theodore pleaded with him to release him, he mocked him and said, “Come with me to Armenia. You can enter Theodosiopolis—Theodosiopolis—with me, bathe, and rest there, and then I will release you.” So he took him and brought him along to Armenia, fully confident that he would enter and capture the city without difficulty.

When the Roman armies learned of this, although they were deeply alarmed at the king’s name, they made thorough preparations to confront him. When he saw their powerful forces, he was greatly dismayed, for they were said to number more than a hundred and twenty thousand. When they challenged him and prepared to fight him, he became frightened and turned away from them to attack another city. But there too they hurried to confront him, met him, and drove him away from there as well. Now that they had tested his strength, they grew still bolder against him and treated him with contempt. After this, when he saw that things had not turned out as he wished, he headed for the northern mountains and turned toward Cappadocia, intending to enter and capture Caesarea.

When the Roman armies saw this, they moved to intercept him and reached Cappadocia ahead of him as well. They stood against him and challenged him there in the mountains of Cappadocia. They checked him and would not let him pass. They skirmished with one another for many days, while he did not dare to draw up his forces against them in an open battle. When he saw that they were more numerous and stronger than he was, and that he could not get past them and march on Caesarea, he became greatly dismayed and distressed. He now began devising a way to get through and escape to his own country, if he could. His Magi reproached him and argued with him.

He then turned and went out into Cappadocia toward Sebaste, while all his men trembled before the Roman armies. Out of shame, so that he would not be reproached for failing to accomplish any of his plans, he attacked Sebaste and burned it down. He found neither plunder nor captives, because the whole region had been evacuated before his arrival. When he passed on from there, he turned back and now headed eastward, hoping to escape to his own country if he could.

The Roman armies now followed him with contempt, having tested his strength; they despised him and grew bold against him. When he saw that they had surrounded him and were pressing him on every side, he was compelled to flee hurriedly into the mountains. He abandoned his entire camp and his pavilion—that is, his tent—with all his equipment and his treasures of gold, silver, and pearls, and all his magnificent royal garments, and fled empty-handed.

The Romans hurried in and took possession of his entire camp. They killed everyone they caught there and carried off all his equipment and that of his nobles, including the shrine of the fire he worshiped and the horses that carried it and bore it in procession. Men grew rich from the spoils there. Indeed, some Romans who found and took royal possessions formed a band, took what they had found, and fled. They were never found or seen again.

Those who fled and escaped from the Persian camp went to the king, weeping and saying, “My lord, the Romans fell upon us and killed many of your servants. They plundered and carried off our entire camp.” When he heard this, he reportedly answered them, “Leave them alone.” He ordered his entire army to surround him and form a wall of shields around him, and he drew them up in ranks. He rode among them, pleading with them and showing them his gray hair, saying, “My brothers and my sons, have pity on my gray hair! Go in and fight for the Persian kingdom, so that it will not be mocked and ridiculed. Look, I myself will fight beside you like one of your cavalrymen.”

His nobles, it is said, were continually arguing with him, saying, “Whether we live or die, Persia will gain a bad name through us. No Persian king has ever done what you have done: you have brought us here to die in these mountains.” The Romans were learning from some of them what was being said among them.

The Persians again resorted to a stratagem and headed in another direction to flee [?] to a city. They came out toward Melitene. Had it not been for the jealousy and divisions among the Roman commanders—had they agreed with one another—they would have destroyed him and his entire army there. They had agreed with one another, divided their forces, and surrounded him. The Persians then turned against Justinian the patrician, the son of Germanus. Justinian became frightened and fled before him, and his fellow commanders did not reach him and come to his aid. When the king saw this, he and his army recovered their spirits, took courage, entered Melitene, and set it on fire.

When the Persian entered the city of Melitene, he immediately gave orders, and the whole city was burned with fire. When he left to cross the Euphrates, heading toward his own country, the commanders of the Roman armies sent him this message:

“What you have done—entering and burning the city—is not how a king should behave, carrying out raids and roaming about. Even for us, who are the king’s servants, doing what you have done would be deeply disgraceful. How much more so for you, who consider yourself not only a king but even the king of kings! It is not fitting for a king to act like men who go out raiding, plundering and fleeing, setting fires and burning things. Rather, a king should stand openly in battle, with authority and confidence, as a king should. When he wins, he should triumph like a king, not enter like a thief, do damage, steal, and run away. So prepare yourself, and let us now face one another openly in battle, so that it may be clearly known to whom victory and defeat belong.”

When he heard this, he ordered a battle for the following day on the plain east of the city, some distance from it. Early that morning, both sides drew up opposite one another, with only a short distance between them. They stood in formation, looking at one another, from morning until the sixth hour. Not a man moved from his place. The king himself stood behind his army, and they watched one another to see who would begin first.

The men who told us all these things, who had been interpreters for the Persians and the Romans, swore to us: “Finally, three of us spurred our horses and rode out from the Roman ranks into the space between the two sides. We galloped as far as the front of the Persian ranks and then galloped back, without coming close to them. We did this three times, galloping our horses at full speed, while both sides turned and watched us. We had ridden out to provoke them to battle. Even so, not one of them moved from his place and came out against us. They stood drawn up like a wall. Nor did they even send a message to one another. But finally he sent word: ‘There will be no battle today now, for the proper time has passed.’”

So the armies withdrew from one another. During the night, before dawn broke, the king and his army were found at the river Euphrates, trying hard to devise a way to cross it. It is six miles from Melitene. The Romans were pursuing him, intending to trap him against the river and destroy him. This they did, and the Persians were thrown into confusion. When the Persian army saw that the Roman army had come up behind them, they plunged into the river on their horses. More than half his army sank and drowned. He and the rest barely escaped across, some on horseback and some swimming.

They hurried through Roman Armenia. As they pressed on at speed, he ordered them to burn every village they encountered. Then he turned aside into the high, bare mountains, where there had never been a road. He was forced to send his army ahead of him to make a road for him. They cut down woodland, and in some places they dug and cut through the mountains themselves to make him a road. Thus, bewildered and deeply troubled, he barely escaped from the Romans and entered his own country with great difficulty. And so, they say, he issued a command and established a law that a king should never again go out to battle unless he was going out against a king.

Now the commanders of the Roman armies had distinguished themselves by great victories, won many battles, and destroyed most of those against whom they were sent. They had conquered and subjected all those northern peoples who had been subject to the Persians. They had invaded and devastated Persian territory for many days’ journey, coming within three stages of the Persian king’s royal city. They had plundered and carried off the Persians’ elephants and filled Constantinople with elephants. They had distinguished themselves by many deeds beyond recounting, and all Persia trembled before them.

Finally, when the Persian king returned to his own country in the year 880 of Alexander, the Romans became carefree and puffed up with pride, like men who had successfully stood against a king. From then on they conducted themselves without fear, thinking that they were now free and at rest from all wars and fighting. All the armies were encamped confidently and at ease, with their armor off and all their horses turned loose to graze.

Suddenly their scouting party—that is, their spies—arrived and said, “Get up! Arm yourselves! The Persian army is coming against you with Tamkhosrau the marzban. Look to yourselves!”

When they heard this, they scoffed at them and treated them with contempt, saying, “Can these men really dare to show themselves before us?” They were not alarmed and took no care to prepare themselves. While they were still speaking, the Persian army suddenly appeared before them, not prepared to fight them, but merely to show themselves.

When the Romans saw them advancing, drawn up in great ranks like walls, trembling and fear fell upon them all at once, and they became confused. Their horses had not even been gathered in, and they themselves were weighed down with food, drink, and indulgence, and were scattered about. Everyone who saw the Persians was shaken, and they began to flee in haste. Others, seeing people fleeing, became alarmed and fled themselves. When the army commanders saw that they had been left with no one and that the army had fled from them, they too fled.

Everyone who could take his weapons and catch his horse mounted and fled. Some fled on foot carrying their weapons, but when they became exhausted from running, they threw their weapons onto the road and fled unarmed. Some who were riding horses with their weapons threw their weapons away when they became weary. If the horse then grew weak, they dismounted and fled on foot.

So the Persians went after them without haste, not pursuing them, but laughing, mocking, and jeering at them. The Romans numbered 120,000, whereas the Persians were no more than 30,000. Yet the Romans were so terrified that they fled from them, although they had neither feared nor fled from the Persian king. In this way all the Roman armies, together with their commanders, finally earned shame and a bad name, although the Persians had not even drawn a sword against them, nor bent a bow and shot a single arrow at them. They gathered up all their weapons and [?], coats of mail, shields, helmets, lances, swords, spears, bows, and quivers filled with countless arrows.

Afterward everyone was saying and repeating that this happened because the Romans had angered God. When they entered those northern regions, whose inhabitants were Christians, the priests would take the Gospel book and crosses and go out to meet them, but the Romans paid them no regard. In the end, behaving outrageously without any fear of God, the Romans would take children one or two years old. Some would seize each child by the foot and fling it upward as high as they could, while others caught the children on spears and swords as they came down, impaled them, and threw them to the dogs.

They also insulted monks, killed them, and plundered them. They brought out recluses, old and venerable men, from the cells where they had lived shut away for many years, suspended them, tortured them, and cut their thighs with swords, saying to them, “Bring us gold and silver!”

They also reportedly tortured nuns in this way until they died in bitter suffering. Through these evil deeds, which they were said to have committed, they angered God, and he put them to shame and broke them before their enemies, so that they could not stand against them.

Concerning the reason why the Armenians under Persian rule came and submitted to the Romans, the period involved, the many battles and the devastation that occurred there, and those who went up to the imperial city and were received by the emperor and honored with high offices and many gifts, and the other events of this kind, we have made brief references in our earlier accounts.

What we now wish to make known in our account is this: our Roman emperor had all these conflicts with the Persians so as not to hand over those who had come and sought refuge with him because of their Christianity. After the emperor had enriched virtually all the Armenians with gifts and generous grants, and had also granted them exemption from taxation for three years, the Persian king kept sending him the demand, “Give me my subjects who have rebelled against me,” but he would not comply. Then the Persian king devised a plan and gave the Armenians his written promise that he would do them no harm and would not hold their offense against them. They then turned away from the Romans and went and handed over the whole country to him, apart from those leaders who were with the emperor in Constantinople. That is, the whole country, some twenty thousand people, turned back, went away, and submitted to the Persians. He once again took possession of Armenia, as before.

As for their leaders—one named Vardan, and the others [?] who were with him—together with the king of the people, named Gurgen, and all his people who had submitted to the Romans, he too remained in the imperial city in great honor, because they had come and submitted to Emperor Justin in the fifth year of his reign, which was the year eight hundred and eighty-two of Alexander. The war on their account, meanwhile, continued for a period of years.

Again, in the year 887, three senators were sent on an embassy to the frontier: Theodore the patrician, the son of Peter the master of offices, and John and Peter, consuls from the family of Emperor Anastasius, together with Zachariah the Syrian, a physician and sophist. And a sophist [?]. From the Persians there also came Mabodes and the others. They took their seats beside Dara, which the Persians were holding, to discuss and examine together what had happened in the two states. Each side turned against the other, saying, “You violated your obligations in such-and-such an affair.” The others, in turn, brought further accusations, saying, “You broke the peace between the two states, crossed the border, and devastated our territories.” The others would say, “Your Arabs crossed over and committed outrages in our territory.”

In this way they sat facing one another, raising accusations, disputes, and inquiries of this kind against one another, until they came to quarrels and insults. They spent a year and more speaking and listening, while each side kept its own king informed. The God-loving Caesar Tiberius gave and received replies, since Emperor Justin was ill. Although both sides wanted peace between them, each showed a stern face to the other, so as not to yield to the other and appear weak.

For the Caesar of the Romans sent word to the Persians: “We rejoice in peace more than in war [?]. If you want peace, we do not shrink from it [?]. But if you want war, we are not inferior to you; we are ready to face you.”

The Persian, however, considered that, since he had been given three hundred-pound weights of gold to make peace for three years, he would likewise receive one hundred-pound weight for every year if he made peace with the Romans. When Caesar learned this, he wrote and sent to him: “You are badly mistaken if you think that the Roman Empire will give you a single mina in exchange for peace, or if you imagine that we buy peace with gold. But if you wish the two empires to deal with one another with equal honor, let there be peace between us. Otherwise, accept war.”

When the Persian received such a decisive answer, he was deeply shaken by its words. He agreed that there should be peace on equal terms, without gold.

Then, when Caesar received this reply, he wrote back: “You should know that the Roman Empire has never been weak. Rather, it is powerful, and it has never been subject to anyone. I do not know how the former emperors stooped to giving the Persians five hundred-pound weights of gold every year. But you should know that the Roman Empire will never again give five minas either to you or to anyone else. For your envoys used to boast to the barbarian nation of the Turks, saying, ‘The Romans are slaves, and like contemptible slaves they pay us tribute.’ Unless you put an end to this, we will have no peace with you.”

When many matters had been settled, he immediately not only issued straightforward instructions but also settled the final terms. He prepared copies of the peace documents and sent them to the envoys at the frontier. Then, when Caesar saw that the Persian had committed himself to these terms, he sent him word: “Give us the city of Dara now, and we will make peace.”

When the Persian received this, he was greatly disturbed by it. He wrote: “I took Dara according to the law of war. But you did not take by war the territories of our subjects, the Armenians, which you are holding. Give me Armenia, and I will give you Dara.”

Caesar, however, was reluctant to hand over the Armenians, because they were Christians and had submitted to the Christian empire for that very reason. Over this matter the envoys of the two sides fell into a great quarrel with one another, until they armed themselves to confront one another with swords. So they parted from one another, embittered against each other, and the prospect of peace was completely cut off. From then on, both empires prepared for battle. The Persian envoy summoned his commanders and instructed them, saying, “Go and be on your guard along the frontiers, for the Romans will not make peace.”

So Adarmahan, the great marzban of the Persians, who had discussed peace with the Roman envoys, gathered an army as soon as they decided that there would be no more peace. Embittered and enraged at having been insulted by the envoys, he marched out and devastated and completely burned the whole territory of Dara, Tella, Telbashmaya, and Reshaina—the fortified villages, churches, monasteries, and the entire countryside. He devastated, burned, and killed, and then came against Tella. He said to them, “Surrender the city to us, so that what happened to the people of Dara does not happen to you too, and you perish. Where are your envoys who were threatening us? Let them come out now and face us!”
