But the people of Tella said to them, “We cannot surrender to you now, because we have received letters saying that the patrician Justinian has set out to come here, and that he has sixty thousand Lombards with him. If we surrender to you now, he will come and immediately wipe us from the face of the earth.”

So they withdrew from them, after burning the great, imposing church of the Mother of God outside the city and committing other outrages besides. They returned to Dara, while he mocked the Romans and boasted of the devastation he had caused, the captives they had taken, and the great quantity of plunder they had carried away.

Now the commanders of the Roman army were not getting along with one another, and they were writing to the emperor about one another and against one another. So the God-loving emperor, having noticed one of his own men named Maurice, whom he had appointed to the position of count of the Excubitors, and who was therefore called count, summoned him and ordered him to go down to the East as chief over all the army commanders. He gave him authority to administer, organize, and command all the generals [?] and tribunes of the entire army. None of them was to dare disobey his orders or the word of his mouth in any way. He also gave him authority to appoint to military service and discharge from service whomever he wished, and sent him with many hundredweights of gold to support the armies. Even before this, he had sent a praetorian prefect named Gregory to administer and attend to the armies’ expenses. He had carried out everything successfully there in Armenia.

When the distinguished Maurice received his orders and was sent out, he first went to his own country, Cappadocia, for he was a Cappadocian. He immediately assembled and enlisted many Romans. He also took with him many Excubitors and Scribones, together with whatever troops were available. He further assembled and enlisted a large body of men from the [?] and the Syrians. He went and encamped between Armenia and Syria, at Citharizon. He sent for all the army commanders, gathered them together, and spoke with them. He organized them, gave them orders, encouraged them, and strengthened their resolve.

He remained there for two months, and his reputation spread. Fear of him fell upon all the Persians, who saw that the Roman armies were more numerous and stronger than their own. While they were there, fear fell upon them, and they devised a trick. They moved toward Persia, into Armenia, and sent word to those stationed in Theodosiopolis: ‘After thirty days, be ready to meet us in battle.’ When the Romans received this message, they sent word to Count Maurice, and he too ordered the entire army to prepare for battle.

But as soon as the Persians had sent this message, they made cunning arrangements to deceive the Romans. They prepared themselves, gathered their army, and marched through their own country. They emerged secretly into Roman territory from the direction of Martyropolis and began devastating and burning the whole region of Sophene, especially all the churches and monasteries, as well as the whole district of Amida and the entire country. They came against Amida and burned all its surroundings, right up to its wall—all the churches and great monasteries around it. They remained before the city for three days. When they saw that they could not overcome its strength, and also feared that Maurice might overtake them with his army and cut them down, they burned and plundered the whole country of Mesopotamia in a swift raid, then turned back and entered their own country.

Thus, while the Romans were preparing for a pitched battle, the Persians deceived them. In the end they came out like thieves and raiders, burned and devastated all Mesopotamia, and carried its people away captive, in the year 888 of Alexander. This was the same year in which Maurice had come down from the imperial city. In their frantic haste, they took captives and everything they could find and fled to their own country out of fear of the Romans. They carried out all this destruction and returned within about eighteen days.

When Count Maurice heard these things, he was deeply disturbed and embittered. He assembled his entire army and headed for Arzan, a fertile region belonging to the Persians, in a furious rage because the Persians had mocked and ridiculed him. They invaded, devastated and destroyed, and took a great many of its people captive. They advanced in conquest as far as the Tigris, and he went down, taking captives, destroying, and burning the whole region. Because the inhabitants were sincere Christians without deceit, they would come out to meet the troops and their commanders with worship, crosses, and the Gospel, asking them for a pledge that their lives would be spared. They said, “Have mercy on us, for we are Christians like you. Like you we are, and indeed we are ready to serve the Christian emperor.” When Maurice and the others heard these things from many of them, they showed mercy, telling them, “Anyone among you who wishes to live and serve the Christian emperor should take his possessions and load everything he has onto his pack animals. He will live, and we will not kill him. But if we find him here after two or three days, he will die.” So most of them—all who escaped the sword—fled and went into Roman territory: the greater part of the population of the region of Arzan. When the emperor learned of these things, he gave orders, and they were sent to the island of Cyprus. They were distributed among the villages throughout the island and remained there. As for those Persians who had slipped across into Roman territory and set fires, they were afraid that Maurice would overtake them in his furious advance. They hurried and burned as much as they could in fifteen days. Then, in fear, they fled and crossed back into their own country before Maurice could overtake them.

Again, Maurice and al-Mundhir son of al-Harith, king of the Arabs, assembled their armies together and crossed into Persian territory by the desert route. They entered and penetrated many stages into Persian territory, as far as Beth Aramaye. When they reached the great bridge in Beth Aramaye, which they had been counting on crossing to capture the great cities of the Persian kingdom, they found the bridge destroyed. The Persians had destroyed it when they learned of their approach. Thus they and their armies, especially the Romans, experienced great hardship. They fell into a quarrel with one another and turned back, having been unable to accomplish anything worthwhile. Only with difficulty, amid hardship, did they manage to escape and return to Roman territory. They wrote bitter accusations against one another. Maurice suspected al-Mundhir of having sent word ahead to inform the Persians, so that they had destroyed the bridge to prevent them from crossing. This was false. The emperor had a great deal of trouble, sending messages to the leaders, and only with difficulty were they reconciled to one another. In the end, Maurice himself went up to the emperor, and it was not known whether he brought an accusation against al-Mundhir.

When the Persians saw that Maurice and Mundhir had gone down into their country, and saw that the country had been emptied of troops, the Persian marzban, whose name was Adarmahan, crossed into Roman territory with a large army. He came to the districts of Tella and Reshaina and demolished and burned what they had left on the earlier occasion. They crossed into the fertile territory of Edessa and burned, demolished, and devastated the whole region of Osrhoene—of Osrhoene [?]. He moved about the country confidently and without fear, as though he were living in his own country, for many days. Wherever he passed, he left no house standing. He mocked the entire Roman army, which had been unable to attack him.

Eventually, when Maurice and Mundhir had come back up from Persian territory in humiliation, and he heard that they intended to march against him, he sent them this mocking message: “Since I have heard that you are preparing to come against me, do not tire yourselves by coming, for you are exhausted by the hardships of the journey. Instead, rest, and I will come to you.”

Finally, after the devastation, plundering, and capture of prisoners that he had carried out, and after taking captives and doing everything he wanted, he heard that they intended to march against him. He took all the plunder and all the prisoners he had captured, fled, and withdrew from the territory of Edessa to his own country. Not one of the two hundred thousand Romans who were living at the emperor’s expense attacked him. Only when he had set off to leave did they march out against him. When they failed to catch up with him, they said, “He has certainly fled!”

Meanwhile, the entire army of the Persian Arabs assembled against Mundhir son of Harith. The Persian king’s own army also made preparations alongside them to go up and attack Mundhir after he had returned from Persian territory. When he learned of this, he did not hesitate, being a warrior. Instead, he immediately gathered his army and headed against them by a desert road. He sent scouts and learned where they were and how many they were. Then he suddenly fell upon them while they were unaware. He threw them into panic and confusion, devastated them, and destroyed them. He captured some of them, bound them, and put them in fetters. Only a few of them escaped. From there he headed straight for their Hira, devastated it, and burned it. Then he departed and returned with great quantities of plunder and many captives, having won a magnificent victory.

After Dara, Apamea, and the other places had been taken captive, the Persians carried all their captives away to Persia. When they were counted before the king at Nisibis, their number came to two hundred and seventy-five thousand. Those remaining who had not been distributed he brought into Antioch and confined there. This was the city that had been built for him after he conquered Antioch and took its people captive: he built a city in his own country bearing its name. There he confined all the captives he had taken from Antioch and its entire district. There he also confined those from Dara and Apamea, together with all the other captives he took afterward.

Even in their confinement, under the strong guard kept over them, they did not stop devising schemes. Hoping, as they thought, to help themselves, they devised a plan [?]. They made a secret agreement with one of the Persians who guarded them and kept watch over the wall. They collected money and gave him five hundred coins to lower two of them by a rope at night from the place where he kept watch. Among those there were some blessed men, Arab monks. One was named Benjamin, and the other, his disciple, was named Samuel. They made preparations so that, if they got out and escaped from there, Benjamin would immediately make his way to the emperor of the Romans and inform him about the captives—the many thousands confined in Antioch.

All the captives also sent this message through him: “There are more than thirty thousand of us confined here, while the Persians guarding us number no more than five hundred men. If one of the Roman commanders is sent and merely appears outside the city, we will kill the Persians, come out, and escape to Roman territory.”

After all the captives had secretly spoken these words to that blessed man, the Persian who had accepted the bribe lowered him and those with him from the wall by ropes at night. They fled and escaped to Roman territory. First he informed the Roman commanders of these things. They in turn wrote and sent him to the emperor. When he reached the imperial city, he came to us. He informed the master of offices of these things, and the latter went in and informed Emperor Tiberius. But he paid no attention and apparently did not consider them true. Thus the matter was neglected, and the deliverance of that whole oppressed body of captives came to nothing.

It is therefore not inappropriate, even though we are writing about a Magian and an enemy, to give an account also of the lifetime and death of Khosrow, king of the Persians. As his own deeds testify, he was shrewd and wise. Throughout his life he was constantly occupied with reading philosophy. It is said that he took care to collect all the books of all the religions, reading and examining them all to learn which were true and wise and which were contemptible and full of falsehood and empty tales. As he read and examined them all, it is said, he praised the writings of the Christians above all the others, saying, “These are truer and wiser than those of all the religions.” For this reason, it is said, he devoted himself particularly to them, reading them and believing their words. For this reason, too, he did not appear to hate the Christians. Even when the Magi stirred him up against the Christians, he was not often seen to order their persecution.

At one time, the catholicos of the Nestorians, who was constantly in his company, brought accusations against the few orthodox bishops in Persia. For all the bishops throughout Persia were Nestorians, and only a few orthodox bishops were to be found among them. When the catholicos brought severe accusations against these men, the king ordered them to come and debate with one another before him about their faith. He wanted to learn for himself and personally examine what was being said by them and between them, judge their statements, and discover which of them spoke reasonably.

When these orthodox bishops arrived, he ordered everyone belonging to both sides to assemble and come before him. They entered his presence, and the two sides stood before him on either side. The leader of the orthodox was a bishop, a holy man named Ahudemmeh. The king ordered them to debate and tell one another what they had to say about their faith. When the catholicos and those with him began to speak to the orthodox, they gave him time to begin and finish. Then they themselves spoke, refuted all his statements, and confounded him, taking the king himself as judge. Since the things spoken in their debate were numerous and are not easy to put in writing, we have left them out.

Then King Khosrow himself accepted and praised what the orthodox had said. He said to the catholicos, “These men know what they are talking about and can establish and confirm their statements, which seem to me also to be entirely true. Yours, however, are confused and muddled and have no foundation. You yourselves do not appear able to establish your statements, nor do they seem to me to have the solidity and truth of what these men have said. From this I have learned that you accused them before me unjustly and without justification. Now that I have seen and heard, I order you not to attack or harass them again.”

When he had given these orders, all the orthodox fell down and bowed before him. They thanked him for his favor, saying, “My lord, they persecute us, attack us, and plunder us. They demolish our churches and monasteries and do not allow us to offer prayers and supplications to God in them for the preservation and protection of your life and your kingdom.”

Then he gave them a firm order, saying, “Go and build your churches and monasteries. No one shall again have authority to harass you.” So, after bowing before him and praying for him, they returned to their own regions with great joy. From then on, all the orthodox in the Persian territories went about openly and without fear. Having received this command, they took courage and undertook a great deed: they too established a catholicos through the blessed Mar Jacob, bishop of the orthodox, from that time onward. This was something that had never before happened or been done in the land of the Persians. From that time until today, the office of catholicos of the faithful has continued and remained established.

Let no one suppose, then, that we have brought his story to mind because we wish to praise the Magian. Rather, it is because, as was said in Samson’s riddle, “From the eater came food, and from the bitter came sweetness.” He was indeed very bitter—and what more need be said about a pagan man who had gone astray? Nevertheless, because of the matters that serve the purpose of these histories, we have turned to recording his story.

We have reached the point where, when peace along the borders broke down, he showed that he was troubled and distressed. Thus, as was reported, when he came against Dara, the documents establishing peace between them went before him, tied up and suspended toward heaven. He said, “See, great God, you know that I did not desire, and do not desire, all this devastation and the shedding of human blood that has taken place in both states.”

Again, when his death was approaching, he showed that he had humbled himself and wanted peace. He expected that, for every year in which he maintained peace, he would receive a hundred pounds of gold, according to the practice of the three years that had passed. When the Roman and Persian envoys met at the border for negotiations and to discuss peace, as we have explained above, the victorious Tiberius—who was still Caesar during Justin’s lifetime, and whom all the Persians feared—showed his courage and took his stand, saying, “The Roman Empire is not inferior to the Persian kingdom, nor is it subject to it. We will not give even a hundred pounds of gold in exchange for peace. Unless there is peace with equal honor for the two empires, I will never make peace with them at all.”

This shook the Persian king considerably. He even assembled his Magi and said to them, “We have now learned that the Caesar who has arisen among the Romans is a young man, youthful and warlike. As for me, you can see that I have grown old, and I can no longer endure the toil of warfare. Let us now make peace with the Romans, for we cannot withstand their strength.”

So they took counsel and sent this message: “So that you may not suppose that I am greedy for gold and value gold more highly than peace, let us now make peace with equal honor for the two empires, and let the devastation cease. I ask for nothing.”

When he had promised this, the victorious Caesar Tiberius fired another shot at him, saying, “Do not suppose, either, that you will receive even one mina more of the gold that you have been receiving from the Romans until now. The Roman Empire has not sunk so low that it must pay tribute to the Persians.”

In reply to this, the Persian sent word: “The gold that is paid was agreed upon by earlier kings; it was not you who established it. But you should know that peace is dearer to me than anything else. I will give up these hundreds of pounds of gold as well, and let us make peace.”

When Caesar saw that the Persian had humbled himself and come to these terms, he sent him this message: “Unless you give us Dara, we will not make peace with you.”

At this the Persians became agitated, and the peace was broken off. They left the border in dispute, intending to fight one another, and devastation immediately began in both states. At that very time King Khosrau died, in the year eight hundred and ninety, and his son became king. According to their reckoning, Khosrau himself had reigned for forty-eight years.

When King Khosrow died, one of his sons, named Hormizd, became king after him. As the accounts of his exploits relate, and as his deeds themselves show, he was indeed a wild, brutish, and featherbrained young man. When he became king, he grew so haughty and conceited, like an arrogant man without sense, that he would not even send a token of his accession to the Roman emperor, as was customary among kings. Yet Caesar Tiberius had not discontinued the customary token of accession, even though the kingdoms were engaged in conflict, strife, and war. Instead, as soon as he took his seat as Caesar, he sent Khosrow gifts as a token of his accession, just as Khosrow, when he became king, had sent them to Emperor Justinian, who had preceded him and had already been ruling for about three years. But this man, in his senselessness, arrogantly said, “Why, why should I send honors to my slaves?” And so he sent nothing.

Not only that, but when the Roman envoys who had been sent to his father with gifts and royal letters reached Antioch, they learned that Khosrow had died and his son had become king. When our peace-loving Roman emperors learned this, they instructed the envoys to write to the new king and proceed to him. He arrogantly ordered them to come, but received them with insults. He kept them in distress for a long time, imprisoned and oppressed, until they were close to perishing and losing their lives. Then his Magi advised him, and he released them, though he would not even allow them to travel by the direct route. He sent men with them and ordered them to take them up into rugged, difficult mountains so that they would perish and die there. They even said to those who were conducting them, “If you want to kill us, why did you not kill us openly at once, rather than bring us here to die in this misery in these mountains?” But God helped them, and they escaped. These things were related to the emperor and to everyone as evidence of that man's cruelty and senselessness.

Now the first cause of its dissolution and of the dissolution of the peace was the defection of the Persian Armenians to the Romans. The second cause, in turn, was the bitter hostility occasioned by the Roman emperor’s sending envoys to those barbarian peoples beyond the Persian territories, who are called Turks, together with many other causes that brought the Persians into distress and hostility.

For Emperor Justin had sent envoys to those called Turks in the seventh year of his reign, appointing one of his officials, named Zemarchus. Never before had a Roman embassy been sent to these great and powerful peoples. After traveling for an entire year, the envoy reached their territories, as he related. One of the kings of these peoples—there were, he said, eight other great kings farther inland than he—learned that a Roman embassy had been sent to them. Immediately he was astonished and shaken, and suddenly gave way to deep mourning and bitter weeping. This became still more intense when he received the envoys and saw them standing before him for a long time, while no one dared to speak to him.

As others related, he was weeping so bitterly that none of his nobles dared to speak to him. “We fell on our faces before him,” they said, “and told the interpreters to say to him, ‘We ask you, O king: is it because you have seen us, sent to you by your brother, the Roman emperor, that you are weeping like this?’ When he heard this, he wept still more bitterly for a long time, without speaking a single word to us for two hours. Then he quieted his sobbing a little and said to us, ‘So that you may know the reason for my present mourning and weeping, I will tell you. From past generations and from our ancestors we have received this tradition: “Whenever you see envoys from the land of the Romans in these territories, know and be certain that the whole world is passing away and coming to an end, and that all kingdoms will cease. At that very time all people will destroy one another with the sword.” Now, when I saw you, I remembered these things. That is why I mourned and wept.’

“After we had spoken at length before him, we brought out many gifts, [?] of gold and silver, pearls, and splendid royal garments, and presented them to him. When he saw them, he was amazed. He accepted them and immediately set apart those that were especially fine and splendid, saying, ‘These belong to a great king.’

“Now Persian envoys happened to be there. He questioned the Roman envoys, asking, ‘Is what the Persians told me true—that the Roman emperor is our slave and pays us tribute like a slave?’ When Zemarchus heard this, he answered him, ‘They are lying in saying this. Many Roman emperors have invaded their country, devastated it, and carried its people off into captivity. When Trajan, the Roman emperor, invaded, he conquered and subjugated them so completely that to this day they tremble and shake before the statue he erected of himself in their country. To this day not one of them dares to pass before it on horseback. Let them be summoned, and we will confront them in person, and they will not be able to deny it.’

“Then he ordered them to be brought, and they came. He said to them, ‘Did you not tell me that the Roman emperor is our slave? Yet, according to what these men say, to this day you are subject even to the statue that the Roman emperor erected of himself in your country, and you tremble before it. How can these men be your slaves, when you yourselves tremble before the statue of the Roman emperor and are subject to it? Is this true?’ They said to him, ‘Yes, my lord, it is true that there is a statue of him in our country.’ But he said to them, ‘Then why did you lie and deceive me? I swear that, if it were not that I would be becoming like you, I would take off your heads at once.’ And so he dismissed them in anger.”

When they returned to their king, they informed him that they had found Roman envoys there, and that these had confronted them about Trajan’s statue. “When we could not deny it,” they said, “he became angry with us and dismissed us in a rage.” When the Persian king heard these things, he was shaken and embittered. Because of this incident, he gave orders, and Trajan’s statue was pulled down. His hostility grew still fiercer, for he supposed that the Romans were stirring up these peoples against them. He himself bestowed greater honors on them than the Romans did. He dealt with the Romans and these peoples in this way, as the envoys related; we have recorded only a few of these things.

The Roman envoys returned after two years, relating great and astonishing things about the vast numbers of these peoples, the wonders of those territories, their organization, and the orderly character of their way of life.

Now this people, whose hair [?], who are called Avars, came and appeared in Roman territory in the days of Emperor Justinian. When he received their envoys, he enriched them with gold, silver, clothing, belts, and golden saddles, besides the other things he gave them and sent through them to their chiefs, so that they would be amazed and send others again. To these too he gave gifts and enriched them. Thus they frequently sent envoys on various pretexts. Not only that, but they would form parties and come, and he would give to them all, load them with gifts, and let them go. He supposed that through them he would subdue all his enemies. Eventually, however, grumbling against him grew strong throughout the senate and the whole city. They said, “Look! He is emptying the empire and giving it to the barbarians.”

When he departed this world and Justin, his sister’s son, became emperor, one party of those who used to come was there, expecting to be loaded with gifts and leave as usual. After a few days they went in to Justin and said to him, “Give us what the man who died used to give us, and let us go to our king.”

But Emperor Justin, who had himself been one of those distressed and grumbling over how much they were taking and carrying away from the empire, said to them, “You will no longer load yourselves with the empire’s possessions and go away without giving anything in return. You will take nothing from me when you leave.”

When they began threatening them, he became angry and said, “You dead dogs! Are you threatening the Roman Empire? Know that I will shave the hair off every one of you, and then take off your heads!” He gave orders, and they were seized, put in boats, and taken out of the city. They were carried across and imprisoned at Chalcedon. There were about three hundred men. Troops were stationed there, together with scribones, scribones, and scholarii, to guard them for six months. Finally he released them and sent them away, threatening them with these words: “If I see any of you here, or anywhere in my dominions, you will not remain alive.” They were so terrified of him that they kept quiet and did not appear before him again. Eventually, however, they sent him envoys offering friendship and submission, and promising to do whatever he commanded them. Thus they remained friends throughout his reign.

They were a powerful people, and they grew still richer and stronger through the many northern peoples they conquered and devastated. Finally, beyond the great river called the Danube, they fell upon another powerful people, the Gepids—Gepids—and destroyed them, took possession of their land, and settled and spread out in that good land.

Later, pretending friendship, they deceitfully sent envoys to Emperor Justin with a request from their king: he was to send him engineers and builders to build him a palace and a bathhouse. He duly sent them. They went and built him a palace and a bathhouse, and when they had finished, they asked to be dismissed and allowed to return. Then he revealed his treachery and showed the deceit in his heart. He seized them and drew his sword against them, saying, “Unless you use your skill to build a bridge across the Danube for us to cross wherever we wish, not one of you will live. I will take off your heads at once.”

Under this pressure they said to him, “Who can, or has ever been able to, build a bridge across a river that is like a sea? Besides, even if we could do this, it would be an act against the Roman state, and the emperor himself would kill us. Whether we die or live, we cannot do this.”

At once he took off the heads of two of them. The rest, terrified of death, promised, “If you bring us many large, strong timbers, we will do it, so that we do not die.” Then a great crowd went out and cut down many large, strong trees. Thus, under the threat of death by the sword, they devised a plan and built an extremely strong bridge.

After Emperor Justin had reigned for thirteen years, he departed this world. The victorious Tiberius, who had held the rank of Caesar alongside him for four years, succeeded him as emperor. This affair, which took place in the third year of his reign after Justin’s death, caused no little distress to him—to him and to the whole state. He tried every means of cutting the bridge, but so far he has been unable to do so. They continue to hold it and remain there, demanding that he either give them the city of Sirmium, on this side of the river, for them to settle in, or else they will wage war against him and devastate his dominions. But he has not been at all disposed to give it to them. And now they are assembled and watching for an opportunity to rise up for war. They have also built another bridge, it is said—something that had never happened before. This too they have done in preparation for evil.

In the third year after the death of Emperor Justin and of the reign of the victorious Tiberius, the accursed people of the Slavs, of the Slavs, came out and overran all Greece, the territories of Thessalonica, of Thessalonica, and all Thrace. They captured cities and many fortresses, devastated and burned, took captives, and gained control of the land. They settled there freely, as though it were their own, without fear, for four years now. Since the emperor was still occupied with the Persian war and had sent all his armies eastward, these people spread over the land and settled in it. They have spread through it for the time being, as long as God allows them. They devastate, burn, and take captives. They have reached as far as the outer wall and have carried off all the emperor’s herds of horses, many thousands, along with other things. Even today, in the year eight hundred and ninety-five, they remain encamped and settled, living at ease in Roman territories, without anxiety or fear. They take captives, kill, and burn. They have become rich and acquired gold and silver, herds of horses, and many weapons. They have learned to fight better than the Romans—these uncivilized men who formerly did not dare to show themselves outside the forests and the shelter of the trees, and did not know what weapons were, apart from two or three small lances, that is, javelins.

After the great devastation that had taken place in both states, the Roman and the Persian, both sides wished to negotiate peace between the two kingdoms. Negotiations were being conducted through the bishops of Nisibis and Reshaina and others, and through, through Zachariah the sophist on the Roman side. Finally, a certain one-eyed Persian marzban intervened. Confident in his strength, puffed up and boasting of his prowess, he said to his king, “Do not give in to the Romans or make peace with them. I will cross over immediately and destroy them all. I will conquer all their territories and spend the winter in Antioch.” Trusting his boasting, the king neglected the peace negotiations, becoming puffed up himself.

So this marzban, whose name was Tamchosro, gathered troops and advanced against Tella of Mauzalat, where there were senior generals, generals, and commanders of the troops stationed there. They arrived and surrounded the city. Then the generals, generals, went out to meet him, particularly a brave and powerful man named Constantine. The day before, he had captured one of their spies and questioned him about the marzban Tamchosro: what he looked like, and where in the army he marched and could be found. When, when he had learned this and gone out to battle on one flank, he saw the marzban in the middle of the army. He hurled himself forward in a charge and plunged into the Persian army, heading straight toward Tamchosro. He struck him with his lance, dislodged him, and threw him from his horse. Then he turned his lance, his lance, and struck and stabbed him. The other Persians surrounded Constantine and killed him there too—a faithful Christian and a fighting man.

When the Persians saw that the man on whom they relied more than on the king had been killed—the man who had boasted that he would take the city immediately in a single assault and lodge in it—and that all the Roman troops had surrounded them on every side, they turned to flee. The Romans and Arabs pursued them, slaughtering and striking down many of them—many thousands, according to the reports. Since we do not know this with certainty, and wish to exclude falsehood [?], we have not recorded it as it was reported. Nevertheless, it became known that many of them had fallen. It was also reported that three other commanders of theirs had been killed. All their boasting was put to shame. They fled and went to encamp beside the river called Beth Washi. They remained there for three months, keeping watch and preparing for battle. When they proved unable to stand against the Romans, they returned to their own country in disgrace, since the things they had planned had not turned out as they intended. This is how these events unfolded.

As for this Maurice, although the narrative has already mentioned him above, he was the man whom the merciful King Tiberius promoted when he became king, because he had served with him as a notary. This happened when Justinian Constantine, the patrician, son of Germanus, who had been placed over all the commanders and armies in the East, departed this world, and the commanders of the armies would not cooperate with one another. Tiberius gave Maurice the position of count of the excubitors. Then he sent him out as commander over all the generals, generals, and commanders of the Roman armies throughout the East. He gave him authority over all the arrangements for war, to fight, to cease fighting, and to do whatever he wished—to do [?].

When he received this commission, he set out with a large army, excubitors, excubitors, and scribones, and reached the region of Cappadocia. He himself came from there, from the city of Arabissus. First he selected many young men from that region and enlisted them as Roman soldiers. He did the same in the region of Hanzit in Armenia, and in Syria when he reached it. First he went and attacked the city of Catharizum. The whole Persian territory was shaken by the first report of him.

The marzban who was stationed in Persian Armenia was alarmed at the report of him and sought an excuse to flee before him. He deceitfully sent word to the commanders stationed in Theodosiopolis: ‘How long shall we sit waiting for one another? In thirty days, let us prepare for battle and fight, and find out who wins and who loses.’ When these words had been spoken, the commanders sent word to Count Maurice. He ordered them to send this reply: ‘We are already prepared.’

While the Romans were relying on this reply, the marzban and his army fled that very night and left the place, passing through their own territory. They came and crossed into Roman territory opposite Martyropolis and began devastating, burning, taking captives, and killing—killing and taking captives throughout Sophanene and the territory of Amida. They came as far as Amida, surrounded it, and remained before it for three days. When they saw that they could not overcome the city's strength, they demanded gold as the city's ransom, so that they would not burn its surroundings. But the inhabitants did not trust them, reasoning that whether they received anything or not, they would certainly burn them.

So the Persians grew angry and burned all the churches and all the monasteries, great and small, and everything else outside the city. They ranged as far as they could. Thus, within fifteen days, they plundered, took captives, and crossed back into their own territory, in haste and great fear of the Romans.

When Count Maurice finally learned of this, he was bitterly distressed. He took his army and set out for Syria, pursuing them, but he did not catch them. Then, in anger and fury, the Roman armies fell upon the districts of Arzanene. They devastated, burned, and ravaged all those districts, took their inhabitants captive, and brought them across into Roman territory, as we related in the preceding account. By the king's command, all the captives brought across from there were sent to the island of Cyprus and distributed among its cities and villages. They remain there to this day.

Now most of the Roman army was stationed opposite Persian Armenia, with the commanders, the two generals John and Cours. The Persian army was also stationed opposite them. But, as we have already explained above, the Roman army split, and about fifty thousand of them stood apart, angry and grumbling. They said, “Unless we receive our customary allowances in full, and each of us is told his regiment, so that we can be sure of our postings, not one of us will go out to battle, and we will not fight anyone.”

When Emperor Tiberius learned of this, he immediately, without delay, sent there the curator of the great imperial household of Hormisdas, whose name was Domnitziolus. He gave Domnitziolus a large amount of gold to distribute among them, to conciliate them and put them at ease. In this way they were made ready for battle.

At that time the Persian commanders sent word to the Roman leaders: “Why, then, are we sitting opposite one another and watching one another like women? Let us go out into the plain and fight one another.”

When Cours, the commander of the Roman army, heard this, he acted as a shrewd man who had served the great Narses and had gained experience alongside him in great battles in Roman territories. He sent them this reply: “We cannot fight now, because our whole army is not here at present. But if you come against us, we will meet you with whatever strength our God gives us.”

When the people of the Magi received this reply, they became very confident and were no longer cautious or afraid of the Romans. That very day, Cours quietly prepared his own force alone, about twenty thousand men, and went out in the night, at the first light of dawn. While the Persians were encamped without a care, at ease and asleep, he fell upon them like fire let loose in a forest, like a flame burning up mountains. He stunned them, threw them into confusion, and slaughtered them, except for a few who escaped. He captured and bound many of them. He also captured one of their commanders and his son. Thus he plundered their entire camp and returned in great triumph, taking their weapons and horses.

After the death of Khosrow, king of the Persians, his son Hormizd succeeded him. In keeping with the foul custom of those who reign there, that a king should kill all his brothers, he too killed some of his brothers and blinded others. But there was one whom, they say, his father had wanted to succeed him, although their entire senate had rejected him and refused to accept him. According to the story, Khosrow himself, while still alive, gave this son provisions and sent him away, saying to him, “Go, my son, flee while I am still alive, so that you do not die.”

After he fled, many stories circulated about him. His countrymen believed and heard reports that he was in many different places. Consequently, a certain deceitful impostor from among the Persians, a young man, went and fabricated grounds for his claim and produced evidence to persuade people that he was the son of Khosrow who had fled. He came to the Roman military commanders in Persian Armenia and told them that he wished to submit to the Roman Empire. “If the Roman emperor will receive me,” he said, “and give me an army, I will conquer all the armies and territories of the Persians. And I will bring my brother Hormizd, who has seized my kingdom, in chains and hand him over to the Roman emperor.”

The Roman military commanders questioned him extensively, and he also produced many people who testified that he was the king’s son who had fled from his brother. So they believed him and wrote to the emperor Tiberius about him and about all the inquiries they had made. They reported that they had found people who knew him and had testified that he was the king’s son, and that he was destitute.

When the victorious emperor received this information and accepted everything the military commanders had written to him, he immediately sent messengers with much gold and silver, many splendid garments, and many horses and mules for his dignity and transportation. He ordered that all the provincial governors should give him a ceremonial escort through all the territories and cities until he reached the imperial city. This was done. He passed through the territories like a king, with great ceremony and magnificent honors. The emperor also sent great honors for his reception.

When he reached Chalcedon, across the water from the imperial city, he was ordered to remain there, because the emperor intended to investigate him thoroughly. For there was a sword-bearer of the Persian king who had come and submitted to him. He knew this man, together with those who had come down as envoys [?]. The emperor ordered them to cross over to him and see whether they too recognized him, and to question him in case he was an impostor, “so that we are not made fools of.”

When they crossed over and saw him, they did not recognize him. The Persian sword-bearer questioned him extensively, but he could not substantiate his claim. He was sitting on a high seat like a king. Then the sword-bearer seized him by the hair, pulled him down, and threw him to the ground, saying, “You impostor, you deserve death! Are you sitting on a high throne while the nobles of the kingdom stand before you?” He also struck him on the neck. In this way he exposed his deceit, and the man could find no easy way out or establish the truth of his claims about himself.

The emperor then gave orders, and he was lodged in a place, without being treated as his deceit deserved. Indeed, the emperor even ordered allowances for him and those with him. The emperor himself never saw him. It was said that more than three hundred pounds of gold had been spent on him. In the end, he also became a Christian.

Now the barbarian people of the Avars had assembled and were holding the two bridges they had built. They remained there, preparing war and devastation against the Roman territories, and sent word to Emperor Tiberius: “If you wish to gain our friendship, give us Sirmium so that we may settle there with your consent. Otherwise, we will take it without your consent and be your enemies.” The emperor put them off with various statements and promises, since he was entirely unwilling to give it to them. Instead, he secretly sent an embassy to the Lombards, to hire them and bring them against the Avars from behind, and also to other peoples. When the Avars pressed him, he decided not to reveal his intention to them. He sent Narses, the chief imperial sword-bearer, to speak with them and keep them waiting. Narses took a great deal of gold, both his own and the empire’s. He was secretly instructed not to travel in haste, and, if those peoples arrived, to receive them and launch them against the Avars, destroying them completely if possible. Meanwhile, the emperor sent the Avars this message: “We have now sent the illustrious Narses, our sword-bearer, to come and speak with you and make peace with you.”

So the illustrious Narses, the sword-bearer, left the imperial capital with great pomp, with a large force, an enormous amount of gold, and clothing of various kinds. He loaded many ships with all sorts of things and began the voyage across the fearsome sea of Pontus. One ship, containing most of the gold and many other things, sank on the very first day of their voyage. One of his officers and some of his trusted men were aboard it to guard its contents. When he learned of this, after leaving the sea and reaching the region of the Danube River, his distress brought on a severe illness. After a period of painful decline, his end overtook him, and he died in great suffering. All his undertakings came to nothing, and he accomplished absolutely nothing. Many other things subsequently happened in connection with the investigation of his affairs.

Since these things had not been accomplished through Narses, and those peoples had not arrived either, the emperor was compelled to send another man, named Callistratus, the praetorian prefect, to the Avars. He went and handed that city over to them. The emperor had decided that this was more advantageous than allowing it to be taken by war and force, after it had endured two years of distress and bitter famine. In their terrible suffering, the inhabitants had eaten all the livestock, all the animals, and everything else, even cats. Their suffering was no less than what Scripture tells us once happened in Samaria.

People also spoke of the compassion these barbarians showed toward those suffering from famine there. It deserved admiration and was a condemnation of Christians, who show no kindness to their fellow servants and have no compassion on their own flesh and blood. They said that when the barbarians entered and saw the deadly suffering of the people in the city, they took pity on them and gave them bread to eat and wine to drink. But because of the wasting caused by famine throughout those two long years, the people snatched the food and ate it, and soon died suddenly. Those who survived went into exile and left the city, and the barbarians took possession of it and settled there.

It was reported that after the barbarians had taken possession of the Christians’ city and lived there for one year, a fire broke out in the city of Sirmium—through what agency, God knows. Suddenly it swept through the city and burned it all. Since the barbarians did not know how to stop or extinguish it, they all fled naked and left the city. It was burned and completely destroyed. There were many things in its history that deserved to be recorded, but because of the length of the many accounts, we have left much of it out.

We have therefore briefly recorded, one after another, the various events of the earlier wars, as we were able to learn them through careful investigation: the campaign of the illustrious patrician Marcian against Nisibis and what happened there; afterward, Khosrau’s invasion of Roman territory with his armies and his capture of Dara, and also of the city of Apamea, and the rest. After these things, we recorded the victorious Maurice’s arrival in the East with great pomp, and the fear of him that fell upon the nation of the Magi; and how, hoping to outwit him by stealth, they crossed into Roman territory from the region near Martyropolis. They burned and moved on, burning and moving on with great haste for fifteen days through the land of Sophene. They came against Amida, and when they saw that they could not capture the city, they set fires in a barbarous frenzy and burned all its surroundings, churches, monasteries, and the rest. They took captives and hurried back to their own country.

We also recorded how, when Count Maurice learned these things, he was stirred to fierce anger and pursued them, but did not overtake them. He rushed toward the territory of Arzanene, burning, uprooting, and taking captives. He brought out all the people of Arzanene whom he had not killed and took them into Roman territory. All of these were sent to the island of Cyprus. He captured fortresses there, taking one called Pum and placing a Roman garrison in it. There was also another Persian fortress opposite it, called Cleimar; he accepted a ransom for it and left it alone. They remained opposite one another and made peace with one another, trading without fear of each other.

Count Maurice likewise took care to build a fortress on a high, rugged mountain called Shmakert. The fortress itself was therefore also called Shmakert. He stationed Romans in it, assigned them provisions, and attended to all its needs. This Shmakert is in Roman territory. He entrusted its construction to an engineer who had defected to him from Persian territory.

Across the river Kallath, which lies along the frontier opposite Martyropolis, there is a rugged mountain. For a long time that accursed nation of the Magi had been planning to build a fortress on it. But since there was an agreement between the Romans and the Persians that neither side was permitted to build within a certain number of miles of the frontier, the Romans opposed them and would not allow them to build. Indeed, it was built and torn down many times. At one point, however, as we explained earlier, the Persians found an opportunity, built the fortress, and occupied it.

Years later, Roman armies attacked it and surrounded it—that is, the general, the general named Ula. He kept it surrounded and maintained the siege for a long time, until those occupying it were so afflicted by hunger and thirst that they were close to losing their lives here in this world. Then, seeing their distress, they asked for a pledge that they would not be killed, seized, taken captive, or transported into Roman territory; in return, they would surrender the fortress and leave it. The commanders agreed to this and gave them their word. They opened it, and all of them came down from it. When they came out, found water, and drank [?], they immediately began falling down and dying, so that only a few of them came out and went away.

The general and his army went up and demolished the entire fortress. They left no stone upon another without tearing it down and throwing it down the mountain. Other commanders and the greater part of the army also gathered there. They then remained divided among various positions, keeping watch against one another.

At the same time that Acbas was captured, in the year eight hundred and ninety-four, a Persian envoy was sent to our Roman emperor. They began discussing peace, and the envoy was received with goodwill. It was agreed that a Roman envoy should be sent to the king of the Persians.
